Buy and Sell Stock.desc: Initialize min_price to +infinity: we have seen no day yet, so ANY real price will count as a new minimum.
Initialize best = 0. Not trading is always allowed, so 0 is the worst we can ever do.
Day 0: the loop picks up price = 7, the first price in the array.
Is 7 < inf? Yes — the very first price is always a new minimum.
Record min_price = 7. Day 0 is currently the cheapest day to buy.
Day 1: price = 1. We move to the next day in the scan.
Is 1 < 7? Yes — day 1 is a cheaper place to buy than day 0.
Update min_price = 1. From now on every sell is measured against buying at 1.
Day 2: price = 5. The scan continues with min_price = 1 in hand.
Is 5 < 1? No — 5 is not a new minimum, so we consider selling today instead.
Selling today: 5 - 1 = 4 profit. Is 4 > best (0)? Yes — a better trade.
Update best = 4: buy at 1 (day 1), sell at 5 (day 2).
Day 3: price = 3. Still holding min_price = 1 and best = 4.
Is 3 < 1? No — 3 is not a cheaper buy day.
Selling today: 3 - 1 = 2. Is 2 > 4? No — keep the old best of 4 and move on.
Day 4: price = 6, the highest price we will meet after the minimum.
Is 6 < 1? No — so we test it as a sell day.
Selling today: 6 - 1 = 5. Is 5 > 4? Yes — this beats our previous best trade.
Update best = 5: buy at 1 (day 1), sell at 6 (day 4). This will turn out to be the answer.
Day 5: price = 4, the final day of the scan.
4 is not < 1, so we test selling: 4 - 1 = 3, which does not beat 5. Nothing changes.
The loop is done. Return best = 5 — the maximum profit (buy day 1 at price 1, sell day 4 at price 6).

Rotate Matrix.desc: Read the size: n = 3 for our 3x3 matrix [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]].
Transpose phase begins. Outer loop takes i = 0 (first row of the upper triangle).
Inner loop starts at j = i+1 = 1, so the diagonal cell (0,0) is skipped and each pair swaps only once.
Swap (0,1) with (1,0): values 2 and 4 trade places across the diagonal.
Inner loop advances to j = 2, still on row i = 0.
Swap (0,2) with (2,0): values 3 and 7 trade places. Row 0 is now [1,4,7] — the old column 0!
Outer loop advances to i = 1: handle the pairs above the diagonal in row 1.
Inner loop starts at j = i+1 = 2 — only one pair left in this row.
Swap (1,2) with (2,1): values 6 and 8 trade places. The transpose is now complete: rows are the old columns.
Outer loop takes i = 2, but range(3, 3) is empty — no cell above the diagonal remains, so the transpose loop ends.
Phase 2 begins: reverse every row. First up is row 0 = [1,4,7].
Row 0 flips left-right: [1,4,7] becomes [7,4,1] — exactly the old first column read bottom-to-top.
Next, row 1 = [2,5,8] steps up for reversal.
Row 1 flips: [2,5,8] becomes [8,5,2]. The center cell 5 stays put, as it must for odd n.
Finally row 2 = [3,6,9] is taken by the loop.
Row 2 flips: [3,6,9] becomes [9,6,3]. The function ends — matrix is now [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]], the 90-degree clockwise rotation.

Merge Overlapping Intervals.desc: Sort by start: the input [[2,6],[1,3],[8,10],[15,18]] becomes [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]], so any overlapping pair now sits side by side.
Start with an empty answer list; we will grow it block by block.
First interval: start = 1, end = 3 is unpacked from the sorted list.
merged is still empty, so the overlap test short-circuits to False — nothing to absorb into.
Open the first block: append [1,3]. merged = [[1,3]].
Overlap test: is 2 <= 3 (the open block's end)? Yes — [2,6] overlaps [1,3] on the points 2 and 3.
Absorb: the open block's end becomes max(3, 6) = 6. merged = [[1,6]] — one block now covers both intervals.
Overlap test: is 8 <= 6? No — there is a real gap (points 7 and below 8 are uncovered), and since starts only grow, block [1,6] is sealed forever.
Open a new block: append [8,10]. merged = [[1,6],[8,10]].
Overlap test: is 15 <= 10? No — another gap, so [8,10] is sealed too.
The sweep is done — return [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]: three disjoint blocks covering exactly the input's points.

Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Sp.desc: i = m - 1 = 2 points at nums1's last REAL value, 3. (nums1 = [1,2,3,0,0,0], nums2 = [2,5,6].)
j = n - 1 = 2 points at nums2's last value, 6.
k = 5 is the last slot of nums1 — the write position where the largest value will land.
j = 2 >= 0: nums2 still has unplaced values, so enter the loop.
Compare tails: nums1[2] = 3 vs nums2[2] = 6. Is 3 > 6? No — nums2's 6 is the largest remaining value overall.
Write 6 into slot k = 5: nums1 becomes [1,2,3,0,0,6]. The biggest value is now locked in the last slot.
Consume nums2's 6: j drops to 1, now pointing at 5.
Slot 5 is filled, so the write position moves left: k = 4.
j = 1 >= 0: keep merging.
Compare tails: nums1[2] = 3 vs nums2[1] = 5. Is 3 > 5? No — 5 wins the slot.
Write 5 into slot k = 4: nums1 becomes [1,2,3,0,5,6].
Consume the 5: j drops to 0, pointing at nums2's 2.
Write position moves left: k = 3.
j = 0 >= 0: nums2 still holds one value (2), keep going.
Compare tails: nums1[2] = 3 vs nums2[0] = 2. Is 3 > 2? YES — for the first time nums1's element wins.
Write nums1's own 3 into slot k = 3: nums1 becomes [1,2,3,3,5,6]. Note the read position i = 2 is LEFT of the write position k = 3 — no unread value is harmed.
Consume nums1's 3: i drops to 1, pointing at the 2.
Write position moves left: k = 2.
j = 0 >= 0: one nums2 value (the 2) still needs a home.
Compare: nums1[1] = 2 vs nums2[0] = 2. Is 2 > 2? No — a tie goes to the else branch, placing nums2's copy.
Write nums2's 2 into slot k = 2: nums1 becomes [1,2,2,3,5,6] (it already held a 2 there, so no visible change — but logically the slot now belongs to nums2's 2).
Consume nums2's last value: j drops to -1 — nums2 is fully placed.
Write position moves to k = 1 (it will not be used again).
j = -1, so the loop exits. nums1's untouched front [1,2] was already sorted and in place — final answer: [1,2,2,3,5,6].

Find Duplicate Number.desc: Both runners start at the chain's head: slow = nums[0] = 1. Think of each index as a node whose arrow goes to nums[index].
fast also starts at nums[0] = 1. The chain from index 0 is: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 4 -> 2 -> 4 ... (a tail, then a loop between 2 and 4).
Phase 1 begins. Because slow and fast start EQUAL, the equality check must happen after they move — hence the do-while shape.
Hare hops twice: first nums[1] = 3, then nums[3] = 2, so fast = 2.
Met yet? slow = 3, fast = 2 — not equal, loop again.
Tortoise hops once more: slow = nums[3] = 2.
Hare hops twice: nums[2] = 4, then nums[4] = 2, so fast = 2. The hare has lapped the loop 2 -> 4 -> 2.
Met yet? slow = 2 and fast = 2 — YES, the runners meet inside the cycle (at node 2, though in general the meeting node need not be the entrance).
Phase 1 ends: a cycle definitely exists and fast sits at the meeting node.
Phase 2: teleport slow back to the head, slow = nums[0] = 1. fast stays at the meeting node 2. Now both will walk ONE hop at a time.
slow = 1, fast = 2 — different, so walk both runners.
slow = 3, fast = 4 — still different, walk again.
fast hops: nums[4] = 2. Both runners now stand on node 2.
slow == fast == 2, so the loop exits. They met exactly at the cycle's entrance — the node with two incoming arrows (from indices 3 and 4).
Return slow = 2: the duplicated number. Indices 3 and 4 both hold the value 2, which is what created the cycle entrance.

Repeat and Missing Number.desc: n = 5: the array [3,1,2,5,3] should have been a shuffle of 1..5.
Closed form: expected_sum = 5*6/2 = 15 — what the sum WOULD be with no repeat/missing.
Closed form: expected_sq = 5*6*11/6 = 55 — the ideal sum of squares 1+4+9+16+25.
Initialize the running sum of the REAL array to 0.
Initialize the running sum of squares to 0. One pass will fill both totals.
Last element: x = 3 again (index 4) — the repeat contributes to the totals a second time; that is exactly the 'signal' the math will decode.
actual_sum = 11 + 3 = 14 (vs 15 expected — the missing 4 and extra 3 net out to -1).
actual_sq = 39 + 9 = 48 (vs 55 expected). The accumulation pass is done.
Equation 1: diff = 14 - 15 = -1, and algebraically diff = R - M. (Indeed 3 - 4 = -1.)
Square-sum clue: sq_diff = 48 - 55 = -7 = R² - M² = (R - M)(R + M).
Divide out the known factor: total = -7 // -1 = 7 = R + M. Two linear equations, two unknowns — solvable!
Return [3, 4]: 3 is the number appearing twice, 4 is the number that vanished. One pass, O(1) space.

Inversion Count.desc: Kick off: call sort_count on the whole array [5,3,2,4]. It will sort a copy and count inversions along the way.
Inside sort_count([5,3,2,4]): length 4 > 1, so this is not a base case — we must split.
mid = 4 // 2 = 2: the halves will be [5,3] and [2,4].
Recurse into the LEFT half [5,3]. (We now follow that inner call.)
Inside sort_count([5,3]): mid = 1, splitting into [5] and [3].
Both sub-calls hit the base case: sort_count([5]) returns ([5], 0) and sort_count([3]) returns ([3], 0) — single elements hold no inversions.
Merge [5] and [3]: i = 0, j = 0, inv starts at 0 + 0 = 0. Both lists have unread values, enter the loop.
Compare fronts: left[0] = 5 <= right[0] = 3? No — the right value must go first, which means it is out of order relative to the left half.
Place 3 into merged before 5.
Count the batch: 3 jumped over len(left) - i = 1 - 0 = 1 remaining left element (the 5). inv = 1 — that is the inversion pair (5,3).
Consume the 3: j = 1, right half exhausted, the while loop ends.
Flush the leftover left values: merged becomes [3,5].
sort_count([5,3]) returns ([3,5], 1) to the outer call: the left half is sorted and contributed 1 inversion.
Back in the outer call: recurse into the RIGHT half [2,4]. It splits into [2] and [4]; the merge takes 2 then 4 with no counting (2 <= 4), returning ([2,4], 0).
Combine the halves' banked counts: inv = 1 + 0 = 1. Now count the CROSS inversions while merging [3,5] with [2,4].
Merge loop: i = 0 (on 3), j = 0 (on 2), merged = []. Both halves have values, so compare fronts.
left[0] = 3 <= right[0] = 2? No — 2 must be placed first, jumping over the whole remaining left half.
Place 2 into merged: merged = [2].
Batch count: 2 is smaller than BOTH remaining left values (3 and 5), so inv += 2 - 0 = 2, giving inv = 3. Those are the pairs (3,2) and (5,2) — certified without comparing 5 to 2 directly!
Consume the 2: j = 1, now pointing at 4.
Next comparison: left[0] = 3 <= right[1] = 4? Yes — 3 is in correct order, no inversion involved.
Place 3: merged = [2,3]. Taking from the left never counts anything.
Consume the 3: i = 1, now pointing at 5.
Compare: left[1] = 5 <= right[1] = 4? No — 4 must be placed before 5.
Place 4: merged = [2,3,4].
Batch count: 4 jumps over len(left) - i = 2 - 1 = 1 remaining left element (the 5). inv = 4 — the final pair (5,4).
Consume the 4: j = 2 — the right half is exhausted, so the merge loop exits.
Flush the leftover left values: the 5 joins the end, merged = [2,3,4,5].
The top-level sort_count returns ([2,3,4,5], 4): a fully sorted array and 4 total inversions (1 from inside [5,3] + 3 cross pairs).
Back at the outer function: total = 4 — the inversion count of [5,3,2,4]. Return it.

Search in a 2D Matrix.desc: Read dimensions: m = 3 rows, n = 4 columns. Target is 16. Flattened row-by-row, the matrix is one sorted list of 12 values.
Set the virtual search window over flat indices: lo = 0, hi = 3*4 - 1 = 11. Virtual index k maps to cell (k // 4, k % 4).
Window check: 0 <= 11, so the window is non-empty — search on.
Un-flatten index 5: row = 5 // 4 = 1, col = 5 % 4 = 1 — so val = matrix[1][1] = 11.
Is 11 < 16? Yes — 16 (if present) must sit AFTER flat index 5, since everything up to index 5 is <= 11.
Discard the left half: lo = 6. The window is now flat indices 6..11 (cells from matrix[1][2] onward).
Un-flatten index 8: row = 8 // 4 = 2, col = 8 % 4 = 0 — so val = matrix[2][0] = 23.
Is 23 == 16? No — not an exact match, so decide which half to discard.
Is 23 < 16? No — 23 is too big, so 16 must lie BEFORE flat index 8.
Discard the right half: hi = 7. The window shrinks to flat indices 6..7 — just cells matrix[1][2] and matrix[1][3].
Un-flatten index 6: row = 6 // 4 = 1, col = 6 % 4 = 2 — so val = matrix[1][2] = 16.
Is 16 == 16? YES — the target is found at cell (1, 2) after only three probes.
Return True. Binary search inspected just 3 of the 12 cells — that is the power of treating the matrix as one sorted list.

Pow(x, n).desc: Call my_pow(x=2.0, n=10). The exponent 10 in binary is 1010 (shown as the array, most-significant bit on the left). We will read it right to left, squaring as we go.
n=10 is already non-negative, so exp = 10. (A negative n would flip to |n| here and we would take a reciprocal at the very end.)
result starts at 1.0, the empty product x^0. Powers of x whose bit is 1 will be folded into it.
base starts as x = 2.0. It will square every round: 2 -> 4 -> 16 -> 256, i.e. x^1, x^2, x^4, x^8 — one power per bit position.
Round 1: exp=10 > 0, enter the loop. We are looking at the lowest bit of 1010 (index 3 in the display).
10 % 2 == 0: the lowest bit is 0, so x^1 = 2.0 is NOT part of the answer. Skip the fold.
Square the base: 2.0 * 2.0 = 4.0. base now represents x^2, the power owned by the next bit.
exp = 10 // 2 = 5 (binary 101). The processed 0-bit is discarded.
Round 2: exp=5 > 0. We are now on the bit at display index 2, which is 1.
5 % 2 == 1: this bit is set, so the current power x^2 = 4.0 belongs in the answer.
Fold it in: result = 1.0 * 4.0 = 4.0. So far the answer holds x^2.
Square again: 4.0 * 4.0 = 16.0. base now represents x^4.
exp = 5 // 2 = 2 (binary 10). Two bits remain.
Round 3: exp=2 > 0. Now on the bit at display index 1, which is 0.
2 % 2 == 0: bit is 0, so x^4 = 16.0 is skipped — 10 = 8 + 2 has no 4 in it.
Square: 16.0 * 16.0 = 256.0. base now represents x^8.
exp = 2 // 2 = 1 (binary 1). One bit left — the most significant one.
Round 4: exp=1 > 0. Final bit, display index 0, value 1.
1 % 2 == 1: the 8s bit is set, so x^8 = 256.0 is part of the answer.
Fold: result = 4.0 * 256.0 = 1024.0 — that is x^2 * x^8 = x^10. The answer is complete.
base squares one last time to 65536.0 (x^16). It is never used again — harmless leftover work.
exp = 1 // 2 = 0. Every bit of the exponent has been consumed.
exp=0, so 0 > 0 is false — the loop exits after just 4 rounds instead of 10 multiplications.
n=10 is not negative, so no reciprocal is owed — skip straight to the return.
Return result = 1024.0. Binary exponentiation computed 2^10 with 4 squarings and 2 folds.

Majority Element (> n/2 times).desc: Call majority_element([2,2,1,1,1,2,2]). n=7, so the majority needs at least 4 occurrences — the 2s have exactly 4.
No candidate yet: candidate = None. The first element will be adopted immediately because count is 0.
count = 0 — it measures the current candidate's surplus of for-votes over against-votes.
i=0: num = 2, the first voter steps up.
count is 0, so adopt 2 as the candidate — with no active candidate, the current value takes the seat.
num (2) equals candidate (2): a vote FOR. count rises to 1.
i=1: num = 2 again — another supporter of the current candidate.
2 == candidate, so count grows to 2. The candidate has a 2-vote lead.
i=2: num = 1 — a rival value appears for the first time.
1 != candidate (2): a vote AGAINST. One 2-vote and this 1-vote cancel; count drops to 1.
i=3: num = 1 — another rival vote arrives.
Cancellation again: count falls to 0. The candidate 2 is now fully neutralized — the next element can seize the seat.
i=4: num = 1 arrives while the seat is vacant (count = 0).
count == 0, so 1 takes over as the new candidate — the algorithm forgets 2 entirely.
1 == candidate, so count = 1. The usurper holds a 1-vote lead.
i=5: num = 2 — the real majority strikes back against candidate 1.
2 != 1: cancellation drops count to 0. Candidate 1 is neutralized after holding the seat for just one element.
i=6: the final element, num = 2, arrives with the seat vacant again.
count == 0, so 2 is re-adopted as candidate. Its surplus vote (4 twos vs 3 ones) guaranteed it could not stay buried.
2 == candidate: count = 1. The scan ends with 2 holding the seat.
Return candidate = 2. Every cancellation killed one 2-vote AND one rival vote, and 2 had more votes than all rivals combined — so it had to survive.

Majority Element II (> n/3 times).desc: Call majority_element_ii([1,1,1,3,3,2,2,2]). n=8, floor(8/3)=2, so winners need at least 3 occurrences: 1 has 3, 2 has 3, 3 has only 2.
Slot 1 starts vacant: cand1 = None with count1 = 0.
Slot 2 starts vacant too. Two slots suffice because at most two values can exceed n/3.
i=0: num = 1. It matches neither slot (both None-with-0), so the vacancy checks will fire.
count1 == 0, so slot 1 adopts 1: cand1 = 1, count1 = 1.
i=1: num = 1 again — it matches slot 1's candidate.
Vote for slot 1: count1 rises to 2.
i=2: num = 1 for a third time — slot 1 keeps strengthening.
count1 = 3. Slot 2 is still vacant; no cancellation has happened yet.
i=3: num = 3 — a brand-new value. It fails 'num == cand1' (3 != 1), fails 'num == cand2', fails 'count1 == 0' (count1 is 3)...
...but count2 == 0, so slot 2 adopts 3: cand2 = 3, count2 = 1.
i=4: num = 3 — it matches slot 2's candidate this time.
Vote for slot 2: count2 = 2. State: slot1 = (1, 3 votes), slot2 = (3, 2 votes).
i=5: num = 2 — a third distinct value while BOTH slots are occupied. The else branch fires: a (1, 3, 2) triple will be cancelled.
Cancel one vote from slot 1: count1 drops to 2. One occurrence of 1 is 'paired off' against this 2.
And one from slot 2: count2 drops to 1. A triple of three DIFFERENT values (1, 3, 2) has been deleted — no true winner can lose its > n/3 status this way.
i=6: num = 2 again — still matches neither slot, and both counters are positive, so another triple dies.
count1 falls to 1 — the 1s are being whittled down by the stream of 2s.
count2 falls to 0 — slot 2's candidate 3 is fully cancelled and the slot becomes vacant.
i=7: num = 2, the final element. It matches neither candidate, count1 is 1 (not 0), but count2 IS 0...
...so slot 2 adopts 2: cand2 = 2, count2 = 1. Pass 1 ends with candidates 1 and 2 — the value 3 was correctly squeezed out.
PASS 2 begins. Surviving candidates are only POSSIBLE winners (in [1,2,3] two would survive yet neither qualifies), so each must be verified by a real count.
threshold = 8 // 3 = 2. A verified winner must appear STRICTLY more than 2 times.
Verify cand1 = 1 first.
nums.count(1) = 3, and 3 > 2 — candidate 1 is a confirmed winner. result = [1].
Now verify cand2 = 2.
nums.count(2) = 3 > 2 — candidate 2 is also confirmed. result = [1, 2]. (Had 3 survived instead, its count of 2 would have failed here.)
Return [1, 2] — both values appear 3 times, strictly more than n/3 = 2. Done in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

Grid Unique Paths.desc: Call unique_paths(m=4, n=4): a 4x4 grid, robot at the top-left (0,0), target at the bottom-right (3,3), moving only down or right.
total = 4 + 4 - 2 = 6: every path makes exactly 3 down-moves and 3 right-moves, six moves in all — only their order varies.
pick = min(3, 3) = 3: we will choose which 3 of the 6 move-slots are downs, i.e. compute C(6, 3). Picking the smaller side keeps the loop short.
result = 1, which is C(3, 0) — the empty choice. Each loop round will grow it into C(4,1), C(5,2), then C(6,3).
Loop round 1: i = 1. We upgrade result from C(3,0) to C(4,1).
result = 1 * (6 - 3 + 1) // 1 = 4. Indeed C(4, 1) = 4. Multiplying BEFORE the // keeps the division exact.
Loop round 2: i = 2. Next upgrade: C(4,1) -> C(5,2).
result = 4 * (6 - 3 + 2) // 2 = 4 * 5 // 2 = 10 = C(5, 2). The product 4*5 of two consecutive integers is guaranteed divisible by 2.
Loop round 3: i = 3, the final round since pick = 3. Upgrade C(5,2) -> C(6,3).
result = 10 * (6 - 3 + 3) // 3 = 10 * 6 // 3 = 20 = C(6, 3). The binomial coefficient is complete.
range(1, 4) is exhausted (i would be 4 > pick), so the loop ends after just 3 multiply-divide rounds.
Return 20: the 4x4 grid has exactly 20 distinct monotone paths — no table, no recursion, just C(6,3).

Reverse Pairs.desc: Start: sort_count runs on the whole array [2, 4, 3, 5, 1]; every reverse pair will be counted while the halves get merged.
This segment is the full array, so n = 5 — far more than one element, so it has to be split.
mid = 5 // 2 = 2, splitting the array into left = [2, 4] and right = [3, 5, 1].
Recurse into the left half [2, 4] first; the parent cannot count anything until it comes back sorted.
Inside the segment [2, 4]: n = 2, so this piece splits as well.
mid = 1 cuts [2, 4] into the single elements [2] and [4].
Segment [2] holds one element, so it is already sorted and can hold no pair: return ([2], 0).
Segment [4] is a single element too, returning ([4], 0) with no pairs inside it.
Cross-counting for left = [2] against right = [4]: the only left value is x = 2, and j starts at 0.
Test 2 > 2 * right[0] = 8? No, so j never advances and 2 beats nothing in the right half.
count += j = 0, so the segment [2, 4] contributes no reverse pair at all.
Merge phase: left[0] = 2 is <= right[0] = 4, so the 2 is written to merged first.
The left half is exhausted, so the leftover right value 4 is copied over: merged = [2, 4].
Return the sorted segment [2, 4] with count 0 back up to the top-level call.
Now the top-level call recurses into its right half, the segment [3, 5, 1].
Here n = 3 and mid = 1, so [3, 5, 1] splits into [3] and [5, 1].
Recurse once more into [5, 1] — this is the first segment that actually contains a reverse pair.
Cross sweep in [5, 1]: left = [5], right = [1]. Is 5 > 2 * 1 = 2? Yes, so the 1 qualifies.
j advances to 1, marking that right value 1 forms a reverse pair with the left value 5.
count += j = 1: the pair (5, 1) is recorded because 5 is more than double 1.
Merge [5] with [1]: left[0] = 5 is bigger than right[0] = 1, so the 1 is emitted first.
The right half is used up, so the leftover 5 is appended: this call returns ([1, 5], 1).
Back in [3, 5, 1]: count = count_left 0 + count_right 1 = 1, inherited from inside the halves.
Cross sweep with x = 3 over the sorted right half [1, 5]: is 3 > 2 * 1 = 2? Yes.
j becomes 1, confirming right value 1 as a partner for the left value 3.
Next test: 3 > 2 * 5 = 10? No, so the while loop stops with j frozen at 1.
count += 1 -> count = 2, adding the cross pair (3, 1) to the pair (5, 1) already found.
Merge [3] with [1, 5]: 3 > 1, so the 1 goes out first and b moves to 1.
Now 3 <= 5, so the 3 is written next: merged = [1, 3] and the left half is finished.
The leftover right value 5 is appended, so this segment returns ([1, 3, 5], 2).
Top level again: count = 0 from the left half plus 2 from the right half = 2 before any cross counting.
x = 2 against right = [1, 3, 5]: is 2 > 2 * 1 = 2? No — the test is strict, so j stays at 0.
count += 0, so the left value 2 forms no cross pair with anything in the right half.
Next left value x = 4: is 4 > 2 * 1 = 2? Yes, so the right pointer can move forward.
j = 1 — the right value 1 pairs with 4, and would pair with any later (larger) left value too.
Check 4 > 2 * 3 = 6? No, so the sweep for x = 4 stops with j = 1.
count += 1 -> count = 3, adding the cross pair (4, 1) found in one linear sweep instead of a nested loop.
Final merge of [2, 4] and [1, 3, 5]: 2 > 1, so the 1 is written first.
2 <= 3, so the 2 is written next: merged = [1, 2].
4 <= 3 is false, so the 3 is taken from the right half: merged = [1, 2, 3].
4 <= 5, so the 4 is written: merged = [1, 2, 3, 4] and the left half is drained.
The single leftover right value 5 is extended on: merged = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
Return total = 3: the reverse pairs of [2, 4, 3, 5, 1] are (4, 1), (3, 1) and (5, 1).

Four Sum.desc: Call four_sum([1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2], target=0). We must find every unique quadruplet of values summing to 0.
Sort a copy: nums = [-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2]. Sorting powers both the two-pointer search and neighbor-based duplicate skipping.
n = 6 — just enough room for quadruplets (we need at least 4 elements).
result starts empty; quadruplets will be appended already sorted internally.
i = 0: first number is nums[0] = -2. The loop stops at n-4 = 2 so three slots always remain after i.
j = 1: second number is nums[1] = -1. Fixed prefix so far: (-2, -1).
need = 0 - (-2) - (-1) = 3: the last two numbers must sum to exactly 3.
Two pointers bracket the remaining window: left = 2 (value 0), right = 5 (value 2).
pair = nums[2] + nums[5] = 0 + 2 = 2.
2 < 3: the pair undershoots. Only a bigger left value can help (right already holds the maximum), so left moves to 3.
pair = nums[3] + nums[5] = 0 + 2 = 2 again — the duplicate 0 gives the same undershoot.
Still 2 < 3, so left advances to 4 (value 1).
pair = nums[4] + nums[5] = 1 + 2 = 3 — exactly what we need!
Record the first quadruplet: [-2, -1, 1, 2]. result = [[-2, -1, 1, 2]].
Step past the used third number: left = 5.
Step past the used fourth number: right = 4. The pointers have crossed.
left=5 < right=4 is false — the window for (i=0, j=1) is exhausted with one quadruplet found.
j = 2: second number becomes nums[2] = 0. Fixed prefix: (-2, 0).
need = 0 - (-2) - 0 = 2: the last two must now sum to 2.
Fresh window: left = 3 (value 0), right = 5 (value 2).
pair = nums[3] + nums[5] = 0 + 2 = 2 — an immediate hit.
Record [-2, 0, 0, 2] — it legally uses BOTH zeros, which live at different indices (2 and 3).
left moves to 4; right will move to 4 as well — the window is about to close.
right = 4. Now left == right, so no third-number/fourth-number pair remains.
4 < 4 is false — done with (i=0, j=2) after one hit.
j = 3: nums[3] = 0 — the SAME second value as the previous round (nums[2] = 0).
j > i+1 and nums[3] == nums[2], so skip: rerunning with an identical second value could only rediscover [-2, 0, 0, 2]. This is dedupe at the source.
j's range is exhausted, so i advances: i = 1, first number nums[1] = -1 (different from -2, no skip).
j = 2: fixed prefix (-1, 0).
need = 0 - (-1) - 0 = 1: the final pair must sum to 1.
Window: left = 3 (value 0), right = 5 (value 2).
pair = 0 + 2 = 2, which overshoots need = 1.
2 > 1: only a smaller right value can help, so right retreats to 4 (value 1).
pair = nums[3] + nums[4] = 0 + 1 = 1 — a hit for prefix (-1, 0).
Record [-1, 0, 0, 1]. result now holds all three expected quadruplets; the pointers then cross and this window ends.
Remaining rounds find nothing new: (i=1, j=3) is skipped as a duplicate 0, and i = 2 with j = 3 needs the last pair to sum to 0 but 1 + 2 = 3 only overshoots, so the window empties without a hit.
Return [[-2, -1, 1, 2], [-2, 0, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 0, 1]] — three unique quadruplets, produced without ever creating a duplicate to clean up.

Largest Subarray with 0 Sum.desc: Call max_len_zero_sum([15, -2, 2, -8, 1, 7, 10, 23]). The hidden zero-sum champion is [-2, 2, -8, 1, 7] (indices 1..5), length 5.
Seed the map with {0: -1}: the EMPTY prefix (before index 0) has sum 0. Without this, any zero-sum window starting at index 0 would be invisible.
prefix = 0 — the running sum of everything scanned so far (currently nothing).
best = 0 — if no zero-sum subarray ever appears, this 0 is the honest final answer.
i=0: num = 15, the first element enters the running sum.
prefix = 0 + 15 = 15 — the 'altitude' after index 0.
15 is a brand-new prefix value, so record its FIRST occurrence: first_seen = {0: -1, 15: 0}.
13 is new too: first_seen = {0: -1, 15: 0, 13: 1}.
i=2: num = 2, prefix = 13 + 2 = 15 — an altitude we have SEEN before (at index 0)!
first_seen[15] = 0, so the slice (1..2) = [-2, 2] sums to 15 - 15 = 0. best = max(0, 2 - 0) = 2. Note the map is NOT updated — index 0 stays as 15's earliest home.
i=3: num = -8, prefix = 15 - 8 = 7.
i=4: num = 1, prefix = 7 + 1 = 8.
i=5: num = 7, prefix = 8 + 7 = 15 — the altitude 15 strikes for a THIRD time.
Against 15's EARLIEST index 0: the slice (1..5) = [-2, 2, -8, 1, 7] sums to 0 with length 5 - 0 = 5. best = max(2, 5) = 5. Keeping the first occurrence is exactly what made this window measure long.
25 is new: recorded at index 6. No zero-sum window ends here.
i=7: num = 23, prefix = 25 + 23 = 48 — the final element.
48 is new as well; the scan ends without another repeat.
Return best = 5: the longest stretch between equal prefix sums — one pass, one dictionary, done.

Count Subarrays with Given XOR.desc: We call solve(A=[4, 2, 2, 6, 4], B=6). xr will hold the XOR of every element seen so far; it starts at 0 because XOR-ing nothing gives 0.
xr_map = {0: 1} seeds the map with 'the empty prefix has XOR 0, and I have seen it once'. Without this seed we would miss every subarray that starts at index 0.
count = 0. This will accumulate the number of subarrays whose XOR equals B = 6.
Iteration 1 of the for loop: val = A[0] = 4.
xr ^= 4 turns the running prefix XOR from 0 into 4. So the XOR of A[0..0] is 4.
target = xr ^ B = 4 ^ 6 = 2. Reason: if some earlier prefix had XOR 2, then the piece between it and here XORs to 2 ^ 4 = 6 = B.
Is 2 a key of xr_map = {0: 1}? No. So no subarray ending at index 0 has XOR 6, and count stays 0.
Record the prefix we just built: xr_map[4] = 1. The map now remembers one prefix with XOR 4.
Iteration 2 of the for loop: val = A[1] = 2.
xr ^= 2 gives 4 ^ 2 = 6. The XOR of A[0..1] is 6.
target = 6 ^ 6 = 0. We are asking: how many earlier prefixes had XOR 0?
0 IS in xr_map with frequency 1 (the seeded empty prefix), so we found a match.
count += xr_map[0] = 1, so count becomes 1. The subarray found is A[0..1] = [4, 2], whose XOR really is 6.
Store the new prefix: xr_map[6] = 1.
Iteration 3 of the for loop: val = A[2] = 2, the second 2.
xr ^= 2 gives 6 ^ 2 = 4. Notice the prefix XOR is 4 again — the same value it had after index 0.
target = xr ^ B = 4 ^ 6 = 2, the same target we already failed to find in iteration 1.
2 is still not a key of xr_map = {0: 1, 4: 1, 6: 1}, so count stays 1.
xr_map[4] was already 1, so get(4, 0) + 1 makes it 2. Two different prefixes now share the XOR value 4.
Iteration 4 of the for loop: val = A[3] = 6, which equals B itself.
xr ^= 6 gives 4 ^ 6 = 2. Prefix XOR of A[0..3] is 2.
target = 2 ^ 6 = 4, and we already know 4 appeared twice as a prefix.
4 is in xr_map with frequency 2 — this is exactly why we count frequencies and not just presence.
count += 2, so count jumps from 1 to 3. The two new subarrays are A[1..3] = [2, 2, 6] and A[3..3] = [6].
Store the prefix: xr_map[2] = 1.
Iteration 5 (last): val = A[4] = 4.
xr ^= 4 gives 2 ^ 4 = 6. The XOR of the whole array is 6.
target = xr ^ B = 6 ^ 6 = 0 once more, so we are hunting for prefixes with XOR 0.
0 is present with frequency 1 (still just the seeded empty prefix).
count += 1 makes count = 4. The fourth subarray is the whole array A[0..4], whose XOR is 6.
Final map update: xr_map[6] becomes 2.
The loop is done after one single pass. return count = 4 — the four subarrays [4,2], [2,2,6], [6] and [4,2,2,6,4].

Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.desc: We call lengthOfLongestSubstring("abba"). char_map will remember the LAST index at which each character was seen; it starts empty.
max_len = 0. This is the best window length found so far; 0 is correct for the empty string too.

left = 0. The window is the stretch of characters from s[left] to s[right] with BOTH ends included — that is why its length is right - left + 1 a few steps below. Both ends start at the beginning of the string.
Iteration 1: right = 0, so the new character entering the window is s[0] = 'a'.
Check the two conditions: is 'a' in char_map? No, the map is empty. The whole condition is False, so left does NOT move.
char_map['a'] = 0 records where 'a' was last seen.
max_len = max(0, right - left + 1) = max(0, 0 - 0 + 1) = 1. Window "a" has length 1.
Iteration 2: right = 1, entering character s[1] = 'b'.
'b' is not in char_map, so again nothing shrinks and left stays 0.
char_map['b'] = 1 records that 'b' was last seen at index 1.
max_len = max(1, 1 - 0 + 1) = 2. Window "ab" has length 2 and no repeats.
Iteration 3: right = 2, entering character s[2] = 'b' — a repeat of the 'b' at index 1.
'b' IS in char_map at index 1, and 1 >= left (0), meaning that old 'b' is still INSIDE the window. Both halves are True, so we must shrink.
left = char_map['b'] + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2. The window jumps in one move to start just after the duplicate, instead of sliding one step at a time.
char_map['b'] = 2 overwrites the stale index 1 with the current one.
max_len = max(2, 2 - 2 + 1) = max(2, 1) = 2. The current window is shorter, so the record stands.
Iteration 4 (last): right = 3, entering s[3] = 'a'. This is the case that breaks naive solutions.
'a' IS in char_map, but at index 0 — and 0 >= left (2) is False. That old 'a' sits BEHIND the window, so it is not a real repeat. left must NOT jump backwards to 1.
char_map['a'] = 3 refreshes the stale entry.
max_len = max(2, 3 - 2 + 1) = max(2, 2) = 2. Window "ba" also has length 2.
The loop is finished after exactly one pass over the string. return max_len = 2 — the longest repeat-free substrings of "abba" are "ab" and "ba".

Remove Nth Node From End.desc: We call removeNthFromEnd(head = 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, n = 2). Counting from the back, the 2nd node is the one holding 4, so the answer must be 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 5.
dummy = ListNode(0) creates a throwaway node that will sit BEFORE the head. It exists only so that deleting the real head needs no special case.
dummy.next = head glues the dummy in front: dummy -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5.
fast = dummy. (A pointer shown as 'off the list' is sitting on the dummy node.)
slow = dummy as well. The two pointers will keep a fixed gap of n + 1 nodes between them.
The for loop will run n = 2 times to open that gap. Turn 1 begins.
fast = fast.next moves fast from dummy onto node 1 (index 0).
Turn 2 of the n-step for loop that opens the gap.
fast = fast.next moves fast onto node 2 (index 1). The gap is now fixed: slow is on dummy, fast is 2 nodes ahead.
while fast.next: fast is node 2 and fast.next is node 3, so we enter the loop and move BOTH pointers in lockstep.
fast = fast.next -> node 3 (index 2).
slow = slow.next -> node 1 (index 0). slow finally steps onto the real list.
Loop check: fast.next is node 4, not None, so we go again.
fast = fast.next -> node 4 (index 3).
slow = slow.next -> node 2 (index 1).
Loop check: fast.next is node 5, still not None.
fast = fast.next -> node 5 (index 4), the last node.
slow = slow.next -> node 3 (index 2). Because of the fixed gap, slow now sits exactly one node BEFORE the node we must delete.
Loop check: fast.next is None (node 5 is the tail), so the while loop ends here.
slow.next = slow.next.next: node 3 stops pointing at node 4 and points at node 5 instead. Node 4 is now unreachable — deleted.
return dummy.next gives node 1, the (unchanged) head. Final list: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 5. One single pass, O(1) extra space.

Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.desc: We call addTwoNumbers(l1 = 2 -> 4 -> 3, l2 = 5 -> 6 -> 4). Reversed digits mean l1 is the number 342 and l2 is 465, so the answer must be 807, i.e. 7 -> 0 -> 8. dummy = ListNode(0) is a placeholder head.
curr = dummy. curr always points at the LAST node of the answer built so far, so appending is just curr.next = new node.
carry = 0. Nothing has overflowed yet, exactly like starting a written addition with no carry.
while l1 or l2 or carry: l1 is node 2, so we enter iteration 1. Notice 'or carry' — it keeps the loop alive for a final carry even after both lists end.
val_sum = carry = 0. Every column starts from whatever was carried in.
if l1: l1 is the node holding 2, so its digit joins this column.
val_sum += l1.val makes val_sum = 0 + 2 = 2.
l1 = l1.next advances to the node holding 4.
if l2: l2 is the node holding 5, so its digit joins too.
val_sum += l2.val makes val_sum = 2 + 5 = 7.
l2 = l2.next advances to the node holding 6.
carry = val_sum // 10 = 7 // 10 = 0. Seven fits in one digit, so nothing is carried.
curr.next = ListNode(val_sum % 10) = ListNode(7) appends the units digit of this column.
curr = curr.next moves the tail pointer onto the new node 7.
Loop check for iteration 2: l1 is node 4, so we continue.
val_sum = carry = 0 again, since the previous column carried nothing.
if l1: node 4 exists.
val_sum += 4 makes val_sum = 4.
l1 = l1.next advances to the node holding 3.
if l2: node 6 exists.
val_sum += 6 makes val_sum = 4 + 6 = 10 — this column overflows.
l2 = l2.next advances to the node holding 4.
carry = 10 // 10 = 1. The overflow is remembered for the next column instead of being lost.
curr.next = ListNode(10 % 10) = ListNode(0) appends the digit 0.
curr = curr.next moves the tail onto the new node 0.
Loop check for iteration 3: l1 is node 3, so we go again.
val_sum = carry = 1. This time the column starts at 1 because of the carry.
if l1 is true, so val_sum += 3 makes val_sum = 1 + 3 = 4.
l1 = l1.next makes l1 None; list 1 is now exhausted.
if l2 is true, so val_sum += 4 makes val_sum = 4 + 4 = 8.
l2 = l2.next makes l2 None; list 2 is exhausted as well.
carry = 8 // 10 = 0, so nothing is carried out of the final column.
curr.next = ListNode(8 % 10) = ListNode(8) appends the last digit.
curr = curr.next moves the tail onto node 8.
Loop check: l1 is None, l2 is None and carry is 0, so 'None or None or 0' is falsy and the loop finally ends. Had carry been 1 here, one extra node would have been created.
return dummy.next skips the placeholder and returns node 7. The answer 7 -> 0 -> 8 reads as 807 = 342 + 465. One pass over the longer list, O(1) extra space beyond the output.

Delete a Given Node.desc: Our list is 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 9 and deleteNode is handed ONLY the node holding 5 (index 1). We get no head pointer, so we can never reach the node holding 4 and re-point it — the usual deletion move is impossible.
The trick the comment describes: since we cannot delete this node object, we instead make it IMPERSONATE its successor — copy the next node's value into it, then unlink the successor.
Evaluating the right-hand side: node.next is the node holding 1 (index 2). This is the successor whose identity we are about to steal.
Reading node.next.val gives 1. Note we only copy the VALUE, not the object.
Assignment happens: node.val = 1. The list momentarily reads 4 -> 1 -> 1 -> 9. The value 5 is gone from the list already, and there is now a duplicated 1 that we must clean up.
The second comment sets up the cleanup: the node we copied from is now redundant, so we bypass it by pointing our node at its successor.
Evaluating the right side: node.next is still the duplicate node at index 2 (value 1).
Then node.next.next is read: that is the node holding 9 at index 3. This is the new successor we want.
Assignment: node.next = node(9). The pointer at index 1 now jumps straight over index 2, shown by the redirected link 1 -> 3.
The old node at index 2 is now unreachable from the head: nothing points to it, so Python's garbage collector reclaims it. We effectively deleted a node we never had a previous pointer to.
Walking from the head now gives 4 -> 1 -> 9. The value 5 has disappeared exactly as required, in O(1) time and O(1) extra space.

The function has no return statement, so it implicitly returns None — the caller sees the change through the mutated list itself. Caveat: this trick cannot delete the LAST node, since node.next would be None and line 3 would crash.

Intersection of Two Linked Lists.desc: Input: list A = 1 -> 9 -> 1 -> 2 -> 4 (length 5) and list B = 3 -> 2 -> 4 (length 3), where the nodes 2 and 4 are the SAME objects in both lists. Neither head is None, so we skip the early return.
pA = headA, so pA sits on node 1 (A index 0).
pB = headB, so pB sits on node 3 (B index 0). The trick: each pointer walks its own list, then jumps to the OTHER head, so both travel lenA + lenB steps and must line up.
while pA != pB: node(1) and node(3) are different objects, so we enter the loop.
pA is not None, so pA = pA.next -> node 9 (A index 1).
pB is not None, so pB = pB.next -> node 2, which is the FIRST shared node (B index 1).
Check again: node(9) is not node(2), keep going.
pA = pA.next -> node 1 (A index 2).
pB = pB.next -> node 4 (the second shared node, B index 2).
Still different objects — note that pA holds a node whose VALUE is 1, but identity, not value, is what we compare.
pA = pA.next -> node 2, the first shared node.
pB = pB.next -> None, because node 4 was the tail of B. pB has now walked all 3 nodes of B.
node(2) != None, so the loop continues. This is the step where the switch is about to happen.
pA = pA.next -> node 4 (A index 4, the tail).
pB IS None, so the conditional expression fires the other branch: pB = headA. pB restarts on node 1 of list A. Total distance pB will cover = lenB + lenA.
Different objects again, loop on.
pA = pA.next -> None; pA has now walked all 5 nodes of A.
pB = pB.next -> node 9 (A index 1).
pA is None and pB is node(9); still not equal, so the loop continues.
pA is None, so pA = headB: pA restarts on node 3, the head of list B. Total distance pA will cover = lenA + lenB, exactly the same as pB.
pB = pB.next -> node 1 (A index 2).
node(3) and node(1) are different objects, so we take one more turn.
pA = pA.next -> node 2, the shared node.
pB = pB.next -> node 2 as well — the very same object. Both pointers have now walked 7 steps, which is why the equal-distance trick works.
while pA != pB is now False: pA and pB are literally the same node object. The loop exits.
return pA gives the node holding 2 — the intersection point. Had the lists never met, both pointers would have become None at the same time and this line would have returned None.

Reverse Nodes in K Group.desc: We call reverseKGroup(head = 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 2). First job: confirm a full group of 2 exists. curr = head = node 1.
count = 0 will tally how many nodes we managed to walk (capped at k).
while curr and count < k: curr is node 1 and 0 < 2, so we take a step.
curr = curr.next moves the counter onto node 2.
count += 1 makes count = 1: one node of the group confirmed.
Check again: curr is node 2 and 1 < 2, so one more step.
curr = curr.next moves the counter onto node 3.
count += 1 makes count = 2: a full group of k = 2 is confirmed.
Now count < k is False (2 < 2 is false), so the counting loop stops with curr parked on node 3 — the head of the NEXT group.
count == k (2 == 2) is True, so a complete group of 2 exists and we are allowed to reverse it.
prev = None. In a reversal, prev is what the current node should point BACK to; for the first node that is None.
curr = head = node 1. We now run the standard iterative reversal exactly k times.
Reversal turn 1 of k = 2 inside the for loop.
next_node = curr.next = node 2. We must save it before we destroy curr.next.
curr.next = prev: node 1 now points at None. Node 1 has become the tail of this group.
prev = curr -> prev is node 1.
curr = next_node -> curr is node 2.
Reversal turn 2 of k = 2, the last one for this group.
next_node = curr.next = node 3 (saved before we overwrite the link).
curr.next = prev: node 2 now points at node 1. The first group reads 2 -> 1.
prev = curr -> prev is node 2, the new head of this reversed block.
curr = next_node -> node 3. The for loop has run k = 2 times and stops. prev = node 2, curr = node 3.
head.next = reverseKGroup(curr, k): head is still node 1 (now the group's tail), and we recurse on node 3 to fix up everything after this group.
[depth 1] The same counting loop on 3 -> 4 -> 5 reaches count = 2, so nodes 3 and 4 form another full group and get reversed.
[depth 1] After its two reversal turns: node 3 points at None, node 4 points at node 3, prev = node 4 and curr = node 5.
[depth 1] head is node 3, so node3.next = reverseKGroup(node 5, 2). Recurse once more.
[depth 2] Only node 5 is left, so the counting loop ends with count = 1. count == k is False — an incomplete tail group must be left untouched.
[depth 2] return head returns node 5 exactly as it is. This is the base case that stops the recursion.
[depth 1] The recursive call handed back node 5, so node3.next = node 5. The tail of the second reversed group is stitched to the leftover.
[depth 1] return prev returns node 4, the head of the second reversed block.
[top level] That returned node 4 becomes head.next, i.e. node1.next = node 4. The first group's tail now joins the second group's head.
[top level] return prev returns node 2 — the final head. Walking the links gives 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 5, exactly the required answer.

Check if Linked List is Palindrome.desc: Check if list has 0 or 1 node.
Initialize slow and fast pointers to head (1)
Iteration 1: Move slow to 2, fast to 2
Iteration 2: fast.next is not None. Move slow to 2 (second 2), fast to None
Reversal of second half: initialize prev = None, curr = slow (2)
Reversal step 1: 2.next becomes None. prev = 2, curr = 1
Reversal step 2: 1.next becomes 2. prev = 1, curr = None
Set left pointer to head (1), right pointer to prev (1)
Compare left.val (1) and right.val (1). Match! Move pointers.
Compare left.val (2) and right.val (2). Match! Move pointers.

Find Starting Point of Loop.desc: Input list: 3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4, and -4 points BACK to the node holding 2 (index 1). So there is a tail of length 1 and a cycle of length 3. The correct answer is the node holding 2.
slow = head, so slow points at node(3) at index 0. slow will move one step at a time.
fast = head as well, so both pointers start on node(3). fast will move two steps at a time, gaining exactly one position per iteration.

while fast and fast.next: fast is node(3) and fast.next is node(2), both non-None, so we enter the loop. Checking fast.next too is essential — without it, fast.next.next would crash on a list that ends.
slow = slow.next moves slow from index 0 to index 1 (node 2). One step.
fast = fast.next.next jumps fast from index 0 over index 1 to index 2 (node 0). Two steps.
Is slow == fast? slow is at index 1 and fast is at index 2 — different objects, so no collision yet. Gap is now 1.
Loop check again: fast is node(0) at index 2 and fast.next is node(-4) at index 3, both exist, so iteration 2 begins.
slow = slow.next: slow goes from index 1 to index 2 (node 0).
fast = fast.next.next: from index 2, one step is index 3 (node -4), and a second step follows the BACK EDGE to index 1 (node 2). fast has wrapped around the cycle.
slow is at index 2 and fast is at index 1 — still not equal. They passed each other in position order but that is fine; only object identity matters.
Iteration 3: fast is node(2) at index 1 and fast.next is node(0) at index 2, so we continue.
slow = slow.next: slow moves from index 2 to index 3 (node -4).
fast = fast.next.next: from index 1, one step to index 2 (node 0), a second step to index 3 (node -4). fast also lands on index 3.
slow == fast is now True — both are the SAME node object, node(-4) at index 3. A collision inside the cycle proves a cycle exists. But this meeting point is NOT the cycle start, so phase 2 begins.

slow = head resets slow back to index 0 (node 3), while fast stays at the meeting point index 3. The maths: the distance from head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle start, going forward.
while slow != fast: slow is at index 0 and fast is at index 3, so they differ and we enter phase 2's loop. Both now move at the SAME speed, one step each.
slow = slow.next moves slow from index 0 to index 1 (node 2).
fast = fast.next moves fast from index 3 along the back edge to index 1 (node 2).
Loop check: slow != fast is now False — both sit on the very same node(2) at index 1. The loop exits after just one step.
return slow gives node(2) at index 1 — exactly the node where the cycle begins, found in O(n) time with O(1) extra space and no hash set.
For contrast: had the list been a plain 3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4 -> None, the while on line 7 would have ended when fast fell off, and this line would return None instead.

Flatten a Linked List.desc: Input: four columns joined by next -- col0 = 5,7,8,30 / col1 = 10,20 / col2 = 19,22,50 / col3 = 28,35,40,45. flatten is called with root = node 5. root.next is node 10, so this is NOT the base case.
root.next = flatten(root.next): before we can merge anything, everything to our right must first become ONE sorted column. Recurse on node 10.
[depth 1] root = node 10 and root.next = node 19 exists, so keep going right.
[depth 1] Recurse again, this time on node 19.
[depth 2] root = node 19, root.next = node 28 exists, still not the base case.
[depth 2] Recurse on node 28, the last column.
[depth 3] root = node 28 and root.next is None -- there is no column to our right, so 'not root.next' is True.
[depth 3] return root hands back the untouched column 28 -> 35 -> 40 -> 45. Recursion now unwinds, merging on the way back up.
[depth 2] The call returned, so root(19).next now points at the flattened column headed by 28.
[depth 2] mergeTwoLists(a = 19 -> 22 -> 50, b = 28 -> 35 -> 40 -> 45). Both are sorted, so a linear merge suffices.
[merge] dummy = Node(0) is a placeholder head so the first append needs no special case.
[merge] temp = dummy. temp always marks the last node of the chain built so far.
[merge] while a and b: a is node 19 and b is node 28, both real, so we enter.
[merge] a.data (19) < b.data (28) is True, so a's node wins this round.
[merge] temp.bottom = a hangs node 19 under the dummy. Merged so far: 19.
[merge] temp = temp.bottom moves temp onto node 19.
[merge] a = a.bottom advances inside column a to node 22.
[merge] Next round: 22 < 28 is True, so a wins again; lines 11-15 append node 22 and advance a to node 50.
[merge] Now a.data (50) < b.data (28) is False, so control falls into the else branch and b wins.
[merge] temp.bottom = b appends node 28. Merged so far: 19 -> 22 -> 28.
[merge] b = b.bottom advances to node 35. The else branch fires three more times in the same way, appending 35, 40 and 45, after which b becomes None.
[merge] while a and b is now False because b is None, so the merging loop stops with node 50 still unused.
[merge] if a: a is node 50, so there IS a leftover tail.
[merge] temp.bottom = a attaches the whole remaining tail in one move -- it is already sorted, so no comparisons are needed.
[merge] return dummy.bottom returns node 19, the real head of the merged column.
[depth 2] return root sends that 7-node sorted column back up to depth 1.
[depth 1] Merge our own column 10 -> 20 with the column just received. 10 wins, then 19, then 20, then a runs out and the rest of b is attached.
[depth 1] return root gives 10 -> 19 -> 20 -> 22 -> 28 -> 35 -> 40 -> 45 -> 50 back to the top-level call.
[top level] Final merge: our column 5 -> 7 -> 8 -> 30 against that 9-node column. 5, 7 and 8 are all smaller than 10, then 10, 19, 20, 22 and 28 come across before 30 is placed.
[top level] return root gives the finished list 5 -> 7 -> 8 -> 10 -> 19 -> 20 -> 22 -> 28 -> 30 -> 35 -> 40 -> 45 -> 50, chained entirely through bottom pointers.

Rotate a Linked List.desc: We call rotateRight(head = 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 2). The guard checks for an empty list, a single node, or k == 0; none applies, so we continue.
tail = head parks a pointer on node 1; it will walk to the real tail.
length = 1, because we are already standing on one node.
while tail.next: node 1 has a successor, so we step.
length += 1 makes length = 2 (we have seen two nodes).
tail = tail.next walks the pointer onto node 2.
tail.next is node 3, so loop again.
length += 1 makes length = 3 (three nodes counted so far).
tail = tail.next walks the pointer onto node 3.
tail.next is node 4, keep going.
length += 1 makes length = 4 (four nodes counted so far).
tail = tail.next walks the pointer onto node 4.
tail.next is node 5, one more turn.
length += 1 makes length = 5, the full size of the list.
tail = tail.next walks the pointer onto node 5, the last node.
tail.next is None, so node 5 really is the tail and the measuring loop ends with length = 5.
tail.next = head closes the list into a RING: 5 now points back at 1. Rotating a ring is just choosing where to cut it.
steps_to_new_tail = length - (k % length) = 5 - (2 % 5) = 5 - 2 = 3. The k % length is what makes k = 7 or k = 102 behave like k = 2.
new_tail = head starts the walk on node 1.
The for loop runs steps_to_new_tail - 1 = 2 times, because starting on node 1 already counts as the 1st of the 3 steps. Turn 1.
new_tail = new_tail.next -> node 2.
Turn 2 of the for loop that walks to the new tail.
new_tail = new_tail.next -> node 3. That is the 3rd node, exactly where the ring must be cut.
new_head = new_tail.next -> node 4. The last k = 2 nodes (4 and 5) are the ones that wrap around to the front.
new_tail.next = None cuts the ring open right after node 3, which becomes the new end of the list.
return new_head gives node 4. Following the links from there: 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3, which is [1,2,3,4,5] rotated right by 2. One pass, O(1) extra space.

Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array.desc: We call removeDuplicates([0, 0, 1, 1, 2]). The array is SORTED, which means every duplicate group is contiguous — that is the fact the whole two-pointer trick rests on. We must compact unique values to the front and return their count.
Guard clause: 'if not nums' is False because [0, 0, 1, 1, 2] is non-empty, so we skip the early return on line 4 and continue.
i = 0. Think of i as the index of the LAST value already accepted as unique. nums[0] = 0 is trivially unique, so the accepted region is just [0].
The for loop starts the scanner at j = 1 (never 0, since element 0 is already accepted).
Compare nums[1] = 0 with nums[0] = 0. They are EQUAL, so this is a duplicate — the if-body is skipped entirely and i does not move.
The scanner advances to j = 2 while i stays at 0.
Compare nums[2] = 1 with nums[0] = 0. They DIFFER, so 1 is a value we have never accepted — the if-body runs.
i += 1 makes i = 1: we are opening up slot 1 as the home for the next unique value.
nums[1] = nums[2] copies the 1 into slot 1. The array becomes [0, 1, 1, 1, 2]. Slots 0..1 now hold the unique prefix [0, 1]; everything after index i is scratch space we no longer care about.
The scanner advances to j = 3; i is now parked at 1.

Compare nums[3] = 1 with nums[1] = 1. Equal, so this second 1 is a duplicate and is skipped. Because the input was sorted, we only ever need to compare against the single last-kept value, never the whole prefix.
j advances to 4, the final index.
Compare nums[4] = 2 with nums[1] = 1. They differ, so 2 is a new unique value.
i += 1 makes i = 2, reserving slot 2 for the value 2.
nums[2] = nums[4] writes 2 into slot 2. The array is now [0, 1, 2, 1, 2] — the first three cells hold [0, 1, 2] and the tail [1, 2] is leftover garbage the caller must ignore.
range(1, 5) is exhausted after j = 4, so the for loop ends. Every element was touched exactly once, giving O(n) time.
return i + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3. We add 1 because i is an INDEX (last unique position) while the caller wants a COUNT. The caller reads nums[0:3] = [0, 1, 2], which is the answer.

Max Consecutive Ones.desc: Start of the scan on nums = [1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1]. max_count is the best run length seen so far; it begins at 0 so an all-zero array correctly answers 0.
current_count is the length of the run of 1s that ends at the element we are looking at right now. Nothing scanned yet, so it is 0.
Iteration 1: the for-loop hands us num = nums[0] = 1.
num == 1 is True, so this element extends the run instead of breaking it.
current_count grows from 0 to 1: there is now a run of one 1 ending at index 0.
max_count = max(0, 1) = 1. The best run so far is length 1.
Iteration 2: num = nums[1] = 1, another one.
current_count grows from 1 to 2 — the run [1, 1] ends at index 1.
max_count = max(1, 2) = 2. Notice we update the maximum immediately, so we never need to remember where runs started.
Iteration 3: num = nums[2] = 0. This is the interesting case.
num == 1 is False for the 0, so control jumps to the else branch on line 13.
current_count is reset to 0 because the run is broken here. max_count keeps the value 2 — the finished run is already banked.
Iteration 4: num = nums[3] = 1. A brand new run starts.
current_count goes 0 -> 1 for the run starting at index 3.
max_count = max(2, 1) = 2. The new run is still shorter than the banked best, so nothing changes.
Iteration 5: num = nums[4] = 1, the run keeps growing.
current_count goes 1 -> 2 (the run [1, 1] covering indices 3 and 4).
max_count = max(2, 2) = 2 — a tie, so the stored maximum is unchanged.
Iteration 6, the last one: num = nums[5] = 1.
current_count goes 2 -> 3: indices 3, 4 and 5 form a run of three 1s.
max_count = max(2, 3) = 3. Because we update inside the loop, the run that touches the end of the array is captured with no extra code after the loop.
The loop is exhausted, so we return max_count = 3 — the longest block of consecutive 1s in [1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1].

Minimum Number of Platforms.desc: arr.sort() puts the arrival times in increasing order: [900, 940, 950, 1100, 1500, 1800]. Sorting is what lets us sweep time forwards.

dep.sort() sorts the departures INDEPENDENTLY: [910, 1120, 1130, 1200, 1900, 2000]. Train i no longer pairs with departure i, and that is fine — we only care how many trains are inside the station, not which ones.
i is the index of the next arrival event we have not processed yet.
j is the index of the next departure event.
platforms_needed counts trains standing at the station right now. It starts at 0 because the station is empty before 900.
max_platforms remembers the busiest moment we have seen, which is the answer we will return.
Loop guard: i = 0 < 6 and j = 0 < 6, so there are still events left to merge.
Compare the next arrival with the next departure: arr[0] = 900 <= dep[0] = 910, so the arrival happens first.
A train pulls in, so platforms_needed rises from 0 to 1.
Consume the arrival event: i moves from 0 to 1.
max_platforms = max(0, 1) = 1.
Next comparison: arr[1] = 940 <= dep[0] = 910 is FALSE, so the earliest event is a departure at 910, not the arrival at 940.
The train that leaves at 910 frees its platform: platforms_needed drops from 1 to 0.
Consume the departure event: j moves from 0 to 1.
max_platforms = max(1, 0) = 1, unchanged — the peak is never lowered.
Now arr[1] = 940 <= dep[1] = 1120 is True, so the 940 arrival is the next event in time order.
platforms_needed rises to 1 (the 940 train is in).
i moves from 1 to 2.
max_platforms stays 1.
arr[2] = 950 <= dep[1] = 1120: another arrival before the next departure.
platforms_needed rises to 2 — the 940 and 950 trains are both standing.
i moves from 2 to 3.
max_platforms = max(1, 2) = 2, a new record.
arr[3] = 1100 <= dep[1] = 1120: a third overlapping arrival.
platforms_needed rises to 3. This is the busiest instant of the whole day.
i moves from 3 to 4.
max_platforms = max(2, 3) = 3 — the eventual answer is locked in here.
arr[4] = 1500 <= dep[1] = 1120 is False, so a departure comes first.
platforms_needed falls to 2.
j moves from 1 to 2.
1500 <= dep[2] = 1130 is still False, so another departure is consumed: platforms_needed 2 -> 1 and j becomes 3.
1500 <= dep[3] = 1200 is False as well: platforms_needed 1 -> 0 and j becomes 4. The station is empty between 1200 and 1500.
Finally arr[4] = 1500 <= dep[4] = 1900 is True, so the 1500 train arrives: platforms_needed 0 -> 1, i becomes 5, max_platforms stays 3.
arr[5] = 1800 <= dep[4] = 1900 is True: platforms_needed 1 -> 2, i becomes 6. Two trains share the evening, still under the peak of 3.
Loop guard again: i = 6 is not < n = 6, so the while loop stops. Every remaining event is a departure, which can only lower the count.
Return max_platforms = 3: three platforms are enough, and never fewer.

Job Sequencing Problem.desc: Sort jobs by profit descending. Sorted: [Job 3 (profit 40), Job 4 (profit 30), Job 1 (profit 20), Job 2 (profit 10)]
Find slot starting at 1. slot 1 is free. Assign schedule[1] = 3.
Find slot starting at 1. slot 1 is occupied. No slot available.
Find slot starting at 4. slot 4 is free. Assign schedule[4] = 1.
Find slot starting at 1. slot 1 is occupied. No slot available.
Return count of scheduled jobs and total profit.

Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick.desc: Call minCost with n = 5 and cuts = [1, 3]: a stick from 0 to 5 that must be cut at positions 1 and 3.
Sort the cuts and wrap them in sentinels: c = [0, 1, 3, 5]. Index 0 and index 3 are the stick ends, never real cuts.
m = 4 positions in total, so the real cuts live at indices 1 and 2 of c.
Allocate a 4x4 dp table of zeros. dp[i][j] will store the cheapest cost of cutting the piece that spans c[i-1] .. c[j+1]; cells with j < i stay 0 and mean 'empty window'.
Outer loop starts at i = m - 2 = 2 and counts DOWN, so windows that start further right are finished before the ones that start left.
Inner loop: j = 2, so the window is (i, j) = (2, 2) - only the cut at c[2] = 3 is pending here.
The piece holding this window spans c[i-1] = c[1] = 1 to c[j+1] = c[3] = 5, so length = 5 - 1 = 4. Any cut made here costs 4.
best starts at infinity so that the very first candidate cost always replaces it.
Only one split point exists in this window: k = 2, i.e. we perform the cut at position 3.
cost = length + dp[2][1] + dp[3][2] = 4 + 0 + 0 = 4. Both sub-windows are empty (j < i), so they cost nothing.
4 < infinity, so this candidate becomes the champion for the window (2, 2).
best = 4 - cutting position 3 while standing on the piece (1, 5) costs 4.
Store dp[2][2] = 4. This small answer will be reused by every bigger window that contains it.
i drops to 1: now we handle windows that begin at the leftmost real cut, c[1] = 1.
j = 1 first, so the window (1, 1) holds only the cut at position 1.
This window sits on the piece from c[0] = 0 to c[2] = 3, so length = 3 - 0 = 3.
The only split is k = 1: cut at position 1 while holding the piece (0, 3).
cost = 3 + dp[1][0] + dp[2][1] = 3 + 0 + 0 = 3, since both neighbouring windows are empty.
best = 3 for the window (1, 1) - there was no alternative to compare against.
dp[1][1] = 3 is stored. The table now knows both single-cut windows.
j moves to 2, giving the window (1, 2): BOTH cuts are pending and the piece is the entire stick.
length = c[3] - c[0] = 5 - 0 = 5: whichever cut we make first, we pay the full stick length 5.
First candidate: k = 1, meaning we cut at position 1 before anything else.
cost = 5 + dp[1][0] + dp[2][2] = 5 + 0 + 4 = 9. Cutting at 1 first leaves the long piece (1, 5), whose own cut costs 4.
best = 9 so far; we still have to test the other opening move.
Second candidate: k = 2, meaning we cut at position 3 first instead.
cost = 5 + dp[1][1] + dp[3][2] = 5 + 3 + 0 = 8. Cutting at 3 first leaves the short piece (0, 3), whose cut costs only 3.
8 < 9, so cutting the middle-ish position first really is cheaper - this single comparison is the whole point of the problem.
best = 8 - the improved plan is 'cut at 3, then cut at 1'.
dp[1][2] = 8 is written; the k-loop is exhausted so this window is final.
Return dp[1][m - 2] = dp[1][2] = 8: cut at 3 (pay 5), then cut at 1 on the piece (0, 3) (pay 3).

Burst Balloons.desc: Call maxCoins with nums = [3, 1, 5]. We must burst all three balloons in the best possible order.
Pad both ends with imaginary 1-balloons: a = [1, 3, 1, 5, 1]. Now index i - 1 and j + 1 always exist.
m = 5, so the real balloons sit at indices 1, 2 and 3 of the padded array.
Create a 5x5 dp table of zeros. dp[i][j] will hold the best coins from bursting every balloon in the window i..j; cells with j < i stay 0 = empty window.
Outer loop starts at i = m - 2 = 3 and counts down, so the rightmost windows are solved first.
j = 3, so the window is (3, 3): just the single balloon a[3] = 5, walled in by a[2] = 1 and a[4] = 1.
best = 0 - the starting value for the maximum inside this window.
Only one candidate for the LAST balloon here: k = 3.
coins = a[2] * a[3] * a[4] + dp[3][2] + dp[4][3] = 1 * 5 * 1 + 0 + 0 = 5. Both side windows are empty.
5 > 0, so best becomes 5 for the window (3, 3).
Store dp[3][3] = 5: bursting balloon 5 alone between two imaginary 1s earns 5 coins.
i drops to 2. Windows starting at balloon a[2] = 1 are next.
j = 2 gives the single-balloon window (2, 2): balloon a[2] = 1 with walls a[1] = 3 and a[3] = 5.
With k = 2: coins = a[1] * a[2] * a[3] + dp[2][1] + dp[3][2] = 3 * 1 * 5 + 0 + 0 = 15. Both real neighbours are still alive, which is why this pop is worth so much.
dp[2][2] = 15 is stored - the best (and only) plan for that window.
j grows to 3: window (2, 3) holds balloons a[2] = 1 and a[3] = 5, walled by a[1] = 3 and a[4] = 1.
8 > 0, so best = 8 for now; one more candidate remains.
30 > 8, so best jumps to 30: it pays to burst the small balloon first and keep the 5 alive next to the 3.
dp[2][3] = 30 is written and becomes reusable by the bigger window starting at i = 1.
i drops to 1 - the last row, containing every window that starts at the first real balloon a[1] = 3.
dp[1][1] = 3 stored: balloon 3 alone, squeezed between the wall 1 and the balloon 1, is only worth 3.
j = 2: window (1, 2) covers balloons 3 and 1, with walls a[0] = 1 and a[3] = 5.
best = 30 for window (1, 2).
8 > 30 is false, so best stays 30 - keeping balloon 3 for last was the better plan.
dp[1][2] = 30 is written.
j = 3: the final window (1, 3) covers ALL three real balloons, with imaginary walls 1 on both sides.
33 > 0, so best = 33 for the full window while two more candidates for the last balloon remain.
k = 2 (burst the middle 1 last): coins = a[0] * a[2] * a[4] + dp[1][1] + dp[3][3] = 1 * 1 * 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, clearly worse.
35 > 33, so best becomes 35 - the winning plan bursts 1, then 3, then 5 last.
dp[1][3] = 35 is stored; the k-loop is finished so this window is final.
Return dp[1][m - 2] = dp[1][3] = 35 coins, the maximum over every burst order of [3, 1, 5].

Palindrome Partitioning II.desc: Call minCut with s = "aab". We want the fewest cuts that leave only palindromic pieces.
n = 3 characters: s[0] = 'a', s[1] = 'a', s[2] = 'b'.
n = 3 is greater than 1, so the trivial shortcut does not fire and we build the tables.
Create the 3x3 palindrome table pal, all False (shown as 0). pal[i][j] will mean 's[i..j] reads the same both ways'.
Outer loop starts at i = n - 1 = 2 and counts DOWN, so the inner window pal[i+1][j-1] is always filled before it is read.
j = 2, so we are testing the window s[2..2] = "b".
s[2] == s[2] is trivially true and j - i = 0 < 2, so a single character skips the inner check and counts as a palindrome.
pal[2][2] = True: "b" is a palindrome.
i drops to 1, so all windows now start at s[1] = 'a'.
j = 1 gives the window s[1..1] = "a", another single character.
Ends match ('a' == 'a') and the window length is 1, so j - i < 2 short-circuits the inner lookup.
pal[1][1] = True: the single character "a" at index 1 is a palindrome.
j = 2 now: the window is s[1..2] = "ab".
s[1] = 'a' but s[2] = 'b', so the ends disagree; the condition fails and pal[1][2] stays False - "ab" is not a palindrome.
i drops to 0, the last row of the table: windows that begin at the very first character.
j = 0: the window s[0..0] = "a" is a single character, so pal[0][0] = True.
j = 1: the window is s[0..1] = "aa", the interesting length-2 case.
s[0] = 'a' equals s[1] = 'a', and j - i = 1 < 2, so the length-2 window needs no inner check - this guard is exactly what stops us from reading the nonsense window pal[1][0].
pal[0][1] = True: "aa" is a palindrome.
j = 2: the window s[0..2] = "aab" has ends 'a' and 'b' which differ, so pal[0][2] stays False. The palindrome table is now complete.
Start phase two. dp = [0, 0, 0] where dp[j] will hold the fewest cuts for the prefix s[0..j].
j = 0: consider the prefix "a".
pal[0][0] is True, so the entire prefix "a" is already a palindrome.
dp[0] = 0 - no cut is needed for "a".
j = 1: consider the prefix "aa".
pal[0][1] is True, so "aa" is itself a palindrome and the else-branch is skipped entirely.
dp[1] = 0: zero cuts for "aa", because one whole palindromic piece means no cut at all.
j = 2: the final prefix "aab", the whole string.
pal[0][2] is False - "aab" is not a palindrome - so we must place at least one cut and enter the else-branch.
best = j = 2, the worst case of cutting between every pair of characters: "a" | "a" | "b".
Try i = 1, meaning the last piece would be s[1..2] = "ab".
pal[1][2] is False, so "ab" is not a legal last piece and this candidate is rejected without even looking at dp[0].
Try i = 2, meaning the last piece is s[2..2] = "b".
pal[2][2] is True, and dp[i - 1] + 1 = dp[1] + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1 is smaller than best = 2, so this split wins.
best = 1: one cut placed just before index 2, giving the pieces "aa" and "b".
The i-loop is exhausted, so dp[2] = 1 is stored. dp is now [0, 0, 1].
Return dp[n - 1] = dp[2] = 1. The optimal partition of "aab" is "aa" | "b" with a single cut.

Kth Largest Element.desc: Start with an empty min-heap. It will hold at most k = 2 numbers: the 2 largest seen so far.
First iteration of the loop: num takes the value 3 at index 0.
Push 3. The heap was empty, so 3 becomes the root: heap = [3].
len(heap) = 1 which is not greater than k = 2, so we keep everything — no eviction.
Second iteration: num moves on to the value 2 at index 1.
Push 2. It is smaller than the root 3, so it bubbles up and the heap becomes [2, 3].
len(heap) = 2 equals k = 2, still within budget, so nothing is evicted yet.
Third iteration: num is now 1, the value at index 2.
Push 1. It is the smallest so far and sifts up to the root: heap = [1, 3, 2].
Now len(heap) = 3 > k = 2, so we are carrying one candidate too many.
Pop the root 1. Out of {1, 3, 2} it is the weakest, so it can never be the 2nd largest — heap = [2, 3].
Fourth iteration: num becomes 5, the value at index 3.
Push 5. It is bigger than the root so it stays low in the tree: heap = [2, 3, 5].
len(heap) = 3 > 2 again, so the weakest of the three must go.
Pop 2. The two largest seen so far are now {3, 5}, stored as heap = [3, 5].
Fifth iteration: num is 6, the largest value in the whole array.
Push 6 — it is the biggest, so it sinks to a leaf: heap = [3, 5, 6].
Size 3 exceeds k = 2 once more, so the eviction branch runs.
Pop 3. The top-2 so far is {5, 6}, held as heap = [5, 6] with 5 at the root.
Sixth and last iteration: num is 4 at index 5.
Push 4. Since 4 < 5 it bubbles to the root, giving heap = [4, 6, 5] momentarily.
len(heap) = 3 > k = 2, so 4 has to prove it belongs in the top 2 — and it does not.
Pop 4, the value we just added. The heap settles back to [5, 6] and the loop ends.
Every number is processed. heap = [5, 6] holds the 2 largest; its root 5 is the 2nd largest, so we return 5.

Top K Frequent Elements.desc: Counter walks [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3] once and tallies each value into a hash map.
Create the empty min-heap. It will never hold more than k = 2 (count, value) pairs.
First map entry: value = 1 with count = 3 (the three 1s at indices 0, 1 and 2).
Push the pair (3, 1) — count first so the heap sorts by frequency. heap = [(3, 1)].
len(heap) = 1 is not greater than k = 2, so nothing is evicted this round.
Second map entry: value = 2 with count = 2 (the two 2s at indices 3 and 4).
Push (2, 2). Since 2 < 3 it sifts up to the root: heap = [(2, 2), (3, 1)].
len(heap) = 2 equals k = 2 — still exactly within budget, so no pop.
Third and last map entry: value = 3 with count = 1 (the single 3 at index 5).
Push (1, 3). Count 1 is the smallest so it becomes the root: heap = [(1, 3), (3, 1), (2, 2)].
Now len(heap) = 3 > k = 2, so we are holding one candidate too many and must evict.
Pop the root (1, 3): value 3 occurs only once, and two values already beat it, so it is out. heap = [(2, 2), (3, 1)].
The for-loop asks for another map entry, but freq is exhausted, so the loop ends.
Two pairs survived: (2, 2) and (3, 1). Strip the counts to return the values [2, 1] — the top 2 in any order.

Merge K Sorted Arrays.desc: Start with an empty min-heap. Input is arrays = [[1, 4], [2, 6], [3, 5]], so it will hold at most 3 candidates.
Seeding loop, first round: i = 0 and arr = [1, 4].
arr = [1, 4] is non-empty, so it has a first element to contribute.
Push (1, 0, 0): value 1, from array 0, at position 0. heap = [(1, 0, 0)].
Second seeding round: i = 1 and arr = [2, 6].
Push (2, 1, 0). It is larger than the root 1, so it stays below: heap = [(1, 0, 0), (2, 1, 0)].
Third seeding round: i = 2 and arr = [3, 5], the last array.
Push (3, 2, 0). Heap now holds one candidate per array: [(1, 0, 0), (2, 1, 0), (3, 2, 0)].
Seeding is done. Create the empty output list that we will fill in sorted order.
The heap is non-empty, so there is still work: enter the main merge loop.
Pop the root (1, 0, 0): value 1 from array 0, index 0. Heap becomes [(2, 1, 0), (3, 2, 0)].
Append 1 to the output. Nothing smaller can exist anywhere, so this position is final. merged = [1].
Array 0 is [1, 4] and j + 1 = 1 < 2, so array 0 still has the element 4 to offer.
Push (4, 0, 1) as array 0's new candidate: heap = [(2, 1, 0), (3, 2, 0), (4, 0, 1)].
Second merge round: pop (2, 1, 0). Heap re-heapifies to [(3, 2, 0), (4, 0, 1)].
Append 2, giving merged = [1, 2].
Array 1 is [2, 6]; j + 1 = 1 < 2, so 6 is still waiting in that array.
Third round: pop (3, 2, 0), the smallest of the three candidates. Heap = [(4, 0, 1), (6, 1, 1)].
Append 3: merged = [1, 2, 3]. Notice we have now taken one element from each array.
Array 2 is [3, 5]; j + 1 = 1 < 2, so it can still offer the value 5.
Push (5, 2, 1). It is bigger than the root 4, so it lands as a leaf: heap = [(4, 0, 1), (6, 1, 1), (5, 2, 1)].
Fourth round: pop (4, 0, 1) — array 0's last element. Heap re-heapifies to [(5, 2, 1), (6, 1, 1)].
Append 4: merged = [1, 2, 3, 4].
j + 1 = 2 is NOT < len(arrays[0]) = 2, so array 0 is exhausted and contributes nothing further.
Fifth round: pop (5, 2, 1). The heap has shrunk to just [(6, 1, 1)].
Append 5: merged = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
Array 2 is [3, 5] and j + 1 = 2 is not less than 2, so it is exhausted too — no push.
Sixth round: pop the last candidate (6, 1, 1). The heap is now completely empty.
Append 6: merged = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Every element has been emitted exactly once.
Array 1 is [2, 6] and j + 1 = 2 is not a valid index, so nothing is pushed back.
The while condition is checked again: the heap is empty, so the merge loop exits.
Return the fully merged sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] — 6 elements, and the heap never exceeded 3 entries.

Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.desc: Input lists are 1->4, 1->3 and 2. Start with an empty min-heap that will hold at most 3 candidates.
Seeding loop, first round: i = 0 and node is the head of list 0, value 1.
The head is not None, so list 0 has something to contribute.
Push (1, 0, node) — value 1, list index 0. heap = [(1, 0, A1)].
Second seeding round: i = 1, node is list 1's head, which also has value 1.

Push (1, 1, B1). The values tie at 1, so the index decides: 1 > 0, so it stays below the root. heap = [(1,0,A1), (1,1,B1)]. Without the index the heap would try to compare two ListNodes and raise TypeError.
Third seeding round: i = 2, node is list 2's head with value 2.
Push (2, 2, C1). heap = [(1,0,A1), (1,1,B1), (2,2,C1)] — one candidate per list.
Create the dummy node. Its .next will end up being the head of the merged list.
tail starts at the dummy; it will always point at the last node stitched into the answer.
The heap is non-empty (3 candidates), so enter the merge loop.
Pop (1, 0, A1): the smallest candidate, list 0's node with value 1. heap = [(1,1,B1), (2,2,C1)].
Stitch it on: dummy.next = A1. We reuse the node itself, allocating nothing.
Move tail onto A1, so the next stitch happens after value 1.
A1.next is the node 4 in list 0, so list 0 can still offer a candidate.
Second round: pop (1, 1, B1), list 1's head with value 1. heap = [(2,2,C1), (4,0,A2)].
Stitch B1 after the current tail (the first 1), so the chain reads 1->1.
tail advances to B1, the second node with value 1.
B1.next is the node 3, so list 1 has more to give.
Third round: pop (2, 2, C1), the only node of list 2. heap = [(3,1,B2), (4,0,A2)].
Stitch C1 on: the chain is now 1->1->2.
tail advances onto C1 (value 2).
C1.next is None — list 2 is exhausted, so nothing is pushed and the heap shrinks to 2.
Fourth round: pop (3, 1, B2), value 3 from list 1. heap = [(4,0,A2)].
Stitch B2 on: the chain is 1->1->2->3.
tail advances onto B2 (value 3).
B2.next is None, so list 1 is finished too — no push.
Fifth round: pop the last candidate (4, 0, A2). The heap is now empty.
Stitch A2 on: the chain is 1->1->2->3->4.
tail advances onto A2 (value 4), the final node of the answer.
A2.next is None — list 0 is drained as well, so no new candidate is pushed.
The while condition is re-checked: the heap is empty, so all 5 nodes have been placed and the loop exits.
Cut the tail: A2.next was already None here, but in general the last node can still point into its original list, which would corrupt the answer.
Return dummy.next, which is A1 — the head of the merged list 1->1->2->3->4.

Find Median from Data Stream.desc: Constructor: `low` starts empty. It will be a max-heap of the smaller half, holding NEGATED values.
`high` also starts empty. It is a plain min-heap holding the larger half as-is.
addNum(1): push -1 into low. Negating turns heapq's min-heap into a max-heap, so low = [-1] represents the value 1.
Pop low's root -1 (the value 1), negate it back to 1, and push it into high. Now low = [] and high = [1].
len(high) = 1 is greater than len(low) = 0, so the halves are lopsided and we must rebalance.
Move high's minimum 1 back: push -1 into low. Now low = [-1] (value 1) and high = [], satisfying 'low is one bigger'.
addNum(2): push -2 into low. Since -2 < -1 it sifts to the root: low = [-2, -1], i.e. the max of the small half is now 2.
Pop low's root -2 (value 2), negate to 2, push into high. low = [-1] (value 1), high = [2]. Every low value is now <= every high value.
len(high) = 1 is not greater than len(low) = 1, so the halves are already balanced — no rebalance.
findMedian(): len(low) = 1 is not greater than len(high) = 1, so the count is even and there are two middles.
Average the two roots: -low[0] = 1 and high[0] = 2, so the median is (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5.
addNum(3): push -3 into low. -3 is the smallest stored value so it becomes the root: low = [-3, -1], meaning the small half now holds {1, 3}.
Pop low's root -3 (value 3) and push 3 into high. low = [-1] (value 1), high = [2, 3] — 3 correctly landed in the big half.
len(high) = 2 is greater than len(low) = 1, so high has grown too large and one element must come back.
Pop high's minimum 2 and push -2 into low. Now low = [-2, -1] (values 2 and 1) and high = [3]; sizes are 2 and 1.
findMedian(): len(low) = 2 IS greater than len(high) = 1, so the count is odd and low carries the extra element.
The median is low's root negated: -(-2) = 2.0. Sorted the stream is [1, 2, 3], whose middle is indeed 2.

Implement Trie II.desc: insert("cat") begins: node points at the root, the node standing for the empty prefix "".
root.cnt_prefix goes 0 -> 1. "" is a prefix of every word, so this counter is simply "how many words the trie holds".
First character ch='c'. root.children is empty, so 'c' is not there yet - no word has ever used the prefix "c".
Grow the branch lazily: a brand new TrieNode is created for prefix "c" and hung under the root.
Descend into "c" and bump its cnt_prefix to 1: exactly one stored word ("cat" so far) passes through the prefix "c".
ch='a' is missing under "c", so a new node is created for the prefix "ca".
Descend into "ca" and set its cnt_prefix to 1 - one word so far walks through "ca".
ch='t' is missing under "ca", so the node for the prefix "cat" is created.
Descend into "cat" and set cnt_prefix = 1. The character loop is now finished.
The word ends here, so cnt_end at the "cat" node becomes 1. Trie now stores exactly one word.
insert("car") starts the same way: root.cnt_prefix 1 -> 2, because the trie will now hold two words.
ch='c': this time root.children already contains 'c', so the condition is False and NO new node is made - the branch is shared.
