Descend into the existing "c" node; its cnt_prefix rises to 2 because "cat" and "car" both pass through it.
Same for "ca": reuse the node and lift cnt_prefix to 2. Two words share the prefix "ca".
ch='r': the "ca" node only has the child 't' (from "cat"), so 'r' is missing - here is where the two words diverge.
A new node for the prefix "car" is created as a second child of "ca", branching away from "cat".
Descend into "car"; its cnt_prefix is 1 - only one stored word walks through this fresh prefix.
cnt_end at the "car" node becomes 1. The trie now stores cat and car, sharing the "ca" spine.
insert("card"): root.cnt_prefix 2 -> 3. Note "car" is a prefix of "card", so the two will stack on one path.
Reuse "c" and raise cnt_prefix to 3 - all three stored words start with the letter c.
Reuse "ca" and raise cnt_prefix to 3 as well; the shared path is being walked, not rebuilt.
Reuse the "car" node: cnt_prefix 1 -> 2 while cnt_end stays 1. Two words pass through "car", but only one ends there.
ch='d' is not a child of "car", so the node for prefix "card" is created one level deeper.
Descend into "card" and set cnt_prefix = 1 - it is used by exactly one word.
cnt_end at "card" becomes 1. Stored multiset is now {cat, car, card} on a shared c-a spine.
countWordsEqualTo("car") delegates to _walk("car") to find the node that represents the whole word.
_walk starts at the root with ch='c'; it IS in root.children, so this is not a dead end and the walk continues.
The walk descends c -> a -> r and lands on the node for the prefix "car", the same node insert built.
_walk returns the "car" node itself (cnt_prefix=2, cnt_end=1) back to the caller.
The node exists, so the answer is its cnt_end = 1: exactly one stored word equals "car". "card" passes through but does not end here.
countWordsStartingWith("car") runs the very same _walk("car") helper - only the counter it reads differs.
The walk again ends on the "car" node after descending the shared path c -> a -> r.
Here we read cnt_prefix = 2, not cnt_end: both "car" and "card" start with "car", so the answer is 2.
erase("card") first guards itself: countWordsEqualTo("card") is 1, not 0, so the word really is present and we may subtract.
node is reset to the root; erase mirrors insert exactly but subtracts instead of adding.
root.cnt_prefix drops 3 -> 2: the trie is about to hold two words instead of three.
ch='c': child = root.children['c']. The path is guaranteed to exist because the guard already found the word.
The "c" node loses one passer-by: cnt_prefix 3 -> 2.
c.cnt_prefix is 2, not 0, so "cat" and "car" still live below - nothing may be pruned here.
Keep descending: node = the "c" node, and the loop moves on to ch='a'.
"ca" also loses one: cnt_prefix 3 -> 2, still non-zero, so no pruning and the descent continues to 'r'.
"car" drops from 2 to 1 passer-by. cnt_end there is still 1, because the word "car" itself is untouched.
Not zero, so node = the "car" node and we take the last character ch='d'.
child = the "card" node, reached through the 'd' edge hanging off "car".
card.cnt_prefix falls 1 -> 0: no stored word uses the prefix "card" any more.
cnt_prefix hit 0, so this is the pruning case - the whole subtree from here down is dead weight.
del node.children["d"] unhooks the "card" node from "car"; the dead branch disappears from the trie entirely.
Return early: everything below the cut is already gone, so no further counters need touching. The trie now holds cat and car.

Maximum XOR of Two Numbers.desc: Input nums = [5, 12, 9, 2, 7]. The biggest value is 12 = 1100, whose bit_length is 4, so high = 3: every number is handled as the 4-bit pattern 5=0101, 12=1100, 9=1001, 2=0010, 7=0111.
The trie starts as a single root, node 0, with children[0] = [-1, -1]: neither a 0-branch nor a 1-branch exists yet. 'node' is just an index into children.
PHASE 1, insertion 1 of 5: num = 5, bit pattern 0101. Its four bits will be laid out as a root-to-depth-4 path.
node = 0: every insertion restarts at the root of the trie.
The bit loop counts down b = 3, 2, 1, 0 — most significant bit first, because a high bit is worth more than every lower bit combined.
bit = (5 >> 3) & 1 = 0: the leading bit of 0101 is 0, so num 5 belongs on the root's 0-branch.
children[0][0] == -1: the root has no 0-branch at all yet, so this branch has to be built.
Node 1 was allocated on line 10 and line 11 links it in as children[0][0] = 1. The trie now has a 0-branch hanging off the root.
node = children[0][0] = 1. We have descended one level and stand on the node that all numbers starting with bit 0 will share.
Bits b = 2, 1, 0 of 5 are 1, 0, 1 and none of those branches exists yet, so line 11 runs three more times, creating nodes 2, 3 and 4. The path root -> 0 -> 1 -> 0 -> 1 now spells out 5.
Insertion 2 of 5: num = 12, bit pattern 1100. It starts with bit 1 while 5 started with 0, so it will share nothing with the path just built.
children[0][1] was -1, and so was every branch below it, so all four bits of 12 create new nodes 5, 6, 7, 8. The trie now has two completely separate top-level subtrees: 0... and 1...
Insertion 3 of 5: num = 9, bit pattern 1001. Its leading bit is 1, the same as 12, so this insertion finally reuses part of an existing path.
b = 3, bit = 1, and children[0][1] = 5 is NOT -1, so line 9 is false and nothing is allocated: node = 5, reusing the branch 12 already built.
At b = 2 the paths split: 12 has bit 1 there, 9 has bit 0, so children[5][0] is created. Nodes 9, 10, 11 finish 9's path 1 -> 0 -> 0 -> 1. Shared prefix, then a fork.
Insertion 4 of 5: num = 2, bit pattern 0010, which begins with 0 just like 5.
b = 3, bit = 0, children[0][0] = 1 already exists, so we simply descend: node = 1, the node 5 created.
2 and 5 diverge immediately at b = 2 (2 has bit 0, 5 has bit 1), so nodes 12, 13, 14 are created for the rest of 0 -> 0 -> 1 -> 0.
Insertion 5 of 5: num = 7, bit pattern 0111. It shares the two-bit prefix 01 with 5, the longest reuse so far.
b = 3 bit 0 descends into existing node 1, then b = 2 bit 1 descends into existing node 2 — line 12 runs twice with no allocation, because 5 = 0101 already paved 01.
At b = 1, 7 has bit 1 where 5 had 0, so the paths fork here: nodes 15 and 16 complete 0 -> 1 -> 1 -> 1. All five numbers are now stored; the trie has 17 nodes.
PHASE 1 is done. best = 0 will hold the largest XOR found. From here the trie is read-only: each number walks down looking for the partner that disagrees with it as early as possible.
PHASE 2, query 1 of 5: num = 5 = 0101 asks the trie for its best partner.
node = 0 and cur = 0: restart at the root and build this number's XOR value one bit at a time, from the top.
b = 3 is the most valuable position — winning it is worth 8, more than all lower bits together. bit = (5 >> 3) & 1 = 0, so want = 1: we need a stored number whose leading bit is 1.
children[0][1] = 5, not -1 — 12 and 9 both start with bit 1 — so the greedy branch really is available.
cur |= 1 << 3, so cur = 8: this XOR is guaranteed to have its top bit set.
node = children[0][1] = 5. We are now inside the subtree of numbers 12 and 9, the ones that disagree with 5 at the top.
b = 2: bit of 5 here is 1, so want = 0. Among {12 = 1100, 9 = 1001} we need one with a 0 at this position — that is 9.
children[5][0] exists (9's path), so cur |= 1 << 2 and cur = 12. Two bits won in a row.
node = children[5][0] = 9. Only the stored number 9 lives below this node now.
b = 1: bit of 5 is 0, so want = 1. But everything under this node is the single number 9 = 1001, whose bit here is 0.
children[9][1] == -1: no stored number can disagree with us here, so the greedy branch is unavailable and this XOR bit is forced to 0.
node = children[9][0] = 10. cur stays 12 — we keep walking so the remaining bits can still be decided.
b = 0: bit of 5 is 1, want = 0, but 9 ends in 1, so line 20 fails again and node = children[10][1] = 11. The walk ends with cur = 12, which is exactly 5 XOR 9.
cur = 12 > best = 0, so num 5's best partner beats everything seen so far (there was nothing).
best = 12. Note the answer is NOT settled: the very next number will beat this.
Query 2 of 5: num = 12 = 1100 walks the trie from the root again.
b = 3: bit is 1, want = 0, and children[0][0] = 1 exists (5, 2 and 7 all start with 0). cur = 8, node = 1.
b = 2: bit is 1, want = 0, and children[1][0] = 12 exists (that is 2 = 0010). cur = 12, node = 12.
b = 1: bit is 0, want = 1, and 2 = 0010 has a 1 exactly there, so children[12][1] = 13 exists. cur = 14, node = 13. Three bits won.
b = 0: bit is 0, want = 1, but 2 ends in 0, so the last bit is forced and node = children[13][0] = 14. cur finishes at 14 = 12 XOR 2 = 1100 XOR 0010 = 1110.
cur = 14 > best = 12, so best = 14 — the pair (12, 2) overtakes (5, 9).
The remaining queries change nothing: 9 greedily finds 7 (9 ^ 7 = 14), 2 finds 12 (14) and 7 finds 9 (14). Each cur = 14 is not > best = 14.
Every number has queried the trie, so return best = 14. Total work was 5 inserts + 5 queries of 4 bits each, not the 10 pairs a brute force would test.

Maximum XOR Queries.desc: Sort nums ascending: [5, 12, 2, 9, 7] becomes [2, 5, 7, 9, 12]. Now the elements legal for a limit m are always a prefix of this array, which is what makes the offline trick work.
Sort the three query ids by their limit m: query 1 has m = 1, query 0 has m = 6, query 2 has m = 15, so order = [1, 0, 2]. We carry ids, never losing the output positions.
top = max(nums) = 12, the widest element the trie has to hold so far.
Scan the queries' x values as well: the first is x = 13, and 13 > top = 12.
top becomes 13. Sizing the trie on nums alone would have truncated the top bit of x = 13; the remaining x values 3 and 9 are both smaller, so top stays 13.
BITS = 13.bit_length() = 4, so every value is spelled as a 4-bit root-to-leaf path, MSB first: 2 = 0010, 5 = 0101, 7 = 0111, 9 = 1001, 12 = 1100.
ans = [-1, -1, -1]: the sentinel already encodes 'no element was <= m', and children = [[-1, -1]] is a lone empty root with added = 0 elements inserted.
First id in order is qi = 1, the query with the smallest limit m = 1.
Query 1 is x = 3, m = 1. The smallest element nums[0] = 2 is already larger than m = 1, so the while loop inserts nothing.
added is still 0, so the trie is genuinely empty: no element of nums is <= 1, and this query has no legal partner at all.
continue - we skip the greedy walk entirely and ans[1] keeps its sentinel -1.
Next id in order is qi = 0, the query with limit m = 6.
Unpack it: x = 13, m = 6. Elements 2 and 5 are <= 6, so exactly those two must enter the trie now.
nums[0] = 2 <= 6, so element 2 becomes legal and is inserted permanently - the trie only ever grows.
v = 2, whose 4-bit spelling is 0-0-1-0, and insertion starts at node 0, the root.
b = 3: bit = (2 >> 3) & 1 = 0, so 2 belongs on the root's 0-branch.
children[0][0] is -1, the branch is missing, so a fresh empty node is appended - it becomes node 1.
node = 1. Bits b = 2, 1, 0 of 2 are 0, 1, 0 and every one of those branches is missing too, so nodes 2, 3 and 4 are created in turn; node ends at 4.
nums[1] = 5 <= 6 as well, so 5 is inserted next.
v = 5, spelled 0-1-0-1. This is where a shared prefix finally matters.
b = 3: bit of 5 is 0 and children[0][0] is already 1, not -1, so nothing is built - 2 and 5 share the root's 0-branch.
b = 2: bit = (5 >> 2) & 1 = 1, whereas 2 had a 0 here. This is the position where the two values diverge.
children[1][1] is -1, so node 5 is created as 5's own branch off the shared prefix.
Bits 0 and 1 finish the path, adding nodes 6 and 7. added = 2: the trie now holds exactly {2, 5}.
nums[2] = 7 is greater than m = 6, so insertion stops here - elements 7, 9 and 12 are not legal for this query.
added = 2 is not 0, so an answer exists. Start the greedy walk for x = 13 at the root with cur = 0.
children[0][0] = 1 is not -1 - both legal elements 2 and 5 start with 0, so the greedy branch is available.
cur |= 1 << 3, so cur = 8 - the most significant bit of the answer is already secured.
b = 2: bit of 13 is 1 so want = 0, and children[1][0] = 2 exists - that is the branch element 2 took, while 5 went the other way.
cur |= 4, so cur = 12. Only element 2 is still reachable below us.
b = 1: bit of 13 is 0 so want = 1, and 2 does carry a 1 there, giving cur = 14; b = 0: want = 0 and 2 ends in 0, so cur = 15. Every bit of 13 got flipped.
ans[0] = 15, written back at the ORIGINAL index 0 even though we answered this query second. Check: 13 ^ 2 = 15 beats 13 ^ 5 = 8.
Last id in order is qi = 2: x = 9, m = 15. Every element is <= 15, so the remaining three get inserted.
v = 7 = 0111 shares the prefix 0-1 with 5 and then diverges, so only nodes 8 and 9 are appended.
9 = 1001 needs the root's missing 1-branch, creating nodes 10 to 13; 12 = 1100 reuses node 10 and adds 14, 15, 16. added = 5, so all of {2, 5, 7, 9, 12} are in the trie.
added = 5 = len(nums), so the while loop is done. Restart the greedy walk at the root with cur = 0, now for x = 9 = 1001.
b = 3: bit of 9 is 1 so want = 0, and children[0][0] = 1 exists because 2, 5 and 7 all start with a 0 bit.
cur = 8. The candidate set has narrowed to {2, 5, 7}.
node = 1. For b = 2 the bit of 9 is 0 so want = 1, taken by {5, 7}, giving cur = 12; for b = 1 want = 1 again and only 7 offers it, giving cur = 14 at node 8.
b = 0: bit of 9 is 1 so want = 0, but children[8][0] is -1 - the only reachable element, 7 = 0111, also ends in 1.
Forced branch: no legal element can flip this last bit, so the greedy choice is simply unavailable.
node = children[8][1] = 9 and cur stays 14 - that final XOR bit is 0.
Return ans = [15, -1, 14], back in the original query order even though we processed them as 1, 0, 2.

LFU Cache.desc: We build LFUCache(2): cap = 2, so at most two keys may live in the cache at any moment.
freq_keys is a defaultdict of OrderedDicts: bucket f will list every key used exactly f times, oldest at the front.
Call put(1, 1). The key is new, and len(key_val) = 0 is not >= cap = 2, so no eviction is needed.
key_val[1] = 1 — the value is now cached.
key_freq[1] = 1: creating a key counts as its first use.
freq_keys[1] becomes an OrderedDict containing key 1, so bucket 1 = [1].
min_freq = 1. Inserting a new key ALWAYS resets the minimum, because nothing can have a smaller count than 1.
Call put(2, 2). Again new, and size 1 is still below cap 2, so no eviction.
After storing the value and frequency, key 2 is appended to bucket 1, which is now [1, 2] — key 1 is older, key 2 is newer.
Call get(1). Key 1 is present, so it is a hit and we must record the extra use via _bump(1).
Inside _bump: f = key_freq[1] = 1, so key 1 currently lives in bucket 1.
Delete key 1 from bucket 1: freq_keys[1] is now [2]. Deleting from an OrderedDict by key is O(1).
Bucket 1 still holds key 2, so it is NOT empty — min_freq stays 1 and no bucket is deleted.
key_freq[1] = 2: key 1 has now been used twice.
Key 1 is appended to bucket 2, so freq_keys = {1: [2], 2: [1]}. get returns the cached value 1.
Call put(3, 3). Key 3 is new and len(key_val) = 2 >= cap = 2, so somebody must go.
Evict from bucket min_freq = 1. popitem(last=False) takes its OLDEST member, which is key 2 — the only key used just once.
del key_val[2] and del key_freq[2]: key 2 is completely gone, which is why a later get(2) will return -1.
Bucket 1 is empty now, so it is deleted. Leaving an empty bucket behind would break the next eviction.
Now insert key 3 with value 3 and frequency 1.
min_freq is reset to 1 because key 3 has count 1 — even though key 1 sits at count 2.
Call get(2). Key 2 is not in key_val, so this is a miss.
get(2) returns -1, and nothing about frequencies or min_freq is touched by a miss.
Call get(3): key 3 is present, so _bump(3) runs.
Removing key 3 leaves bucket 1 empty AND f = 1 equals min_freq, so this is the case where the minimum must move.
min_freq = 2. The bumped key itself is the least-used key now, so the new minimum is exactly f + 1 — never 1.
Key 3 joins bucket 2 AFTER key 1, so freq_keys = {2: [1, 3]}: key 1 is the older member. get(3) returns 3.
Call put(4, 4). Key 4 is new and the cache is full again, so we must evict.
Both surviving keys have frequency 2, so the tie is broken by recency: popitem(last=False) on bucket 2 removes the OLDER key, which is key 1.
Key 1 is deleted from key_val and key_freq. Bucket 2 still holds key 3, so it is not removed.
Insert key 4 with value 4.
min_freq drops back to 1 because the fresh key 4 has count 1. Final state: freq_keys = {1: [4], 2: [3]}.
get(1) now returns -1 (key 1 was evicted), while get(3) returns 3 and get(4) returns 4 — exactly the expected LFU behaviour.

Online Stock Span.desc: Construct the spanner: the monotonic stack starts empty. Incoming prices will be 100, 80, 60, 70, 75.
Call 1 with price = 100. span starts at 1 because today always counts.
The while condition fails immediately: the stack is empty, so there is nothing to absorb. Checking 'self.stack' first is what prevents an IndexError.
Push (100, 1) — day 1 represents itself only.
Return 1: the span of the very first day is always 1.
Call 2 with price = 80. span resets to 1 for this new day.
Top of stack is 100, and 100 <= 80 is false, so nothing is absorbed — day 1 is strictly more expensive and stops the walk.
Push (80, 1). The stack is [(100, 1), (80, 1)], still strictly decreasing from bottom to top.
Return 1 for price 80.
Call 3 with price = 60. span = 1 again.
Top price is 80 and 80 <= 60 is false, so again nothing is popped.
Push (60, 1): stack = [(100, 1), (80, 1), (60, 1)]. Three falling days means three entries and three spans of 1.
Return 1 for price 60.
Call 4 with price = 70 — the first day that will actually absorb something. span starts at 1.
The stack is non-empty and its top price 60 is <= 70, so that day is absorbed: we enter the loop.
Pop (60, 1). That popped span of 1 tells us the entry represented exactly one day.
span = 1 + 1 = 2: today plus the day it swallowed. Day 3 can never matter again, because any future price that beats 60 must first get past 70.
Loop again: the new top price is 80, and 80 <= 70 is false, so the absorption stops here.
Push (70, 2): this single entry now stands for two days. Stack = [(100, 1), (80, 1), (70, 2)].
Return 2 — days 3 and 4 both had prices <= 70.
Call 5 with price = 75. span = 1 to begin with.
Top price 70 is <= 75, so this block gets absorbed too.
Pop (70, 2). Notice we absorb TWO days in one pop — this is why the stored span matters instead of re-walking day by day.
span = 1 + 2 = 3: today plus the two days that entry summarised (days 3 and 4).
Check again: the top price is now 80 and 80 <= 75 is false, so we stop. Day 2 is the previous strictly greater day.
Push (75, 3). Stack = [(100, 1), (80, 1), (75, 3)] — still strictly decreasing, and three entries summarise five days.
Return 3 for price 75: days 3, 4 and 5 all had prices <= 75, and day 2's 80 stopped the count.

Power Set.desc: Input s = "dbca", so n = 4. Bit 0 of a mask will mean "keep d", bit 1 "keep b", bit 2 "keep c", bit 3 "keep a".
result = [] will collect all 2^4 - 1 = 15 non-empty subsequences before they get sorted.
mask = 1 = 0001 in binary, the first of the 15 masks. Only bit 0 is on, so this mask should keep just s[0] = 'd'.
pick = [] — a fresh empty basket for the characters this mask (0001) decides to keep.
Inner loop starts at i = 0, so we are asking whether s[0] = 'd' belongs to mask 1.
mask & (1 << 0) = 1 & 1 = 1, a non-zero value, so bit 0 IS switched on and 'd' is kept.
pick.append(s[0]) puts 'd' into the basket, so pick = ['d'] for mask 0001.
i = 1: mask & (1 << 1) = 1 & 2 = 0, so bit 1 is off and 'b' is dropped from this subsequence.
i = 2: mask & 4 = 1 & 4 = 0, so 'c' is dropped as well; the basket still holds only 'd'.
i = 3: mask & 8 = 1 & 8 = 0, so the last character 'a' is dropped and the inner loop is finished.
''.join(['d']) = "d" is appended, so result now holds its first subsequence: ["d"].
mask = 2 = 0010. Only bit 1 is on this time, which points at s[1] = 'b'.
i = 1: mask & (1 << 1) = 2 & 2 = 2, non-zero, so 'b' is the single character this mask keeps.
pick.append(s[1]) makes pick = ['b']; bits 0, 2 and 3 all tested zero for mask 0010.
Result grows to ["d", "b"] — note it is being built in mask order, which is NOT alphabetical order.
mask = 3 = 0011. Two bits are on at once, so for the first time this mask keeps TWO characters.
pick = [] is reset before scanning mask 0011; every mask starts from an empty basket.
i = 0: 3 & 1 = 1, bit 0 is on, so s[0] = 'd' is kept first.
pick = ['d'] after appending s[0]; the scan continues left to right so order is preserved.
i = 1: 3 & 2 = 2, bit 1 is on too, so s[1] = 'b' joins the same subsequence.
pick = ['d', 'b'] — 'd' before 'b' because i walks the string left to right, never rearranging.
Joined into "db" and appended, so result = ["d", "b", "db"] after three masks.
mask = 4 = 0100. The bits that are on select s[2]='c'.
The inner loop collected "c", which becomes entry number 4 of result.
mask = 5 = 0101. The bits that are on select s[0]='d', s[2]='c'.
The inner loop collected "dc", which becomes entry number 5 of result.
mask = 6 = 0110. The bits that are on select s[1]='b', s[2]='c'.
The inner loop collected "bc", which becomes entry number 6 of result.
mask = 7 = 0111. The bits that are on select s[0]='d', s[1]='b', s[2]='c'.
The inner loop collected "dbc", which becomes entry number 7 of result.
mask = 8 = 1000 keeps "a"; result is now 8 subsequences long and still unsorted.
mask = 9 = 1001 keeps "da"; result is now 9 subsequences long and still unsorted.
mask = 10 = 1010 keeps "ba"; result is now 10 subsequences long and still unsorted.
mask = 11 = 1011 keeps "dba"; result is now 11 subsequences long and still unsorted.
mask = 12 = 1100 keeps "ca"; result is now 12 subsequences long and still unsorted.
mask = 13 = 1101 keeps "dca"; result is now 13 subsequences long and still unsorted.
mask = 14 = 1110 keeps "bca"; result is now 14 subsequences long and still unsorted.
mask = 15 = 1111 keeps "dbca"; result is now 15 subsequences long and still unsorted.
All 15 masks are done. result.sort() reshuffles ["d", "b", "db", "c"]... into dictionary order, so "a" jumps from position 8 to position 1.
Return the 15 sorted subsequences of "dbca": a, b, ba, bc, bca, c, ca, d, da, db, dba, dbc, dbca, dc, dca.

Maximum XOR Subarray.desc: Input arr = [1, 2, 3, 4]. The array is not empty, so we skip the guard and continue.
The largest element is 4 = 100, which needs 3 bits, so BITS = 3. Every prefix XOR of these numbers also fits in 3 bits.
Create the trie with only the root, node 0, and both branches missing.
Now seed the trie with the prefix value 0 (binary 000): nodes 1, 2 and 3 are created along the all-zero path. Without this seed, no subarray could start at index 0.
prefix = 0 before the sweep starts.
best = 0, the floor for an all-non-negative array.
Iteration 1: num = arr[0] = 1.
prefix ^= 1 makes prefix = 1 (binary 001): the XOR of everything up to index 0.
Start the greedy query walk at the root. Only the seeded prefix 0 is stored so far.
cur = 0: the XOR value we will build bit by bit for prefix = 1.
b = 2: our bit is (1 >> 2) & 1 = 0, so want = 1 — we hope for a stored prefix with a 1 in the 4s place.
children[0][1] is -1 — the only stored prefix is 0, which has no 1 bits at all. The wish fails.
Forced into the matching branch: node = 1, and the 4s bit of cur stays 0. The same happens at b = 1, taking us to node 2.
At b = 0 our bit is 1 so want = 0, and children[2][0] = 3 exists (the last 0 of the seeded prefix). cur |= 1 gives cur = 1 — that is 1 ^ 0, the subarray [1].
cur = 1 beats best = 0.
best = 1, achieved by the subarray [1].
Now insert prefix = 1 (001) so later positions can pair with it. The first two 0 bits reuse nodes 1 and 2; only the final 1 bit needs a new node 4.
Iteration 2: num = arr[1] = 2.
prefix = 1 ^ 2 = 3 (binary 011), the XOR of arr[0..1].
Query for 3 = 011. At b = 2 our bit is 0, want = 1, but children[0][1] is still -1, so we are forced to node 1 with cur = 0.
At b = 1 our bit is 1, want = 0, and children[1][0] = 2 exists (from prefix 0), so cur = 2 and node = 2. At b = 0 our bit is 1, want = 0, and children[2][0] = 3 exists, so cur = 3.
cur = 3 (that is prefix 3 ^ the seeded prefix 0) beats best = 1, so best = 3 — the subarray [1, 2].
Insert prefix 3 (011): it shares only the top 0 bit with what is stored, so nodes 5 and 6 are created. The trie now holds {0, 1, 3}.
Iteration 3: num = arr[2] = 3.
prefix = 3 ^ 3 = 0. The whole array so far XORs to zero — which is a real signal: it means arr[0..2] itself has XOR 0.
Query for 0 = 000: at b = 2 want = 1 fails again, but at b = 1 children[1][1] = 5 exists (from prefix 3) and at b = 0 children[5][1] = 6 exists, giving cur = 3 (0 ^ 3).
cur = 3 is not greater than best = 3, so best is unchanged.
Insert prefix 0 again. Every bit reuses the existing all-zero path 1 -> 2 -> 3, so no new node is allocated — duplicates are harmless.
Iteration 4: num = arr[3] = 4, the last element.
prefix = 0 ^ 4 = 4 (binary 100), the XOR of the whole array.
b = 2: our bit is 1 this time, so want = 0 — and children[0][0] = 1 certainly exists.
cur |= 4 gives cur = 4 and node = 1. At b = 1 our bit is 0, want = 1, children[1][1] = 5 exists (prefix 3), so cur = 6 and node = 5.
At b = 0 our bit is 0, want = 1, children[5][1] = 6 exists, so cur = 7. The chosen partner is the stored prefix 3.
cur = 7 beats best = 3.
best = 7. The partner prefix 3 was the value right after index 1, so the winning subarray is arr[2..3] = [3, 4], and indeed 3 ^ 4 = 7.
The sweep is finished, so we return best = 7 — the maximum XOR of any contiguous block of [1, 2, 3, 4].

Fractional Knapsack.desc: Enter fractionalKnapsack with capacity W = 50 and n = 6 items given in the caller's order: (v120,w30), (v60,w10), (v100,w20), (v90,w30), (v140,w20), (v48,w6). The cells below are the weights in that original order.
The sort key is value/weight. Computing all six ratios: 120/30 = 4.0, 60/10 = 6.0, 100/20 = 5.0, 90/30 = 3.0, 140/20 = 7.0, 48/6 = 8.0. No two items tie, so the greedy order is unambiguous.

After sorting descending by ratio the items are (v48,w6) at 8.0, (v140,w20) at 7.0, (v60,w10) at 6.0, (v100,w20) at 5.0, (v120,w30) at 4.0, (v90,w30) at 3.0. The weight cells are now [6, 20, 10, 20, 30, 30].
total_value starts at 0.0. Keeping it a float from the very beginning means the fractional cut later mixes cleanly instead of surprising us with integer division.
Iteration 1 begins: i = 0, the densest item (value 48, weight 6, ratio 8.0). Remaining capacity is still the full 50.
Does item 0 fit whole? Its weight 6 is compared against remaining capacity 50. 6 <= 50 is True, so we take the entire item.
Take all of item 0: total_value goes from 0.0 to 0.0 + 48 = 48.0.
Charge the weight: W drops from 50 to 50 - 6 = 44 units of remaining capacity.
Iteration 2: i = 1, the item (value 140, weight 20) whose ratio is 7.0. Capacity left is 44.
Compare weight 20 against the remaining capacity 44. 20 <= 44 is True, so this item also goes in whole.
total_value climbs from 48.0 to 48.0 + 140 = 188.0 after loading item (140, 20) completely.
Remaining capacity W falls from 44 to 44 - 20 = 24.
Iteration 3: i = 2, the item (value 60, weight 10) with ratio 6.0, against 24 units of space left.
Weight 10 versus capacity 24: 10 <= 24 is True, so item 2 is the third one taken whole.
total_value rises from 188.0 to 188.0 + 60 = 248.0.
Capacity shrinks from 24 to 24 - 10 = 14. Only 14 units of the knapsack are still empty.
Iteration 4: i = 3, the item (value 100, weight 20) with ratio 5.0. This is the item that will have to be cut.
Now the test fails for the first time: arr[3].weight = 20 is NOT <= W = 14, so the whole-item branch is skipped.
Control falls into the else branch — this is the case that makes the problem fractional rather than 0/1. We take only as much of item 3 as the leftover 14 units allow.
The fraction taken is W / weight = 14 / 20 = 0.7, so we collect 100 * 0.7 = 70.0 value. total_value goes from 248.0 to 318.0.
The knapsack now holds exactly 6 + 20 + 10 + 14 = 50 weight, so it is full and we break. Items 4 (120, 30) and 5 (90, 30) are never even examined.
Return the accumulated maximum value 318.0 for capacity 50 — three whole items plus 70 percent of the (100, 20) item.

Greedy Coin Change.desc: Sort denominations in descending order. coins becomes [1000, 500, 100, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1]
Loop starts: coin = 1000. 70 >= 1000 is False, skip while loop.
Loop continues: coin = 500. 70 >= 500 is False, skip while loop.
Loop continues: coin = 100. 70 >= 100 is False, skip while loop.
Loop continues: coin = 50. 70 >= 50 is True, enter while loop.
Check V >= coin (20 >= 50). False, exit while loop.
Loop continues: coin = 20. 20 >= 20 is True, enter while loop.
Check V >= coin (0 >= 20). False, exit while loop.
Loop finishes, return coin_count and chosen_coins.

Subsets II.desc: Sort the input [3, 1, 2, 2] into [1, 2, 2, 3] so the two copies of 2 sit next to each other.
result starts empty; every subset the walk visits gets copied into it.
Kick off the walk with backtrack(0, []): index 0 is the first usable element, nothing chosen yet.
Record the empty subset [] — each call records whatever it is holding before it branches.
Loop i from start = 0 to 3; the first candidate is nums[0] = 1.
Choose 1: current_subset = [1].
Recurse with backtrack(1, [1]) so only elements after index 0 can extend this subset.
Record [1]; result now holds 2 subsets.
At start = 1 the first candidate is nums[1] = 2, the first of the two 2s.
Choose that 2: current_subset = [1, 2].
Recurse with backtrack(2, [1, 2]).
Record [1, 2]; result_size is now 3.
i = 2 equals start = 2, so the duplicate guard i > start is false and this second 2 is allowed.
Choose the second 2: current_subset = [1, 2, 2] — legal, because the two 2s are at different depths.
Recurse with backtrack(3, [1, 2, 2]).
Record [1, 2, 2]; result_size is 4.
Choose nums[3] = 3: current_subset = [1, 2, 2, 3], the whole multiset.
Record [1, 2, 2, 3] in the deepest call (start = 4), whose loop range is empty.
Pop the 3, and when the loop at start = 3 ends pop the second 2 as well: back to [1, 2].
Back at start = 2 with i = 3: i > start holds, but nums[3] = 3 differs from nums[2] = 2, so no skip.
Choose 3 as the sibling of the popped 2: current_subset = [1, 2, 3].
Record [1, 2, 3]; result_size is 6.
Pop the 3, then pop the first 2 when that loop finishes: current_subset is back to [1].
Now i = 2 at start = 1: i > start is true AND nums[2] == nums[1] == 2 — this is the duplicate case.
continue skips this 2 entirely; taking it here would rebuild [1, 2] which is already in result.
i = 3 instead: choose 3, giving current_subset = [1, 3].
Record [1, 3]; result_size is 7.
Pop the 3, then pop the 1: the walk is back at the empty subset in the top-level call.
Top level, i = 1: i > start = 0 is true, but nums[1] = 2 differs from nums[0] = 1, so 2 may start a branch.
Choose 2: current_subset = [2], opening the branch of subsets that contain no 1.
Record [2]; result_size is 8.
Inside backtrack(2, [2]) the second 2 is allowed because i == start = 2: current_subset = [2, 2].
Record [2, 2]; result_size is 9.
Extend once more with 3: current_subset = [2, 2, 3].
Record [2, 2, 3]; result_size is 10.
Pop the 3 and then the second 2, unwinding back to [2].
Try the sibling 3 at i = 3: current_subset = [2, 3].
Record [2, 3]; result_size is 11.
Pop the 3 and then the 2: current_subset is empty again at the top level.
Top level i = 2: nums[2] == nums[1] == 2 and i > start = 0, so this whole branch is a repeat.
continue prunes it — without this line every subset starting with 2 would be produced twice.
Last candidate i = 3: choose 3, giving current_subset = [3].
Record [3]; result_size is 12.
The loop is exhausted: return all 12 unique subsets, with [2] and [1, 2] appearing exactly once each.

Combination Sum.desc: candidates [7,3,2,6,5] are sorted in place to [2,3,5,6,7]; ascending order is what makes the prune-and-break at line 15 legal.
result starts empty. It will collect every distinct multiset of candidates adding up to 6.
Kick off the search: backtrack(start=0, path=[], remaining_target=6). start=0 means every candidate is still allowed.
Top frame, i=0: the candidate under consideration is candidates[0] = 2.
2 <= 6 so it is usable: append 2, path becomes [2].
Recurse with start=i=0 (2 may be reused) and remaining 6-2 = 4.
Inside backtrack(0,[2],4): i=0 again, 2 <= 4, so a second 2 is pushed. path = [2,2].
Recurse again: backtrack(0, [2,2], 2). The same element is being reused, which the problem allows.
i=0 once more: 2 <= 2, push a third 2 so path = [2,2,2].
Recurse into backtrack(0, [2,2,2], 0) - the remaining target has just been driven to zero.
remaining_target == 0 is finally True: the path [2,2,2] sums to exactly 6.
A COPY of the path is appended to result - list(current_combination) matters, because the live path is about to be mutated by the pops.
Return from this frame; the search rewinds to the caller backtrack(0,[2,2],2) at i=0.
The undo step: pop the third 2, so path shrinks back to [2,2] before the loop tries a sibling.
Sibling i=1 in frame backtrack(0,[2,2],2): candidates[1]=3 exceeds the remaining 2, and since the array is sorted everything further right is worse - break out of the loop.
That frame is done, so its caller backtrack(0,[2],4) pops the second 2: path = [2].
Back in backtrack(0,[2],4) the loop advances to i=1, candidate 3, with 4 still to cover.
3 <= 4, so push it: path = [2,3].
Recurse backtrack(1, [2,3], 1). start=1 forbids going back to 2, which is how duplicate combinations like [3,2] are avoided.
In that frame i starts at 1: candidates[1]=3 is bigger than the remaining 1, so this path is dead.
break - no candidate from index 1 rightwards can fit into 1, so the frame ends with nothing recorded.
Pop the 3: path returns to [2] and the loop in backtrack(0,[2],4) moves on.
i=2: candidates[2]=5 > remaining 4, so break. Frame backtrack(0,[2],4) is exhausted.
Back in the top frame, pop the first 2 as well: path is empty again and i is about to become 1.
Top frame, i=1: try starting a whole new combination with candidates[1] = 3.
3 <= 6, push it: path = [3].
Recurse backtrack(1, [3], 3) - start=1, so 2 is off the table from now on.
i=1 there: 3 <= 3, push a second 3 giving path = [3,3].
Recurse backtrack(1, [3,3], 0): remaining hits zero again.
Second solution recorded: [3,3] is copied into result.
Pop the second 3 on the way out; path = [3].
In backtrack(1,[3],3) the loop reaches i=2 where candidates[2]=5 > 3, so break.
Top frame pops the 3: path empty, ready for i=2.
Top frame i=2: 5 <= 6 so push 5, path = [5].
Recurse backtrack(2, [5], 1) - only 1 left to cover from candidates 5,6,7.
5 > 1, break immediately: nothing can complete [5] into 6.
Pop the 5, path empty again.
Top frame i=3: candidates[3]=6 <= 6, push it so path = [6].
Recurse backtrack(3, [6], 0): the single candidate 6 already meets the target exactly.
Third solution recorded: [6].
Pop the 6; the top frame's path is empty for the last time.
Top frame i=4: candidates[4]=7 is larger than the full target 6.
break ends the top-level loop as well - the entire search tree has been explored.
Return the three combinations that sum to 6: [2,2,2], [3,3] and [6].

Combination Sum II.desc: candidates = [10,1,2,7,6,1,5] is sorted in place to [1,1,2,5,6,7,10]. Sorting puts the two 1s next to each other (so duplicates can be spotted) and puts big values last (so we can stop early).
result = [] will collect every combination summing to 8. Expect four of them.
Kick off the search: backtrack(start=0, current_combination=[], remaining_target=8).
remaining_target = 8, not 0, so nothing is recorded yet; fall through to the candidate loop.
Loop over i = 0..6. First candidate is i = 0, candidates[0] = 1.
The duplicate guard needs i > start; here i = 0 == start = 0, so the FIRST copy of a value is always allowed through.
Pruning check: candidates[0] = 1 is not greater than remaining_target = 8, so this candidate is usable.
Choose 1: current_combination = [1].
Recurse with start = 1 (each element may be used once) and remaining_target = 8 - 1 = 7.
Depth 2, i = 1: candidates[1] = 1 — the second copy of 1.

candidates[1] == candidates[0], but i = 1 is NOT > start = 1, so this duplicate is kept. That is the whole subtlety: a repeat is banned only as a sibling choice, never as the next position in the path.
Choose the second 1: current_combination = [1, 1], remaining_target still 7 until we recurse.
Recurse with start = 2 and remaining_target = 7 - 1 = 6.
Depth 3, i = 2: candidates[2] = 2, which fits inside remaining_target = 6.
Choose 2: current_combination = [1, 1, 2].
Recurse with start = 3 and remaining_target = 6 - 2 = 4.
Depth 4, i = 3: candidates[3] = 5 > remaining_target = 4. Since the array is sorted, every later candidate is at least 5 too.
break — abandon the whole i = 3..6 tail at once. This is the pruning that sorting bought us.
Backtrack: pop the 2, current_combination = [1, 1] again, remaining_target back to 6.
Next sibling at depth 3: i = 3, candidates[3] = 5, and 5 <= 6, so try it.
Choose 5 -> [1, 1, 5] and recurse with start = 4, remaining_target = 1.
At depth 4, candidates[4] = 6 > 1, so break immediately: [1, 1, 5] is a dead end.
Pop the 5. current_combination = [1, 1], and the loop at depth 3 moves on.
i = 4: candidates[4] = 6 <= 6, so choose it: current_combination = [1, 1, 6].
Recurse with start = 5 and remaining_target = 6 - 6 = 0.
remaining_target == 0 is finally True — the path sums to exactly 8.
Record a COPY of the path: result = [[1, 1, 6]]. Copying matters because current_combination keeps mutating.
Return, then pop the 6: current_combination = [1, 1].
i = 5: candidates[5] = 7 > remaining_target = 6, so break out of depth 3 entirely.
Pop the second 1: current_combination = [1] at depth 2, remaining_target = 7.
i = 2 at depth 2: choose 2 -> [1, 2], recurse with start = 3 and remaining_target = 5.
Depth 3 picks candidates[3] = 5, remaining_target hits 0, so result = [[1, 1, 6], [1, 2, 5]].
Unwind twice: pop 5, then (after 6 and 7 are pruned) pop 2, leaving current_combination = [1].
i = 3 gives [1, 5] (dead end, 6 > 2) and i = 4 gives [1, 6] (dead end, 7 > 1). Now i = 5: choose 7 -> [1, 7].
backtrack(6, [1, 7], 0) hits the base case at once: result = [[1, 1, 6], [1, 2, 5], [1, 7]].
Pop the 7, then i = 6 gives candidates[6] = 10 > 7 and breaks, so pop the leading 1 too: current_combination = [] back at depth 1.
Depth 1, i = 1: now i = 1 > start = 0 AND candidates[1] == candidates[0] == 1. This is a duplicate SIBLING.
continue — skip it. Starting a path with the second 1 would regenerate [1,1,6], [1,2,5] and [1,7] verbatim.
i = 2: choose 2 -> current_combination = [2], recursing with start = 3 and remaining_target = 6.
Inside that branch, 5 fails (6 > 1) but 6 works: result gains [2, 6] and is now [[1,1,6], [1,2,5], [1,7], [2,6]].
Back at depth 1, starts of 5, 6 and 7 all dead-end, and at i = 6 candidates[6] = 10 > 8, so the outermost loop breaks.
Return the four unique combinations: [[1,1,6], [1,2,5], [1,7], [2,6]] — no duplicates, and each element used at most once per combination.

Palindrome Partitioning.desc: s = "cabba", five characters. result starts empty and will collect every way of cutting the string into palindromic pieces.
Kick off the search with backtrack(0, []): nothing consumed yet, the whole string still to cut.
Frame start = 0. The first candidate is i = 0, the substring s[0:1] = "c".
is_palindrome(0, 0): start_idx is not less than end_idx, so the while body never runs and a lone character is trivially a palindrome.
Push "c" onto the path, so current_partition = ["c"].
Recurse into backtrack(1, ["c"]) - the tail "abba" still has to be cut.
Frame start = 1. First candidate is i = 1, the substring s[1:2] = "a".
"a" is a single character so it passes; push it, giving current_partition = ["c", "a"].
Recurse into backtrack(2, ["c", "a"]); the tail left to cut is "bba".
Frame start = 2: candidate i = 2 is s[2:3] = "b", a palindrome, so the path becomes ["c", "a", "b"].
Frame start = 3: candidate "b" passes too, so the path grows to ["c", "a", "b", "b"].
Frame start = 4: the final character "a" is pushed, giving ["c", "a", "b", "b", "a"].
Inside backtrack(5): start = 5 equals len(s) = 5, so every character has been consumed by some palindromic piece.
Record a COPY: result = [["c", "a", "b", "b", "a"]]. Copying matters because the path itself is about to be mutated.
Backtrack: pop "a" in the start = 4 frame, path back to ["c", "a", "b", "b"]. That frame is exhausted and returns.
Back in the start = 3 frame, pop the second "b": the path is ["c", "a", "b"] and a sibling can be tried.
Sibling candidate in the start = 3 frame: i = 4, the substring s[3:5] = "ba".
is_palindrome(3, 4) compares s[3] = 'b' against s[4] = 'a' - they differ on the very first comparison.
return False, so "ba" is rejected: no push, no recursion. The start = 3 frame has no candidates left and returns.
Back in the start = 2 frame, pop "b": the path is ["c", "a"] again.
Sibling candidate in the start = 2 frame: i = 3, the two-character substring s[2:4] = "bb".
is_palindrome(2, 3) compares s[2] = 'b' with s[3] = 'b' - equal, so there is no early exit this time.
The pointers cross to start_idx = 3, end_idx = 2, the loop ends, and "bb" is confirmed as a palindrome.
Push the two-character piece: current_partition = ["c", "a", "bb"].
Recurse into backtrack(4, ["c", "a", "bb"]) - this branch jumps two characters at once, unlike the previous one.
Frame start = 4: the trailing "a" is a palindrome, so the path becomes ["c", "a", "bb", "a"].
start reaches 5 again, so a second partition is recorded: ["c", "a", "bb", "a"] joins the result list.
Pop "a" in the start = 4 frame; the path is back to ["c", "a", "bb"].
Back in the start = 2 frame, pop "bb": the path is ["c", "a"].
Last candidate in the start = 2 frame: i = 4, the substring s[2:5] = "bba".
is_palindrome(2, 4) compares s[2] = 'b' with s[4] = 'a', they differ, so "bba" is rejected and the start = 2 frame is finished.
Back in the start = 1 frame, pop "a": the path is just ["c"].
Sibling candidate in the start = 1 frame: i = 2, the substring s[1:3] = "ab".
s[1] = 'a' differs from s[2] = 'b', so "ab" is not a palindrome and this whole branch is pruned before any recursion happens.
Next candidate in the same frame: i = 3, the substring s[1:4] = "abb".
is_palindrome(1, 3) compares s[1] = 'a' with s[3] = 'b' - different, so "abb" is rejected too.
Final candidate in the start = 1 frame: i = 4, the whole tail s[1:5] = "abba".
is_palindrome(1, 4): s[1] = 'a' matches s[4] = 'a', so the two pointers move inward to start_idx = 2 and end_idx = 3.
s[2] = 'b' matches s[3] = 'b', the pointers cross, and the four-character "abba" is confirmed a palindrome.
Push the whole tail as one piece: current_partition = ["c", "abba"].
backtrack(5) fires immediately and records the third partition, ["c", "abba"].
Pop "abba"; the start = 1 frame has now tried i = 1, 2, 3 and 4, so it returns and the outermost frame pops "c".
Frame start = 0 tries its siblings: i = 1 gives "ca".

s[0] = 'c' differs from s[1] = 'a', so "ca" fails. The remaining candidates "cab", "cabb" and "cabba" all start with 'c' and end with 'b', 'b' and 'a', so every one of them fails the very first comparison too.
The outermost loop is exhausted, so return all three palindromic partitions of "cabba".

K-th Permutation Sequence.desc: n = 4, k = 9. The loop for i in range(1, 4) builds numbers = [1, 2, 3] and multiplies fact up to 1*2*3 = 6, which is (n-1)! — the size of each block of permutations sharing a first digit.
Append the last digit so numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]. This list is always kept sorted, which is what makes index arithmetic give lexicographic order.
Convert k to 0-indexed: k = 9 - 1 = 8. Now 'the 9th permutation' means 'skip 8 permutations'.
ans is the answer string we build one digit at a time; it starts empty.
First digit. Permutations starting with 1 occupy slots 0-5, with 2 slots 6-11, and so on in blocks of fact = 6. index = 8 // 6 = 1, so the answer sits in block 1.
numbers[1] = 2, so the first digit is 2. ans = '2'.
Remove the digit we just used: numbers = [1, 3, 4]. It stays sorted, so the same block logic works at the next position.
len(numbers) is 3, not 0, so there are still digits to place and the loop continues.
Move inside the chosen block: k = 8 % 6 = 2. We now want the 3rd (0-indexed 2nd) permutation of [1, 3, 4].
Blocks shrink as digits are used up: fact = 6 // 3 = 2, i.e. 2! permutations share each remaining first digit.
Second digit: index = 2 // 2 = 1.
numbers[1] = 3, so ans = '23'.
Pop the 3: numbers = [1, 4].
Two digits remain, so we keep going.
k = 2 % 2 = 0 — we are now at the very first permutation of what is left, so the rest of the digits come out in plain ascending order.
Shrink the block size again: fact = 2 // 2 = 1, so each remaining digit heads a block of exactly one permutation.
Third digit: index = 0 // 1 = 0.
numbers[0] = 1, so ans = '231'.
Pop the 1: numbers = [4].
k = 0 % 1 = 0 and only one digit is left.
fact = 1 // 1 = 1 — with a single digit left the block size can no longer shrink.
Fourth digit: index = 0 // 1 = 0, the only choice available.
numbers[0] = 4, so ans = '2314'.
Pop the 4: numbers is now empty.
len(numbers) == 0 is True, so we break out of the while loop — every position has been filled.
Return '2314'. We produced the 9th permutation of [1,2,3,4] after only 4 divisions, never building the other 23.

Sudoku Solver.desc: solveSudoku is called on a board that is complete except for four holes: (0,0), (0,1), (8,0) and (8,1). Line 43 fires the recursive solve() for the first time.
Depth-1 solve() starts its row scan at i=0. It walks the grid left-to-right, top-to-bottom looking for the FIRST '.' it can find.
Inner loop starts at j=0, so we are looking at cell (0,0).
board[0][0] is '.', so this cell is empty — we must try digits here instead of scanning further.
First candidate: c='1'. We ask isValid(0,0,'1') before touching the board.
Inside isValid, at i=2 the column test board[2][0] == '1' is TRUE — row 2 already holds a 1 in column 0, so '1' is rejected.
isValid returns False for '1'. The for-loop on line 26 moves on to the next digit.
Candidate c='2': row and column are clean, but at i=5 the 3x3-box test board[1][2] == '2' hits — the top-left box already contains a 2.
Candidate c='3' survives all 9 iterations: column 0 has no 3 (the old 3 at (8,0) was blanked), row 0 has no 3, box 0 has no 3. isValid returns True.
We optimistically write board[0][0] = '3'. It is locally legal — but 'legal now' does not mean 'correct'; that is exactly why we need backtracking.
Line 32 recurses: solve() is called again (depth 2) to fill the remaining holes given that (0,0) is a 3.
Depth-2 scan skips (0,0) (now '3') and stops at (0,1), which is still '.'.
At (0,1) we try '1': board[5][1] is 1, rejected. '2': board[4][1] is 2, rejected. '3': our own new board[0][0]='3' blocks it via the row test.
'4' clashes with board[0][2]='4', '5' with board[3][1]='5', '6' with board[0][3]='6', '7' with board[1][1]='7', '8' with board[0][5]='8', '9' with board[2][1]='9'. Every digit 1-9 fails.
No digit fits at (0,1), so depth-2 solve() returns False. This is the contradiction that proves the 3 we placed at (0,0) was wrong.
Back at depth 1: the `if solve():` on line 32 was False, so control falls into the else branch on line 34.
BACKTRACK. board[0][0] is reset to '.', erasing the bad 3 so the next candidate starts from a clean board.
The digit loop resumes with c='4'. isValid(0,0,'4') fails immediately at i=2 because board[0][2]='4' sits in the same row.
c='5': column 0 holds 6,1,8,4,7,9,2 — no 5; row 0 holds 4,6,7,8,9,1,2 — no 5; box 0 holds 4,7,2,1,9,8 — no 5. isValid returns True.
board[0][0] = '5' is written. This one is actually the unique correct value for the cell.
Recurse again into depth 2 with the 5 in place.
Depth 2 finds the next hole at (0,1). Digits '1' and '2' clash with board[5][1]='1' and board[4][1]='2'.
c='3' is valid this time (nothing in row 0, column 1 or box 0 is a 3 now that (0,0) holds 5), so board[0][1] = '3'.
Depth 2 recurses into depth 3.
Depth 3 scans rows 0-7 without finding a '.', then hits (8,0) — the third hole.
'1' clashes with board[2][0]='1' and '2' with board[8][3]='2', but '3' passes every test, so board[8][0] = '3'.
Recurse into depth 4 to handle the last hole.
Depth 4 finds (8,1) empty. '1' clashes with board[5][1], '2' with board[8][3], '3' with our new board[0][1]='3' in column 1.
c='4' is valid — column 1, row 8 and box 6 are all 4-free — so board[8][1] = '4'. The grid is now completely filled.
Depth 4 recurses one last time into depth 5.
Depth 5 sweeps all 81 cells on lines 21-22 and finds no '.' at all, so it falls through to line 40 and returns True — the board is solved.
True bubbles up: depth 4 sees `if solve():` succeed and returns True on line 33, and depths 3, 2 and 1 do exactly the same, so no further backtracking happens.
solve() returns True to line 43. The function returns nothing — the answer is the mutated `board`, solved in place: row 0 is now 5 3 4 6 7 8 9 1 2 and row 8 is 3 4 5 2 8 6 1 7 9.

M Coloring Problem.desc: Graph has N = 5 vertices with edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 1-4, 2-4, 3-4, and only m = 3 colours are allowed. color = [0,0,0,0,0], where 0 means uncoloured.
solve(0) starts the search at vertex 0. Vertices are coloured strictly in order 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Vertex 0: try the first colour, col = 1. Its neighbours 1 and 2 are both still uncoloured.
isSafe(0, 1) scanned all 5 vertices and found no neighbour already wearing colour 1, so it returns True.
color[0] = 1. Vertex 0 is now colour 1 and the array reads [1, 0, 0, 0, 0].
solve(1) recurses one level deeper to colour vertex 1 while vertex 0 keeps colour 1.
isSafe(1, 1): at i = 0 the scan finds graph[1][0] == 1 and color[0] == 1, exactly the colour we wanted.
Conflict, so isSafe returns False — vertex 1 cannot take colour 1 because neighbour 0 already has it.
The colour loop moves on to col = 2 for vertex 1.
isSafe(1, 2) is True: neighbour 0 is colour 1 and neighbours 2, 3, 4 are still uncoloured.
color[1] = 2, giving [1, 2, 0, 0, 0]. Vertices 0 and 1 are adjacent and now differ.
solve(2) descends to vertex 2, which is adjacent to BOTH already-coloured vertices 0 and 1.
isSafe(2, 1) fails at i = 0: vertex 2 is joined to vertex 0, which is already colour 1.
isSafe(2, 2) fails at i = 1: vertex 2 is also joined to vertex 1, which is colour 2.
Only one colour is left to try for vertex 2: col = 3, the last of the m = 3 colours.
isSafe(2, 3) is True — no neighbour of vertex 2 wears colour 3 yet.
color[2] = 3, so the triangle 0-1-2 now uses all three colours: [1, 2, 3, 0, 0].
solve(3) descends to vertex 3, whose only coloured neighbour is vertex 1 (colour 2).
isSafe(3, 1) is True: vertex 3 touches only vertices 1 (colour 2) and 4 (uncoloured), so colour 1 looks free.
color[3] = 1 — a locally legal but, as we are about to discover, globally fatal choice.
solve(4) descends to the last vertex 4, which is adjacent to vertices 1, 2 and 3.
isSafe(4, 1) fails: neighbour 3 was just painted colour 1.
isSafe(4, 2) fails: neighbour 1 is colour 2.
isSafe(4, 3) fails too: neighbour 2 is colour 3. Vertex 4 sees all three colours around it.
All m = 3 colours were rejected for vertex 4, so solve(4) returns False and the recursion unwinds.
Back inside solve(3): the recursive call failed, so undo the choice — color[3] = 0. This is the backtrack.
The colour loop of vertex 3 continues with the sibling choice col = 2.
isSafe(3, 2) fails at i = 1: vertex 3 is adjacent to vertex 1, which is colour 2.
Try the last sibling for vertex 3: col = 3.
isSafe(3, 3) is True — vertex 3 is not adjacent to vertex 2, so reusing colour 3 is legal here.
color[3] = 3 gives [1, 2, 3, 3, 0]; vertices 2 and 3 share colour 3 but have no edge between them.
solve(4) is retried, this time with vertex 3 coloured 3 instead of 1.
isSafe(4, 1) now succeeds: neighbours 1, 2, 3 wear colours 2, 3, 3 — nobody is using colour 1.
color[4] = 1 completes the assignment: [1, 2, 3, 3, 1].
solve(5) is called with v = 5.
v == N == 5, so every vertex is coloured and the base case returns True.
True propagates back up through solve(4), solve(3), solve(2), solve(1) and solve(0) without any further search.
graphColoring returns True: 5 vertices, 7 edges, 3 colours [1, 2, 3, 3, 1], found only after one backtrack at vertex 3.

Rat in a Maze.desc: Maze m = [[1,1,0],[0,1,0],[1,1,1]] with n = 3. Guard clause first: m[0][0] = 1 and m[2][2] = 1, so both ends are open and we may search.
Mark the start cell as visited so no later move can step back onto it.
Call solve(0, 0, '') — the rat is at the top-left with an empty move string.
Are we already home? row = 0 is not n-1 = 2, so no. Keep exploring.
First direction in the fixed D, L, R, U order: 'D' gives next_row = 1, next_col = 0.
(1,0) is inside the grid, but m[1][0] = 0 — that cell is a wall. The move is rejected without any recursion.
Next direction 'L' gives next_col = -1, which fails the boundary test 0 <= next_col < 3 on line 24.
Direction 'R' gives (0,1): inside the grid, not visited, and m[0][1] = 1. This move is legal.
Mark (0,1) visited BEFORE recursing — that is what stops the rat walking back and forth forever.
Recurse: solve(0, 1, 'R').
From (0,1) try 'D' -> (1,1). m[1][1] = 1 and it is unvisited, so the move is allowed. ('R' would hit the wall at (0,2) and 'U' would leave the grid.)
Mark (1,1) visited before stepping onto it, so the rat cannot come back through the centre later in this branch.
Recurse: solve(1, 1, 'RD').
From (1,1) direction 'D' gives (2,1), which is open. ('L' hits the wall at (1,0), 'R' hits the wall at (1,2), 'U' goes back to the visited (0,1).)
Mark (2,1) visited; the path string so far is 'RD' and it is about to become 'RDD'.
Recurse: solve(2, 1, 'RDD'). We are one square away from the goal, but the loop still tries D and L first.
Direction 'D' from (2,1) gives next_row = 3, which fails the boundary test.
Direction 'L' gives (2,0): open and unvisited, so the rat takes it — even though it leads away from the goal.
Mark (2,0) visited too — the algorithm has no idea yet that this corner is a dead end.
Recurse: solve(2, 0, 'RDDL').
DEAD END. From (2,0): 'D' and 'L' leave the grid, 'R' goes back to the visited (2,1), and 'U' hits the wall m[1][0] = 0. The for-loop ends with nothing appended to result.
THE BACKTRACK. solve(2,0,...) returned, so its caller un-marks (2,0). Without this line the wasted detour would block every other path through that cell.
Back inside solve(2,1,'RDD') the loop advances to 'R', giving (2,2).
(2,2) is inside the grid, unvisited, and m[2][2] = 1 — legal.
Mark (2,2) visited, exactly as for any other cell — the destination gets no special treatment on the way in.
Recurse: solve(2, 2, 'RDDR').
row == n-1 and col == n-1, so the destination is reached: append 'RDDR' to result and return at once (the destination is never explored past).
Unwind: un-mark (2,2) so other branches could still use it.
Back at (2,1) the last direction 'U' leads to (1,1), which is still marked visited, so it is rejected and solve(2,1,...) finishes.
Un-mark (2,1) on the way out of solve(1,1,...).
Un-mark (1,1) on the way out of solve(0,1,...); the remaining directions there are all walls or visited cells.
Un-mark (0,1) back in the root call. The root's remaining direction 'U' leaves the grid, so the search is over.
Return result = ['RDDR'] — the single path through this maze, discovered after one dead-end detour that backtracking cleanly erased.

Word Break.desc: word_set = set(['apple', 'pen']) gives O(1) membership tests instead of scanning a list.
dp gets len(s) + 1 = 9 slots, all False. dp[i] will mean 'the first i characters are segmentable'.

vars.dp: [False, False, False, False, False, False, False, False, False]

Word Break.desc: Base case: the empty prefix needs zero words, so dp[0] = True. Every other answer is built from this one.

vars.dp: [True, False, False, False, False, False, False, False, False]

Word Break.desc: Outer loop starts with i = 1, asking: can the prefix 'a' be segmented?
Inner loop tries the only cut point, j = 0, which splits the prefix as '' + 'a'.
dp[0] is True, but s[0:1] = 'a' is not in word_set, so the condition fails and dp[1] stays False.
i = 2, 3 and 4 behave the same way: 'ap', 'app', 'appl' are not words and no earlier dp[j] is True, so dp stays all False up to index 4.

vars.dp: [True, False, False, False, False, False, False, False, False]

Word Break.desc: Now i = 5, asking about the prefix 'apple'.
Inner loop starts at j = 0, the cut that leaves the whole prefix as one candidate word.
dp[0] is True AND s[0:5] = 'apple' is in word_set — both halves of the condition hold, so this cut works.
Mark dp[5] = True: the first five characters 'apple' are segmentable as exactly one dictionary word.

vars.dp: [True, False, False, False, False, True, False, False, False]

Word Break.desc: break — once one valid cut is found for length 5 there is nothing to gain from testing j = 1..4.
i = 6 asks about 'applep'. No cut works: 'applep' is not a word, and the only True dp is dp[0] and dp[5] with leftover 'p'.
Concretely at i = 6, j = 5: dp[5] is True but s[5:6] = 'p' is not in word_set, so dp[6] stays False. i = 7 fails the same way ('pe').
i = 8, the final length — this asks the real question: is the whole string 'applepen' segmentable?
The inner loop walks j = 0..4 first; every one of those has dp[j] False except dp[0], and s[0:8] = 'applepen' is not a word.
j reaches 5, the cut that splits 'applepen' into 'apple' + 'pen'.
dp[5] is True AND s[5:8] = 'pen' is in word_set, so the whole string is segmentable.
Set dp[8] = True — 'applepen' = 'apple' + 'pen'.

vars.dp: [True, False, False, False, False, True, False, False, True]

Word Break.desc: break out of the inner loop; the outer loop has also finished since i reached len(s).
Return dp[len(s)] = dp[8] = True. The answer for 'applepen' with ['apple', 'pen'] is True.

vars.dp: [True, False, False, False, False, True, False, False, True]

Nth Root of a Number.desc: Start the answer range at low = 1 — the smallest candidate root worth testing for n = 3, m = 27.
high = m = 27. The true root can never exceed m itself, so this bound is safe (if loose).
Loop check: low <= high (1 <= 27) is True, so there are still candidates left to test.
mid = (1 + 27) // 2 = 14 — we test the middle candidate instead of stepping through them one by one.
Call check(14) to classify 14^3 against m = 27.
Inside check: ans starts at 1 and will be multiplied by mid n times.
Multiplication 1 of 3: ans = 1 * 14 = 14.
Is 14 > 27? No, so keep multiplying — the early-exit guard has not fired yet.
Multiplication 2 of 3: ans = 14 * 14 = 196.
196 > 27, so we return 2 ('too big') immediately without computing the third multiplication.
Back in the search: mid_state == 1? No, it is 2, so 14 is not the root.
mid_state == 0? No — 14^3 overshot rather than undershot.
Since 14 is too big, every candidate above it is too big as well: high = 14 - 1 = 13. Half the range is gone in one step.
Loop check: 1 <= 13 is True, keep searching.
check(7): ans goes 7, then 49 which already exceeds 27, so it returns 2 after only two multiplications.
Too big again, so high = 7 - 1 = 6. The range is now just 1..6.
Loop check: 1 <= 6 is True.
mid = (1 + 6) // 2 = 3 — this is the candidate that will turn out to be the answer.
Inside check(3) the multiplications run fully: ans = 3, then 9, then 27, and none of them exceed 27.
The loop finished without overshooting, so now compare ans == m: 27 == 27 is True.
check returns 1, the 'exact match' code.
mid_state == 1 is True — 3^3 is exactly 27, so we have found an integer root.
Return mid = 3. Only three candidates (14, 7, 3) were ever tested instead of walking 1..27.

Matrix Median.desc: C = 3 columns, so there are 9 elements in total and the median is the 5th smallest.
low = min of the first column = min(1, 2, 3) = 1. No matrix element can be smaller than that.
high = max of the last column = max(5, 9, 9) = 9. The median must live somewhere in the value range 1..9.
required_count = (3 * 3) // 2 = 4. The median is the smallest value with MORE than 4 elements <= it.
Loop check: low < high (1 < 9) is True, so the value range still has more than one candidate.
mid = (1 + 9) // 2 = 5. We now ask: how many matrix elements are <= 5?
Call countLessEqual(5) to answer that question row by row.
Inside the helper, count starts at 0 before scanning the rows.
Row 0 is [1, 3, 5]; bisect_right(row, 5) = 3 because all three values are <= 5. count = 3.
Row 1 is [2, 6, 9]; only 2 is <= 5, so bisect_right returns 1 and count becomes 4.
Row 2 is [3, 6, 9]; only 3 is <= 5, so count becomes 5. Each row cost O(log C), not O(C).
The helper returns 5: exactly five matrix elements are <= 5.
Is 5 <= required_count (4)? No — 5 already has enough elements below it, so the median is at most 5: high = mid = 5.
Loop check: 1 < 5 is True, so keep narrowing the value range.
countLessEqual(3) = 2 (from [1,3]) + 1 (from [2]) + 1 (from [3]) = 4, and 4 <= 4 is True.
Only 4 elements are <= 3, which is not more than half, so 3 is too small: low = 3 + 1 = 4.
Loop check: 4 < 5 is True, one candidate value (4) still separates the bounds.
mid = (4 + 5) // 2 = 4. Note 4 is not even an element of the matrix — that is fine, we are searching values.
countLessEqual(4) is still 4 (nothing new became eligible between 3 and 4), and 4 <= 4 is True.
So 4 is too small as well: low = 4 + 1 = 5. Now low and high have met.
Loop check: 5 < 5 is False — the range has collapsed to a single value and the loop ends.
Return low = 5. Sorting all nine values gives [1,2,3,3,5,6,6,9,9] whose middle element is indeed 5.

Find Single Element in Sorted Array.desc: low = 0, the first index of nums = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4].
high = len(nums) - 1 = 6, the last index. The single element is somewhere inside [0, 6].
Loop check: low < high (0 < 6) is True, so more than one candidate remains.
mid = (0 + 6) // 2 = 3, which holds the value nums[3] = 3.
mid = 3 is odd, so mid ^ 1 = 2 (its partner on the LEFT). nums[3] = 3 vs nums[2] = 2 — not equal, so the pairing is already broken at or before index 3.
The break is at or to the left of mid, so keep mid as a candidate: high = mid = 3.
Loop check: 0 < 3 is True, the range [0, 3] still holds several indices.
mid = 1 is odd, so mid ^ 1 = 0. nums[1] = 1 equals nums[0] = 1 — this pair is intact, so everything up to index 1 is perfectly paired.
Intact pair means the odd one out lies strictly to the right: low = mid + 1 = 2.
Loop check: 2 < 3 is True, two indices are still in play.
mid = 2 is even, so mid ^ 1 = 3 (its partner on the RIGHT). nums[2] = 2 vs nums[3] = 3 — not equal, so index 2 itself is suspicious.
Keep mid in the range: high = mid = 2. Now low and high are both 2.
Loop check: 2 < 2 is False — the two pointers have converged, so the search is over.
Return nums[low] = nums[2] = 2, the element that appears exactly once. Only three probes were needed for seven elements.

Median of Two Sorted Arrays.desc: Input nums1 = [1, 3], nums2 = [2]. len(nums1) > len(nums2) is 2 > 1, which is True.
Swap so the binary search always runs over the SHORTER array: nums1 = [2], nums2 = [1, 3].
m = len(nums1) = 1 — this is the array we will cut.
n = len(nums2) = 2. Total length is 3, an odd number, so the median will be a single element.
low = 0: the smallest number of elements we may take from nums1 into the left half.
high = m = 1: the largest number of elements we may take from nums1.
Loop check: low <= high (0 <= 1) is True, so a cut position is still untested.
partition1 = (0 + 1) // 2 = 0 — take ZERO elements from nums1 into the left half.
partition2 = (1 + 2 + 1) // 2 - 0 = 2 — so all of nums2 goes into the left half to keep it size 2.
partition1 == 0 means nothing from nums1 is on the left, so maxLeft1 = -inf (a value that loses every comparison).
partition1 (0) != m (1), so minRight1 = nums1[0] = 2.
partition2 (2) != 0, so maxLeft2 = nums2[2 - 1] = nums2[1] = 3.
partition2 (2) == n (2), so nothing from nums2 is on the right: minRight2 = inf.
Validity test: maxLeft1 <= minRight2 is -inf <= inf (True), but maxLeft2 <= minRight1 is 3 <= 2 (False). The cut is wrong.
Which side is wrong? maxLeft1 > minRight2 is -inf > inf, which is False — nums1's cut is not too far right.
So nums1's cut is too far LEFT: we need more elements from nums1 on the left. low = partition1 + 1 = 1.
Loop check: 1 <= 1 is True, one cut position remains.
partition1 = (1 + 1) // 2 = 1 — take the single element of nums1 into the left half.
partition2 = 2 - 1 = 1, so the left half is nums1[:1] + nums2[:1] = [2] + [1], exactly 2 of the 3 values.
partition1 != 0, so maxLeft1 = nums1[0] = 2.
partition1 (1) == m (1): nums1 has nothing left on the right, so minRight1 = inf.
maxLeft2 = nums2[1 - 1] = nums2[0] = 1.
minRight2 = nums2[1] = 3.
Validity test: 2 <= 3 (True) and 1 <= inf (True). Every left value is <= every right value, so this is the correct partition.
(m + n) % 2 == 1 -> (1 + 2) % 2 == 1 is True, so the total length is odd and the median is a single value.
Return max(maxLeft1, maxLeft2) = max(2, 1) = 2.0 — the largest value on the left half, which is the median of [1, 2, 3].

Kth Element of Two Sorted Arrays.desc: Calculate size n1 of first array [2, 3, 6]
Calculate size n2 of second array [1, 4, 8, 10]
Check if first array is larger than second array (3 > 4 is False)
Initialize low as max(0, 4 - 4) = 0
Initialize high as min(3, 4) = 3
Check binary search condition low <= high (0 <= 3 is True)
Calculate cut1 partition position (0 + 3) // 2 = 1
Calculate cut2 partition position (4 - 1) = 3
Get left element from arr1: l1 = arr1[0] = 2
Get right element from arr1: r1 = arr1[1] = 3
Get left element from arr2: l2 = arr2[2] = 8
Get right element from arr2: r2 = arr2[3] = 10
Compare boundaries (l1 <= r2 and l2 <= r1 -> 2 <= 10 and 8 <= 3 is False)
Check if l1 > r2 (2 > 10 is False)
The cut in arr1 is too far left, so we need more of arr1 on the left side: low = cut1 + 1 = 2.
Check binary search condition low <= high (2 <= 3 is True)
Calculate cut1 partition position (2 + 3) // 2 = 2
Calculate cut2 partition position (4 - 2) = 2
Get left element from arr1: l1 = arr1[1] = 3
Get right element from arr1: r1 = arr1[2] = 6
Get left element from arr2: l2 = arr2[1] = 4
Get right element from arr2: r2 = arr2[2] = 8
Compare boundaries (l1 <= r2 and l2 <= r1 -> 3 <= 8 and 4 <= 6 is True)
Partition is correct. Return max(l1, l2) = max(3, 4) = 4

Implement Stack Using Array.desc: We create st = MyStack(). Python runs __init__ to set up the backing storage.
self.arr becomes a fixed block of 1000 slots pre-filled with -1. Only the first 6 slots are drawn; -1 here just means 'never written'.
self.top_idx = -1 is the whole trick: -1 means 'no element yet', so the next push will land at index 0.
Operation 1: st.push(10).
top_idx moves first: -1 + 1 = 0. We always make room before writing.
arr[0] = 10. The stack now logically holds [10] even though 998 slots are still -1.
Operation 2: st.push(20).
top_idx becomes 0 + 1 = 1.
arr[1] = 20. Stack is [10, 20] with 20 on top.
Operation 3: st.push(30).
top_idx becomes 1 + 1 = 2.
arr[2] = 30. Stack is [10, 20, 30]; every push was O(1) — no shifting of any kind.
Operation 4: st.top() — peek without removing.
top_idx is 2, not -1, so the stack is non-empty and it is safe to read.
Return arr[2] = 30. Nothing changed: top_idx is still 2 and the stack is still [10, 20, 30].
Operation 5: st.pop().
top_idx == -1 is False (it is 2), so we skip the empty guard and do the real work.
val = arr[2] = 30. We grab the value BEFORE moving the pointer, otherwise we would lose it.
top_idx drops to 1. Note arr[2] still physically holds 30, but it is now beyond the top, so it is garbage the stack will overwrite on the next push.
Return 30 — LIFO honoured: the last value pushed is the first popped.
Operation 6: st.size().
Size is top_idx + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2, because indices 0 and 1 are live.
Operation 7: st.isEmpty().
top_idx == -1 is False, so isEmpty() returns False.
Operation 8: st.pop() again. val = arr[1] = 20.
top_idx drops to 0 and 20 is returned. Stack is [10].
Operation 9: st.pop(). val = arr[0] = 10.
top_idx drops to -1 and 10 is returned. The stack is now logically empty again.
Operation 10: st.pop() on the empty stack — the underflow case.
This time top_idx == -1 is True, so the guard fires.
Return the sentinel -1 instead of crashing with an IndexError. Final state: arr still shows old numbers, but top_idx = -1 means the stack is empty.

Implement Queue Using Array.desc: We create q = MyQueue(). Python runs __init__ to lay out the circular buffer.
capacity = 1000 fixes the ring size once and for all; only the first 6 slots are drawn here.
arr becomes 1000 slots pre-filled with -1. The -1s are just 'never written yet', not real data.
front_idx = 0 marks where the next dequeue will read from.
rear_idx = 0 marks where the next enqueue will write. Both pointers start together.
count = 0 is the tie-breaker: front_idx == rear_idx means empty when count is 0 and full when count is capacity.
Operation 1: q.enqueue(5).
Full check: count (0) == capacity (1000)? No, so there is room and we continue.
Write arr[rear_idx] = arr[0] = 5. Nothing else in the array moves — that is the whole point.
rear_idx = (0 + 1) % 1000 = 1. The modulo is what lets the pointer wrap back to 0 after slot 999.
count = 1. The queue logically holds [5].
Operation 2: q.enqueue(6) writes arr[1] = 6 at the current rear.
rear_idx advances to (1 + 1) % 1000 = 2.
count = 2. Queue is [5, 6] with 5 still at the front.
Operation 3: q.enqueue(7) writes arr[2] = 7.
rear_idx becomes 3 and count becomes 3. Queue is [5, 6, 7]; three enqueues, zero element shifting.
Operation 4: q.front() — look at the oldest element without removing it.
count is not 0, so return arr[front_idx] = arr[0] = 5. Nothing changed.
Operation 5: q.dequeue().
Empty check: count (3) == 0? No, so we have something to hand back.
val = arr[front_idx] = arr[0] = 5 — read BEFORE moving the pointer, or the value would be lost.
front_idx = (0 + 1) % 1000 = 1. Slot 0 still physically holds 5, but it is now outside the live window.
count drops to 2. Queue is [6, 7].
Return 5 — FIFO honoured, the first value enqueued is the first one out, and it cost O(1) with no shifting.
Operation 6: q.size().
Return count = 2 directly; we never have to subtract pointers or worry about wrap-around.
Operation 7: q.dequeue() reads val = arr[1] = 6.
front_idx moves to 2 and count drops to 1. Queue is [7].
Operation 8: q.dequeue() reads val = arr[2] = 7.
front_idx moves to 3 and count drops to 0. front_idx and rear_idx are equal again — the ring is empty.
Operation 9: q.isEmpty().
count == 0 is True, so isEmpty() returns True even though front_idx == rear_idx would also be true when full.
Operation 10: q.dequeue() on the empty queue — the underflow case.
This time count == 0 is True, so the guard fires.
Return the -1 sentinel instead of handing back the stale 5 still sitting in slot 0.

Implement Stack Using Queue.desc: We create st = MyStack(). __init__ runs to build the single queue that will pretend to be a stack.
self.q = deque() — an empty double-ended queue. The rule we will maintain: the FRONT of q is always the stack's TOP.
Operation 1: st.push(1).
Append 1 to the back: q = [1].
len(q) - 1 = 0, so the rotation loop runs zero times. With one element, front is already the top.
Operation 2: st.push(2).
Append 2 to the back: q = [1, 2]. Right now the front is 1, but a stack must expose 2 — so we rotate.
len(q) - 1 = 1, so we rotate exactly once.
popleft() removes 1 and append() puts it at the back: q = [2, 1]. Now the newest element, 2, is at the front. That is the whole trick.
Operation 3: st.push(3).
Append 3: q = [2, 1, 3]. The new element is at the back and needs to travel to the front.
len(q) - 1 = 2, so the loop rotates twice.
Rotation 1 of 2: popleft() takes 2 and appends it. q = [1, 3, 2].
Rotation 2 of 2: popleft() takes 1 and appends it. q = [3, 2, 1] — exactly reverse insertion order, which is stack order.
Operation 4: st.top().
The queue is non-empty, so the guard does not fire.
Return q[0] = 3 without removing anything — peeking is O(1) because the invariant already put the top at the front.
Operation 5: st.pop().
q is not empty, so we skip the -1 fallback.
popleft() removes and returns 3 — the last value pushed. q = [2, 1]. Pop is O(1); all the cost was paid up front in push.
Operation 6: st.top() again.
Return q[0] = 2, the new top. The invariant survived the pop for free.
Operation 7: st.pop() returns 2 and leaves q = [1].
Operation 8: st.pop() returns 1 and leaves q = []. All three values came out in 3, 2, 1 order — perfect LIFO.
Operation 9: st.empty().
len(q) == 0 is True, so empty() returns True.
Operation 10: st.pop() on the empty stack.
`if not self.q` is now True — the guard catches the underflow.
Return -1 instead of raising IndexError from popleft(). Final state: q = [], stack empty.

Implement Queue Using Stack.desc: Create q = MyQueue(). __init__ builds the two-stack machine: one stack absorbs arrivals, the other serves departures.
self.input_stack = [] — every push lands here first. The right end of the list is its top.
self.output_stack = [] — the reversed copy that answers pop and peek. Its top is the queue's FRONT element.
Operation 1: q.push(1). Pushing never touches the output stack, so it is always O(1).
input_stack.append(1) — the input stack is now [1] and 1 sits on top of it.
Operation 2: q.push(2). Again straight into the input stack.
input_stack.append(2) makes the input stack [1, 2]. Note that 1, the oldest element, is now buried at the bottom.
Operation 3: q.push(3), the third arrival.
input_stack.append(3) gives [1, 2, 3]. In LIFO order 3 would come out first, but FIFO demands 1 — that inversion is what the second stack fixes.
Operation 4: q.pop(), which must return the oldest element, 1.
output_stack is empty, so the guard is True and we must do the one-time transfer that reverses the arrival order.
The while loop runs as long as input_stack has something. It currently holds [1, 2, 3], so we enter.
input_stack.pop() yields 3 (its top) and we append it to output_stack. output_stack = [3], input_stack = [1, 2].
Next transfer: 2 comes off the input stack and lands on the output stack. output_stack = [3, 2], input_stack = [1].
Last transfer: 1 moves across. output_stack = [3, 2, 1] with 1 on TOP — the arrival order has been flipped exactly once.
input_stack is now empty so the while condition is False and the transfer loop ends. Each element was moved exactly once, which is where the amortised O(1) comes from.
output_stack is not empty, so we skip the -1 sentinel path used for popping an empty queue.
output_stack.pop() returns 1 — the oldest element, exactly what FIFO requires. output_stack is left as [3, 2].
Operation 5: q.push(4) while the output stack still holds [3, 2]. The new arrival must NOT jump ahead of them.
input_stack.append(4). The queue conceptually holds 2, 3, 4 but it is split across two stacks: output [3, 2] and input [4].
Operation 6: q.push(5), the fifth arrival, again straight to the input side.
input_stack.append(5) gives input [4, 5] while output still holds [3, 2].
Operation 7: q.peek(). It should report 2, the front, without removing it.
output_stack = [3, 2] is NOT empty, so the guard is False and the transfer loop is skipped entirely. Moving 4 and 5 across now would wrongly put them in front of 2 and 3.
Return output_stack[-1] = 2 without popping. The stacks are unchanged: input [4, 5], output [3, 2].
Operation 8: q.pop(). The expected front is 2.
output_stack still has [3, 2], so no transfer happens — the lazy refill only fires when the output side runs dry.
output_stack.pop() returns 2 and leaves output as [3]. Elements 4 and 5 are still waiting on the input side.
Operation 9: q.pop() again. The front should now be 3.
output_stack = [3] is non-empty, so the transfer is skipped one more time.
Return 3. output_stack is now completely empty while input_stack still holds [4, 5].
Operation 10: q.pop(). This is the pop that triggers the SECOND transfer, and the front should be 4.
output_stack is empty again, so the guard is True and we refill it from the input stack for the second time in this run.
Move 5 (the input top) onto output_stack. output = [5], input = [4].
Move 4 across. output = [5, 4] with 4 on top — the later arrivals are reversed among themselves, which is exactly right.
output_stack.pop() returns 4 and leaves [5]. Every element has crossed between the stacks exactly once so far.
Operation 11: q.empty(). The queue should report False because 5 is still queued.
input_stack is empty but output_stack = [5] is not, so 'not [] and not [5]' evaluates to False. The queue is not empty, and the answers 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 came out in perfect FIFO order.

Next Greater Element.desc: Start with greater_map = {} — an empty dictionary that will remember, for each value of nums2, the first larger value standing to its right.
stack = [] will hold values from nums2 that are still WAITING for someone bigger. It stays decreasing from bottom to top.
First iteration of the loop over nums2: num = 1 (index 0). Nothing has been seen yet.
While-check: the stack is empty, so `stack and ...` is False straight away — there is nobody waiting for a bigger neighbour yet.
Push 1 onto the stack: stack = [1]. Value 1 is now waiting for the first value greater than it to appear on its right.
Second iteration: num = 3 (index 1 of nums2). This is the moment the waiting value 1 may finally be resolved.
While-check: stack is non-empty and stack[-1] = 1 < 3 is True, so the top of the stack has found its next greater element.
Pop 1 and record greater_map[1] = 3. The answer for value 1 is locked in forever: the first bigger value to its right is 3. Stack is now [].
Loop back to the while-check: the stack is empty now, so we stop popping and fall through.
Push 3: stack = [3]. Value 3 becomes the new waiting candidate.
Third iteration: num = 4 (index 2). Again the incoming value is larger than the stack top.
While-check: stack[-1] = 3 < 4 is True, so 3's long wait is over.
Pop 3 and record greater_map[3] = 4. Notice each value is pushed once and popped at most once — that is why the whole scan is O(n).
While-check again: the stack drained to empty, so the popping stops.
Push 4: stack = [4]. Value 4 now waits for something larger than itself.
Fourth and last iteration: num = 2 (index 3 of nums2).
While-check: stack[-1] = 4 < 2 is False, so nothing is popped — 4 is bigger than 2 and keeps waiting.
Push 2 on top of 4: stack = [4, 2]. The stack is still decreasing from bottom to top, exactly as intended.
nums2 is exhausted, so the for-loop ends. Values 4 and 2 are still on the stack, which means nothing greater ever appeared to their right — they simply never get a map entry.
Final step: look up each element of nums1 = [4, 1, 2] in greater_map, defaulting to -1. 4 is absent -> -1, 1 -> 3, 2 is absent -> -1. Return [-1, 3, -1].

Sort a Stack.desc: Top-level call sortStack([2, 1]) (bottom = 2, top = 1). The stack is not empty, so the base case does not fire.
Pop the top: temp = 1 and the stack shrinks to [2]. temp now lives in THIS call frame, which is our only allowed storage.
Recurse on the smaller stack: sortStack([2]). We will not touch temp = 1 again until that call returns.
Depth 1: stack is [2], still not empty, so keep peeling.
Depth 1 pops temp = 2, leaving the stack completely empty.
Depth 1 recurses again: sortStack([]).
Depth 2: `not stack` is True for the empty stack — an empty stack is trivially sorted.
