Return immediately. This is the bottom of the recursion; now the frames unwind and start rebuilding.
Back at depth 1: insert its saved temp = 2 into the sorted (empty) stack via sortedInsert([], 2).
sortedInsert base case: `not stack` is True (the stack is empty), so 2 can simply go on top.
append(2) — the stack becomes [2].
Return from sortedInsert. Depth 1 is finished: its sub-stack [2] is sorted.
Back at depth 0: now insert its saved temp = 1 into the sorted stack [2] via sortedInsert([2], 1).
Base case check: the stack is not empty, and element > stack[-1] is 1 > 2 which is False. So 1 does NOT belong on top.
Pop the blocking top: temp = 2 and the stack becomes []. This temp is saved in the sortedInsert frame.
Recurse to place 1 deeper: sortedInsert([], 1).
Inner call: the stack is empty, so the base case fires and 1 can be placed.
append(1) — the stack becomes [1], with 1 now at the bottom position it deserves.
Return from the inner sortedInsert.
Push the saved temp = 2 back on top: the stack becomes [1, 2] — ascending, with the largest on top. Sorting is done.

Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size.desc: The input is arr = [3, 7, 5, 8, 2, 6], so n = 6 and six window sizes need an answer.
left[] starts as six -1 values: until proven otherwise no bar has a smaller bar to its left.
right[] starts as six 6s, where 6 = n means 'no smaller bar anywhere to the right'.
The stack is empty; it will hold indices whose values increase from bottom to top.
Sweep 1 starts at i = 0 with arr[0] = 3.
The stack is empty, so left[0] keeps -1, and index 0 is pushed as a boundary candidate.
i = 1, value 7. The top is index 0 with value 3, and 3 >= 7 is false, so nothing pops.
left[1] = 0: the nearest strictly smaller value to the left of 7 is the 3 at index 0.
Push index 1; bottom to top the stack now reads values 3, 7.
i = 2, value 5. The top index 1 holds 7 and 7 >= 5, so that bar has to go.
Pop index 1: a 7 can never be the nearest smaller bar for anything to the right of this 5.
The new top is index 0 with value 3, and 3 >= 5 is false, so the popping stops.
left[2] = 0 — the 3 at index 0 is what bounds the 5 on its left.
Push index 2; the stack values are 3, 5, increasing again.
i = 3, value 8. The top value 5 is not >= 8, so nothing pops for this bar.
left[3] = 2, and index 3 is then pushed, so the stack holds values 3, 5, 8.
i = 4, value 2 — smaller than everything on the stack. The top index 3 holds 8, and 8 >= 2.
Pop index 3 (value 8), then index 2 (value 5), then index 0 (value 3): all are >= 2, so the stack empties.
With an empty stack left[4] stays -1: nothing smaller than 2 exists to its left. Push index 4.
i = 5, value 6: the top index 4 holds 2, which is smaller, so left[5] = 4 with no popping.
Push index 5. Sweep 1 is finished with left = [-1, 0, 0, 2, -1, 4].
Reset the stack to empty; the mirror sweep must not see leftovers from sweep 1.
Sweep 2 walks right to left and begins at i = 5, value 6.
The stack is empty, so right[5] keeps 6 (= n, nothing smaller to its right); push index 5.
i = 4, value 2: the top index 5 holds 6 and 6 >= 2, so it pops.
Pop index 5. The stack is empty again, so right[4] stays 6 — nothing to the right of the 2 is smaller.
Push index 4; the 2 will now bound every bar to its left.
i = 3, value 8: the top index 4 holds 2 < 8, so right[3] = 4 immediately.
i = 2, value 5: the top is index 3 with value 8, and 8 >= 5, so it pops.
Pop index 3; the exposed top is index 4 (value 2), which is smaller than 5, so popping stops.
right[2] = 4: the next smaller bar to the right of the 5 is the 2 at index 4.
i = 1, value 7: the top is index 2 (value 5), already smaller, so right[1] = 2 with no pops.
i = 0, value 3: pop index 1 (7 >= 3) and then index 2 (5 >= 3); index 4 with value 2 survives.
right[0] = 4, so the leading 3 rules as minimum only until the 2 at index 4.
ans gets n + 1 = 7 slots so it can be indexed by window size; slot 0 is deliberately unused.
i = 0: length = right[0] - left[0] - 1 = 4 - (-1) - 1 = 4, so the 3 claims window size 4 and ans[4] = 3.
i = 1: length = 2 - 0 - 1 = 1, so the 7 only rules a single cell and ans[1] = 7.
i = 2: length = 4 - 0 - 1 = 3, so the 5 is the minimum of a width-3 window and ans[3] = 5.
i = 3: length = 4 - 2 - 1 = 1, and ans[1] = max(7, 8) = 8 — the biggest single element wins.
i = 4: length = 6 - (-1) - 1 = 6, so the 2 is the minimum of the whole array and ans[6] = 2.
Sizes 2 and 5 were claimed by nobody. i = 5: ans[5] = max(0, ans[6] = 2) = 2.
i = 4: ans[4] = max(3, ans[5] = 2) = 3, so the direct claim by the 3 survives.
i = 3: ans[3] = max(5, 3) = 5, and then i = 2 inherits it: ans[2] = max(0, 5) = 5.
Drop the unused slot 0 and return [8, 5, 5, 3, 2, 2] for window sizes 1 through 6.

LRU Cache.desc: Create cache = LRUCache(2), a cache that can hold at most two keys.
self.capacity = 2 is remembered so put() knows when it must evict.
self.cache = {} maps key -> NODE (not key -> value), which is what makes O(1) unlinking possible later.
Create the dummy head sentinel. It holds no real data; it only marks the most-recently-used end.
Create the dummy tail sentinel, marking the least-recently-used end.
head.next = tail links the two sentinels together.
tail.prev = head completes the empty doubly linked list. No real node can ever be first or last, so _remove/_add need zero special cases.
Operation 1: cache.put(1, 1).
Is key 1 already in the map? No, so we take the 'insert new key' branch.
Capacity check: len(cache) = 0 >= capacity = 2 is False, so nothing has to be evicted.
Build a fresh Node holding key 1 and value 1.
Register it in the map: cache = {1: Node(1)}.
_add splices the node in right after head, so the list becomes head <-> 1 <-> tail.
Operation 2: cache.put(2, 2).
Key 2 is new too; len(cache) = 1 >= 2 is still False, so again no eviction.
Create a fresh Node holding key 2 and value 2.
_add puts it directly after head: head <-> 2 <-> 1 <-> tail. Key 1 has drifted one step towards the tail.
Operation 3: cache.get(1) — a read, which must also count as a USE.
Key 1 is present in the map, so this is a hit.
node = cache[1] gives us the node object directly — O(1), no list walking.
_remove(node) unlinks it: its prev (node 2) and next (tail) are stitched together, leaving head <-> 2 <-> tail.
_add(node) reinserts it just after head: head <-> 1 <-> 2 <-> tail. Key 1 is now the most recently used.
Return node.value = 1.
Operation 4: cache.put(3, 3) — the interesting one, because the cache is full.
Key 3 is not in the map, so we go to the insert branch.
len(cache) = 2 >= capacity = 2 is True — something must be thrown out first.
lru_node = tail.prev = Node(2, 2). By our convention the node just before tail is the least recently used, and key 2 has not been touched since it was inserted.
_remove(lru_node) unlinks node 2 from the list: head <-> 1 <-> tail.
del cache[2] drops it from the map as well — both structures must stay in sync or the cache leaks memory.
Now create the new Node(3, 3).
Store it in the map: cache = {1: Node, 3: Node}.
_add places it at the front: head <-> 3 <-> 1 <-> tail.
Operation 5: cache.get(2) — the key we just evicted.
Key 2 is no longer in the map, so the `if` is False and we fall through.
Return -1 for the miss. Final state: keys {3, 1} with 3 as most recently used — every operation touched only O(1) pointers.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram.desc: We call largestRectangleArea([2, 1, 5, 6]). stack = [] will hold INDICES of bars whose heights are increasing, never the heights themselves.
max_area = 0 is the best rectangle found so far. Every rectangle we ever measure will be compared against it.
n = len(heights) = 4. We will loop to n inclusive so index 4 acts as a virtual bar of height 0.
Iteration i = 0. The loop runs over range(5), so indices 0..3 are real bars and 4 is the sentinel.
i = 0 < n, so current_height = heights[0] = 2, the first bar.
While-check: the stack is empty, so there is no taller bar waiting to be closed. The body is skipped.
Push index 0. Meaning: bar of height 2 is still 'open' — we do not yet know how far right it can stretch.
Iteration i = 1 begins with index 0 still open on the stack.
current_height = heights[1] = 1. This bar is SHORTER than the bar on the stack, which means bar 0 can go no further right.
While-check: stack top is index 0 and heights[0] = 2 > 1 is True, so we close bar 0 now.
Pop index 0 and read its height: h = heights[0] = 2. The stack becomes empty.
Width: the stack is now empty, which means nothing shorter blocked bar 0 on the LEFT, so it stretches from index 0 to i-1. w = i = 1.
max_area = max(0, 2 * 1) = 2. The rectangle of height 2 and width 1 is our first candidate.
While-check again: the stack is empty, so the popping loop ends.
Push index 1. The stack now holds the open bar of height 1.
Iteration i = 2: current_height = heights[2] = 5.
While-check: heights[stack[-1]] = heights[1] = 1 > 5 is False. Heights are still increasing, so nothing is closed.
Push index 2. stack = [1, 2] and the heights it points at, 1 and 5, are increasing — that is the invariant.
Iteration i = 3: current_height = heights[3] = 6, taller again.
While-check: heights[2] = 5 > 6 is False, so bar 2 stays open.
Push index 3. stack = [1, 2, 3] pointing at heights 1, 5, 6.
Iteration i = 4 — the sentinel index. There is no real bar here.
Because i = 4 is not < n = 4, current_height = 0. A height of 0 is shorter than everything, which forces the whole stack to drain.
While-check: heights[3] = 6 > 0 is True.
Pop index 3: h = heights[3] = 6. stack = [1, 2].
Stack is not empty, so bar 3 is blocked on the left by index stack[-1] = 2. w = i - stack[-1] - 1 = 4 - 2 - 1 = 1.
max_area = max(2, 6 * 1) = 6.
The while condition still holds (heights[2] = 5 > 0), so pop index 2: h = heights[2] = 5. stack = [1].
w = i - stack[-1] - 1 = 4 - 1 - 1 = 2: bar 2 (height 5) spreads over indices 2 and 3, because bar 3 is taller than it.
max_area = max(6, 5 * 2) = 10. This is the winning rectangle: bars 5 and 6 give height 5 across width 2.
Condition holds once more (heights[1] = 1 > 0): pop index 1, h = heights[1] = 1, and the stack empties.
Stack is empty, so bar 1 (height 1) is the minimum of the whole array and spans everything: w = i = 4.
max_area = max(10, 1 * 4) = 10 — the full-width rectangle of height 1 has area 4, which does not beat 10.
While-check: the stack is empty, so the drain finishes.
Push the sentinel index 4 (harmless — the loop is over).
Return max_area = 10. Every index was pushed once and popped once, so the whole scan is O(N).

Sliding Window Maximum.desc: maxSlidingWindow([1, 3, -1, -3, 5], k = 3). dq starts empty and will hold INDICES whose values are in decreasing order.
res = [] will collect one maximum per window. With n = 5 and k = 3 we expect 3 answers.
Iteration i = 0, value nums[0] = 1.
Out-of-window check: dq is empty, so there is no stale front index to drop.
Monotonic check: dq is empty, so nothing behind us is smaller than 1.
Append index 0. dq = [0], representing the values [1].
Window-full check: i = 0 >= k - 1 = 2 is False. The first window is not complete yet, so we record nothing.
Iteration i = 1, value nums[1] = 3.
Front index dq[0] = 0 and the window starts at i - k + 1 = -1. 0 < -1 is False, so index 0 is still inside the window.
Monotonic check: nums[dq[-1]] = nums[0] = 1 < 3 is True. Index 0 can never be a maximum again while 3 is present, so evict it.
dq.pop() removes index 0 from the BACK. dq = [].
Re-check: dq is empty, so the eviction loop ends.
Append index 1. dq = [1], representing [3].
i = 1 >= 2 is still False — one more element is needed to fill the first window.
Iteration i = 2, value nums[2] = -1. The window [0, 1, 2] is about to be complete.
dq[0] = 1 and window_start = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0. 1 < 0 is False, so the front is still valid.
nums[dq[-1]] = nums[1] = 3 < -1 is False, so -1 does NOT evict 3; it just queues up behind it.
Append index 2. dq = [1, 2], holding values [3, -1] — still decreasing, the invariant holds.
i = 2 >= 2 is True: the window [1, 3, -1] is full, so an answer is due.
The front of the deque is always the window maximum: res.append(nums[dq[0]]) = nums[1] = 3. res = [3].
Iteration i = 3, value nums[3] = -3. Window slides to [1, 2, 3] = [3, -1, -3].
dq[0] = 1 and window_start = 3 - 3 + 1 = 1. 1 < 1 is False, so index 1 has NOT left the window yet.
nums[dq[-1]] = nums[2] = -1 < -3 is False, so nothing is evicted.
Append index 3. dq = [1, 2, 3] holding [3, -1, -3] — decreasing as required.
Window is full again: res.append(nums[1]) = 3. res = [3, 3].
Iteration i = 4, value nums[4] = 5 — the last element and a big one.
window_start = 4 - 3 + 1 = 2 and dq[0] = 1. Now 1 < 2 is True: index 1 has slid out of the window.
dq.popleft() drops the stale index 1 from the FRONT. dq = [2, 3].
nums[dq[-1]] = nums[3] = -3 < 5 is True, so index 3 is useless from now on.
Pop index 3 from the back. dq = [2]. The condition still holds because nums[2] = -1 < 5, so we pop again next.
Pop index 2 as well. dq = [] — the new value 5 has wiped out every smaller candidate behind it.
Append index 4. dq = [4], holding just [5].
Window [2, 3, 4] = [-1, -3, 5] is full: res.append(nums[4]) = 5. res = [3, 3, 5].
Return [3, 3, 5]. Each index entered and left the deque at most once, so despite the inner while loop the scan is O(N).

Rotten Oranges.desc: orangesRotting([[2, 1], [1, 1]]). rows = len(grid) = 2. Cell (0,0) is rotten (2) and the other three oranges are fresh (1).
cols = len(grid[0]) = 2, so the grid is 2x2.
queue = deque() will hold triples (row, col, minute). Seeding it with EVERY rotten orange is what makes this a multi-source BFS.
fresh_count = 0 will count how many oranges still need to rot, so we can detect unreachable ones at the end.
Scan cell (0,0): grid[0][0] == 2 is True — an initially rotten orange, i.e. a BFS source.
Push (0, 0, 0) — row 0, col 0, rotten since minute 0.
Scan cell (0,1): it is not 2, so the elif fires — grid[0][1] == 1, a fresh orange.
fresh_count becomes 1 — one orange that still has to rot.
Row 1 is scanned the same way: (1,0) is fresh, so fresh_count = 2.
(1,1) is fresh too, so fresh_count = 3. The scan is finished: 1 source, 3 fresh oranges.
minutes = 0 records the largest minute stamp we ever pop, which is the answer at the end.
BFS starts: the queue holds one item, so we enter the loop.
Pop the front: r = 0, c = 0, time = 0 — the original rotten orange.
minutes = max(0, 0) = 0. Nothing has spread yet.
Check the four neighbours in order: (-1,0), (1,0), (0,-1), (0,1) added to (0,0).
First direction (-1, 0) gives nr, nc = -1, 0.
Bounds check fails immediately: 0 <= -1 is False, so we never index the grid. This is why the bounds test comes FIRST in the and-chain.
Second direction (1, 0) gives nr, nc = 1, 0.
In bounds and grid[1][0] == 1, a fresh orange next to a rotten one — it rots this minute.
grid[1][0] = 2. Overwriting the cell doubles as marking it visited, so it can never be queued twice.
fresh_count drops from 3 to 2.
Push (1, 0, 1): this orange became rotten at minute time + 1 = 1.
Direction (0, -1) gives nc = -1 and fails the bounds check; direction (0, 1) gives (0, 1), which is in bounds and fresh.
grid[0][1] = 2 — the second orange rots at the same minute as the first, because both are neighbours of the same source.
fresh_count drops to 1.
Push (0, 1, 1). The queue now holds the whole 'minute 1' layer: [(1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1)].
Next pop: r = 1, c = 0, time = 1.
minutes = max(0, 1) = 1 — the rot has advanced one minute.
Neighbours of (1,0): (0,0) is already 2, (2,0) and (1,-1) are out of bounds, and (1,1) is fresh — condition True.
grid[1][1] = 2: the last fresh orange rots.
fresh_count reaches 0 — every orange has rotted, though the BFS still has queued cells to drain.
Push (1, 1, 2): this one rotted at minute 2, one layer deeper than its parent.
Pop (0, 1, 1). minutes stays max(1, 1) = 1, and all of its neighbours are already 2, so nothing is queued.
Pop the last item, (1, 1, 2).
minutes = max(1, 2) = 2. This deepest BFS layer is the true answer.
The queue is empty, so the BFS loop exits.
fresh_count == 0, so nothing was unreachable: return minutes = 2.

Min Stack.desc: We create st = MinStack(). The goal: push, pop, top AND getMin must all be O(1).
self.stack = []. Each entry will be a PAIR (value, minimum-of-everything-at-or-below-it), so every level remembers its own history.
Operation 1: st.push(5).
current_min starts as the value itself, 5.
self.stack is empty, so there is no previous minimum to compare against — the if body is skipped.
Append (5, 5): the value is 5 and the minimum of the stack so far is also 5.
Operation 2: st.push(3).
current_min tentatively equals 3.
The stack is non-empty, so we must compare with the minimum stored in the top pair.
current_min = min(3, self.stack[-1][1]) = min(3, 5) = 3. The new value is smaller, so it becomes the running minimum.
Operation 3: st.push(7).
current_min tentatively equals 7.
current_min = min(7, 3) = 3. Even though we are pushing a big number, the pair carries the OLD minimum forward — that is what keeps getMin O(1).
Operation 4: st.getMin().
Return self.stack[-1][1] = the second field of (7, 3) = 3. No scanning of the stack at all — a single index lookup.
Operation 5: st.top().
Return self.stack[-1][0] = the FIRST field of (7, 3) = 7. Field 0 is the value, field 1 is the minimum — do not mix them up.
Operation 6: st.pop().
The whole pair (7, 3) is discarded. Stack = [(5, 5), (3, 3)].
Operation 7: st.getMin() now reads (3, 3)[1] = 3. Still correct.
Operation 8: st.pop() removes (3, 3) — we just deleted the minimum itself. Stack = [(5, 5)].
Operation 9: st.getMin() reads (5, 5)[1] = 5. The old minimum 5 is restored automatically, because it was frozen inside the pair below — no recomputation needed.
Operation 10: st.push(2).
current_min = min(2, 5) = 2 — a new record low.
Operation 11: st.getMin() returns 2.
Operation 12: st.top() returns (2, 2)[0] = 2. Every operation in this trace touched only the last element, so all of them ran in O(1) time.

Stock Span Problem.desc: We create sp = StockSpanner(). self.stack = [] will hold PAIRS (price, span) for the days that are still 'visible' — the ones no later day has swallowed.
Day 1: sp.next(100) is called with price = 100.
span = 1 because today always counts itself.
While-check: self.stack is empty, so there is no earlier day at all and the loop body never runs.
Push (100, 1): price 100 with a span of 1 day.
Return 1. Day 1 always has span 1.
Day 2: sp.next(80) arrives; the stack still remembers day 1.
span = 1 again — today always counts itself first.
While-check: top pair is (100, 1) and 100 <= 80 is False. Yesterday was more expensive, so it blocks the view immediately.
Push (80, 1). Notice the stack prices 100, 80 are decreasing — that is the invariant of this monotonic stack.
Return 1: day 2 is cheaper than day 1, so its span is just itself.
Day 3: sp.next(60) — prices are still falling.
Top price 80 <= 60 is False, so again nothing is absorbed.
Return 1. Three falling prices in a row, three spans of 1.
Day 4: sp.next(70) — the first interesting call, because 70 is higher than yesterday's 60.
span = 1 to start, before we look at any earlier day.
While-check: top price 60 <= 70 is True. Day 3 is cheaper than today, so today can see straight past it.
Pop (60, 1) and absorb its span: span = 1 + 1 = 2. Absorbing the whole span, not just one day, is the trick that keeps this O(1) amortised.
Re-check: the new top price is 80 and 80 <= 70 is False, so day 2 blocks the view and the loop stops.
Push (70, 2): price 70 already carries the two days it dominates.
Return 2 — days 3 and 4 both had prices <= 70.
Day 5: sp.next(60), a dip after the higher price of 70.
Top price 70 <= 60 is False, so nothing is popped.
Push (60, 1). stack = [(100, 1), (80, 1), (70, 2), (60, 1)], prices still decreasing.
Return 1, because yesterday's 70 already blocks the view.
Day 6: sp.next(75) — this one will collapse several stack entries at once.
span = 1 to start today's count before any absorbing happens.
Top price 60 <= 75 is True.
Pop (60, 1) and absorb its span: span = 1 + 1 = 2.
Re-check: top price is now 70 and 70 <= 75 is True as well.
Pop (70, 2) and absorb its span of 2 in one shot: span = 2 + 2 = 4. Those two days were already summarised by day 4, so we never re-scan them.
Re-check: top price 80 <= 75 is False, so day 2 finally blocks today.
Push (75, 4) so a later day can absorb all four in one pop.
Return 4: days 3, 4, 5 and 6 all had prices <= 75, so the answer sequence so far is [1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 4].

Reverse Words in a String.desc: reverseWords is called with s = '  the sky   is blue  ' (21 characters, including 2 leading, 3 middle and 2 trailing spaces).

Before splitting, note the key fact: s.split() with NO argument is different from s.split(' '). The no-argument form treats any RUN of whitespace as one separator and drops empty pieces, so all the messy spacing is handled for free.
split() begins scanning at index 0. Characters 0 and 1 are spaces, so they are skipped — no empty word is produced.
From index 2 it collects 't','h','e' and stops at the space at index 5. First word: 'the'.
Skips the single space at index 5, collects 's','k','y' (indices 6-8), stops at index 9. Second word: 'sky'.
Indices 9, 10 and 11 are three consecutive spaces. Because split() collapses whitespace runs, they produce ZERO empty strings — this is why the answer will have single spaces.
Collects 'b','l','u','e' at indices 15-18, then the trailing spaces at 19-20 are discarded. Fourth word: 'blue'.
Line 3 finishes: words = ['the', 'sky', 'is', 'blue']. All whitespace noise is gone and we are left with a clean 4-element list.
Next we reverse the ORDER of the words — not the letters inside them. 'blue' must end up first.
words[::-1] is a slice with step -1: it starts at the last element, index 3 ('blue'), and walks backwards.
Step -1 again lands on index 2, 'is'. reversed_words = ['blue', 'is'].
Then index 1, 'sky', and finally index 0, 'the'. The slice builds a NEW list; the original `words` is untouched.
Last step: glue the words back together. Using ' '.join guarantees exactly ONE space between neighbours, which is what the problem asks for.
join walks the list: 'blue', then ' ' + 'is' → 'blue is', then ' ' + 'sky' → 'blue is sky', then ' ' + 'the'.
Return 'blue is sky the' — words reversed, all extra whitespace normalised to single spaces, no leading or trailing space.

Longest Palindromic Substring.desc: longestPalindrome('cbbd'). The guard `if not s` is False because the string has 4 characters, so we keep going.
start, end = 0, 0. These indices describe the best palindrome found so far — right now just the empty/first slot.
expandAroundCenter(left, right) is defined. It pushes two pointers apart while the characters match and reports how long the match grew.
Main loop, i = 0: we try character 'c' as a centre.
Odd case: call expandAroundCenter(0, 0), both pointers on 'c'.
Loop test: left = 0 >= 0, right = 0 < 4, and s[0] == s[0] ('c' == 'c') — trivially true, so we expand.
left -= 1 makes left = -1.
right += 1 makes right = 1.
Loop test again: left = -1 >= 0 is False, so we fell off the front of the string and stop.
Both pointers overshot by one, so the matched length is right - left - 1 = 1 - (-1) - 1 = 1. len1 = 1 (just 'c').
Even case: expandAroundCenter(0, 1) starts with the two pointers straddling the gap between 'c' and 'b'.
s[0] = 'c' and s[1] = 'b' differ, so the while body never runs — there is no even-length palindrome centred here.
Return right - left - 1 = 1 - 0 - 1 = 0. len2 = 0.
max_len = max(1, 0) = 1, the best palindrome centred at index 0.
Is max_len = 1 greater than end - start = 0? Yes, so record this palindrome.
start = i - (max_len - 1) // 2 = 0 - 0 = 0.
end = i + max_len // 2 = 0 + 0 = 0. Best so far is s[0:1] = 'c'.
i = 1: centre on the first 'b'.
Odd case expandAroundCenter(1, 1): s[1] == s[1] matches, so the pointers step apart to left = 0 and right = 2.
Test again: s[0] = 'c' vs s[2] = 'b' — mismatch, so the odd expansion stops.
len1 = 2 - 0 - 1 = 1: only the single 'b' itself.
Even case: expandAroundCenter(1, 2) puts the pointers on the two neighbouring characters s[1] and s[2].
s[1] = 'b' and s[2] = 'b' are equal, so this even-length centre really is a palindrome and we expand.
left -= 1 makes left = 0.
right += 1 makes right = 3.
Test: s[0] = 'c' vs s[3] = 'd' — mismatch, so the expansion stops with the pointers one step too wide.
len2 = right - left - 1 = 3 - 0 - 1 = 2, the length of 'bb'.
max_len = max(1, 2) = 2.
2 > end - start = 0, so this beats 'c' and we update the bounds.
end = 1 + 2 // 2 = 2. The best palindrome is now s[1:3] = 'bb'. This formula handles odd and even lengths alike.
i = 2: centre on the second 'b'.
expandAroundCenter(2, 2) returns 1 (s[1]='b' vs s[3]='d' mismatch) and expandAroundCenter(2, 3) returns 0, so max_len = 1.
1 > end - start = 2 - 1 = 1 is False, so 'bb' survives as the champion.
i = 3: the last centre, character 'd'.
expandAroundCenter(3, 3) returns 1 and expandAroundCenter(3, 4) returns 0 (right = 4 is past the end), so max_len = 1.
1 > 1 is False again, so nothing changes and the loop is finished.
Return s[start:end+1] = s[1:3] = 'bb'. We tried 2*4 - 1 = 7 centres, each expanding in O(N), hence O(N^2) time and O(1) extra space.

Roman to Integer.desc: romanToInt is called with s = 'MCMXCIV'. The expected answer is 1994 — let's see how one left-to-right pass gets there.
Build the lookup dict: I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000. Dict lookups are O(1) average, so each character costs constant time.
total = 0 — the running answer.
n = len(s) = 7. We will need n to know when there is no 'next' character.
Iteration 1: i = 0, character 'M'.
curr_val = roman['M'] = 1000.
Is there a next char? i+1 = 1 < 7, yes: s[1] = 'C' worth 100. Is 1000 < 100? No — the value does not grow to the right, so this is a normal additive numeral.
total += 1000 → total = 1000.
Iteration 2: i = 1, character 'C'.
curr_val = roman['C'] = 100.
Next char is s[2] = 'M' = 1000, and 100 < 1000 is TRUE. A smaller numeral sitting immediately left of a bigger one means subtraction: 'CM' = 900.
total -= 100 → total = 900. We do not look ahead and combine; we just pay -100 now and +1000 on the next step. Same result, far simpler code.
Iteration 3: i = 2, character 'M'.
curr_val = roman['M'] = 1000.
Next is s[3] = 'X' = 10, and 1000 < 10 is False, so we add.
total += 1000 → total = 1900. Together, steps for i=1 and i=2 contributed 900, which is exactly what 'CM' means.
Iteration 4: i = 3, character 'X', curr_val = 10.
Next is s[4] = 'C' = 100, and 10 < 100 is TRUE → subtract ('XC' = 90).
total -= 10 → total = 1890.
Iteration 5: i = 4, character 'C', curr_val = 100.
Next is s[5] = 'I' = 1, and 100 < 1 is False → add.
total += 100 → total = 1990. The 'XC' pair has now netted +90.
Iteration 6: i = 5, character 'I', curr_val = 1.
Next is s[6] = 'V' = 5, and 1 < 5 is TRUE → subtract ('IV' = 4).
total -= 1 → total = 1989.
Iteration 7 (last): i = 6, character 'V', curr_val = 5.
The first half of the condition, i + 1 < n, is 7 < 7 = False. Python short-circuits and never evaluates roman[s[7]], which would have crashed. So the last character is always simply added.
total += 5 → total = 1994.
i reaches 7, range(7) is exhausted, and the loop ends after exactly one pass over the string.
Return 1994. Verify: M(1000) + CM(900) + XC(90) + IV(4) = 1994. Time O(n), space O(1).

String to Integer (atoi).desc: myAtoi is called with s = '   -42abc' (spaces drawn as _). Expected answer: -42.
INT_MAX = 2**31 - 1 = 2147483647, the largest 32-bit signed integer.
INT_MIN = -2**31 = -2147483648. Anything outside [INT_MIN, INT_MAX] must be clamped.
i = 0 — our scanning cursor.
n = len(s) = 9, the number of characters we may scan.
Phase 1, skip whitespace. i = 0 < 9 and s[0] is a space, so the loop body runs.
i advances to 1, still inside the leading-whitespace run.
s[1] is also a space — keep going.
i advances to 2, the third and final leading space.
s[2] is the third and last space.
i advances to 3, which is the first non-space character.
s[3] is '-', not a space, so the while condition fails and whitespace skipping ends with i = 3.
Guard: is i == n? 3 != 9, so the string was not all spaces and we have real content to parse.
Phase 2, the sign. Assume positive: sign = 1.
s[3] == '-' is True.
sign = -1. We remember the sign separately and build the digits as a positive number — much easier than negating as we go.
i advances past the sign to 4.
Phase 3, the digits. res = 0 will accumulate the magnitude.
i = 4 < 9 and s[4] = '4' is a digit, so we enter the accumulation loop.
digit = int('4') = 4.
Overflow guard BEFORE multiplying: is res > (INT_MAX - digit) // 10, i.e. 0 > (2147483647 - 4) // 10 = 214748364? No. Checking first avoids ever creating the oversized number.
res = 0 * 10 + 4 = 4. Multiplying by 10 shifts the old digits left, exactly like writing the number by hand.
i advances to 5 so the loop can look at the next character.
s[5] = '2' is a digit, so we loop again.
digit = int('2') = 2.
i advances to 6, moving past the last digit of 42.
s[6] = 'a' — isdigit() is False, so the loop stops. Trailing junk like 'abc' is simply ignored, not an error.
For contrast: had the digits been '9999999999', this line would have fired once res exceeded 214748364 and returned INT_MIN = -2147483648 (because sign is -1) instead of overflowing.
Return sign * res = -1 * 42 = -42. One left-to-right pass, O(n) time and O(1) space.

Longest Common Prefix.desc: The list holds 5 strings, so it is not empty and the early exit is skipped.
The optimistic start: prefix = strs[0] = "flowerpot", 9 characters long. It can only shrink from here.
i=1: check the candidate prefix against strs[1] = "flowering".
"flowering" does not start with "flowerpot" - they agree on "flower" but then p vs i. Enter the shrink loop.
Chop the last character: prefix = "flowerpo".
prefix is still non-empty, so keep going rather than bailing out with "".
"flowering" still does not start with "flowerpo", so shrink once more.
Chop again: prefix = "flowerp".
"flowering" does not start with "flowerp" either - the mismatch is at position 6 (p vs i).
Chop the p: prefix = "flower".
"flowering".startswith("flower") is True, so the while loop exits after 3 shrinks.
i=2: the next string is "flowchart", which will force more shrinking.
"flowchart" does not start with "flower" - they diverge at position 4 (e vs c).
Chop the r: prefix = "flowe", now five characters long.
Still non-empty, so the search for a shorter common prefix continues.
"flowchart" does not start with "flowe" either, because its 5th character is c.
Chop the e as well: prefix = "flow", four characters.
"flowchart".startswith("flow") is True - the prefix has settled at 4 characters.
i=3: compare the current prefix "flow" with strs[3] = "flown".
"flown" already starts with "flow", so the while loop body never runs and nothing shrinks.
i=4: the last string is "flow" itself, the shortest in the list.
A string is a prefix of itself, so this check passes immediately too - and it caps the answer at the shortest string.
Every string survived the test, so return "flow" as the longest common prefix.

Rabin Karp.desc: We search for pattern "cab" inside text "abcab". n = len(text) = 5 and m = len(pattern) = 3.
Guard check: is m (3) greater than n (5)? No, so the pattern can still fit and we continue.
base = 256 — we treat each character as a digit in base 256 (one byte per character).
prime = 101 — every hash is taken modulo 101 so the numbers stay small instead of exploding.
h = 1 for now. h will become base^(m-1) % prime = 256^2 % 101, the weight of the leftmost character.
Loop to build h runs m-1 = 2 times, multiplying h by 256 each time (mod 101).
p_hash = 0 — the rolling hash accumulator for the pattern starts empty.
t_hash = 0 — the accumulator for the first window of text starts empty too.
Now one loop computes BOTH hashes over the first m = 3 characters: pattern "cab" and window "abc".
i=2: pattern[2] = 'b' (98). p_hash = (256*90 + 98) % 101 = 23138 % 101 = 9. Pattern hash is fixed at 9.
Sliding loop starts, i = 0. There are n-m+1 = 3 windows to test: "abc", "bca", "cab".
i=0: compare hashes — p_hash = 9 but t_hash = 90. Different, so "abc" cannot equal "cab"; no string compare needed.
i=0 < n-m = 2, so another window exists — roll the hash instead of recomputing it from scratch.
Drop 'a' (weight h=88) and add text[3]='a': t_hash = (256*(90 - 97*88) + 97) % 101 = 28. Window "bca" hashes to 28.
Python's % already returns a non-negative value, so t_hash = 28 is not negative and we skip the fix-up.
Next iteration: i = 1, window is text[1:4] = "bca".
i=1: p_hash = 9 vs t_hash = 28 — still different, so "bca" is rejected in O(1) time.
Roll again: drop 'b' (98*88) and add text[4]='b': t_hash = (256*(28 - 98*88) + 98) % 101 = 9.
Next iteration: i = 2, the last window text[2:5] = "cab".
i=2: p_hash = 9 equals t_hash = 9 — a hash hit! But equal hashes can still be a collision, so we must verify.
Verify literally: text[2:5] = "cab" and pattern = "cab" — the characters really do match, no collision.
Return i = 2: the pattern "cab" starts at index 2 of "abcab". Final answer is 2.

Z Function.desc: Input string is s = "aabaab", so n = 6. The Z-array will say, for each index, how long a prefix of s restarts there.
z = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] — one slot per index, all zero for now. z[0] is left as 0 by convention here.
l = 0 and r = 0 define the current Z-box: the rightmost window we already know matches the prefix.
First iteration: i = 1. We ask how many characters starting at index 1 match the start of "aabaab".
Is i = 1 inside the box [l, r] = [0, 0]? 1 <= 0 is false, so there is nothing to reuse; z[1] stays 0 and we compare by hand.
Expand: s[z[1]] = s[0] = 'a' vs s[1 + 0] = s[1] = 'a'. They match, so enter the loop body.
z[1] becomes 1 — one character of the prefix ("a") is repeated at index 1.
Try to extend: s[1] = 'a' vs s[1 + 1] = s[2] = 'b'. Mismatch, so the while loop stops with z[1] = 1.
Does this match reach past r? i + z[i] - 1 = 1 + 1 - 1 = 1, and 1 > r = 0, so yes — record a new box.
l = 1: the new Z-box starts at index 1.
r = i + z[i] - 1 = 1. The box is [1, 1], meaning s[1..1] equals s[0..0].
Second iteration: i = 2, the character 'b'.
Is 2 <= r = 1? No, i sits outside the box, so again no reuse and z[2] stays at 0.
Compare s[0] = 'a' with s[2] = 'b'. Mismatch on the very first character, so z[2] stays 0.
i + z[i] - 1 = 2 + 0 - 1 = 1, which is not greater than r = 1, so the box [1, 1] is left unchanged.
Third iteration: i = 3. Note s[3:] = "aab", which is the whole prefix again — expect a big value.
3 <= r = 1 is false, so we start from z[3] = 0 and compare characters directly.
s[0] = 'a' vs s[3 + 0] = 'a' — match.
z[3] = 1 after the first matching character.
Loop again: s[1] = 'a' vs s[4] = 'a' match, so z[3] = 2.
Loop again: s[2] = 'b' vs s[5] = 'b' match, so z[3] = 3 — the entire prefix "aab" repeats at index 3.
Condition i + z[i] = 3 + 3 = 6 is not < n = 6, so we have run off the end of the string and the while loop exits.
3 + 3 - 1 = 5 > r = 1, so a bigger box is found: l = 3.
r = 5. Box is now [3, 5]: we know s[3..5] = "aab" equals the prefix s[0..2].
Fourth iteration: i = 4. This is where the box pays off.
4 <= r = 5, so index 4 lies inside the known box and we can copy an earlier answer instead of comparing from scratch.
z[4] = min(r - i + 1, z[i - l]) = min(5 - 4 + 1, z[1]) = min(2, 1) = 1. Free work reused from index 1.
Try to grow past the copied value: s[1] = 'a' vs s[4 + 1] = s[5] = 'b'. Mismatch, so z[4] stays 1.
4 + 1 - 1 = 4 is not greater than r = 5, so the box [3, 5] survives unchanged.
Last iteration: i = 5, the final character 'b'.
Verify by hand anyway: s[0] = 'a' vs s[5] = 'b' — mismatch, so z[5] correctly remains 0.
The loop is finished. Return z = [0, 1, 0, 3, 1, 0]: index 3 restarts the full prefix "aab".

KMP Algorithm.desc: We look for pattern = "abab" inside text = "abcabab". m = len(pattern) = 4.
n = len(text) = 7. KMP will scan the text exactly once, never moving i backwards.
Is m == 0? No, the pattern has 4 characters, so we do not take the empty-pattern shortcut.
Phase 1 — build the LPS table. lps = [0, 0, 0, 0], one slot per pattern character.
length = 0 tracks the length of the current longest prefix that is also a suffix.
i = 1: lps[0] is always 0 (a single character has no proper prefix), so we start comparing at index 1.
i=1: pattern[1] = 'b' vs pattern[length] = pattern[0] = 'a'. They differ, so go to the else branch.
length is 0, so there is no shorter border to fall back to — take the inner else.
lps[1] = 0: prefix "ab" has no proper prefix that is also a suffix.
i advances to 2, so next we compare pattern[2] with pattern[0].
i=2: pattern[2] = 'a' vs pattern[0] = 'a' — a match!
length grows to 1 because one prefix character matched here.
lps[2] = 1: in "aba" the prefix "a" is also a suffix.
i advances to 3, the last character of the pattern "abab".
i=3: pattern[3] = 'b' vs pattern[length] = pattern[1] = 'b' — match again.
length grows to 2 because "ab" now matches at both ends.
lps[3] = 2: in "abab" the prefix "ab" is also the suffix "ab".
i becomes 4, which is not < m = 4, so the LPS build ends with lps = [0, 0, 1, 2].
Phase 2 — search. i = 0 walks the text "abcabab".
j = 0 walks the pattern "abab". j also doubles as "how many characters currently match".
i=0, j=0: pattern[0] = 'a' equals text[0] = 'a' — the first character lines up.
Both advance: i = 1, j = 1. We have matched "a" so far.
Is j = 1 equal to m = 4? Not yet, the pattern is not fully matched.
i=1, j=1: pattern[1] = 'b' equals text[1] = 'b'. Advance again to i = 2, j = 2; matched "ab".
i=2, j=2: pattern[2] = 'a' but text[2] = 'c' — mismatch after 2 matched characters.
j = 2 is not 0, so instead of restarting the text pointer we consult the LPS table.
j = lps[j-1] = lps[1] = 0. "ab" has no reusable border, so the pattern slides fully past — but i stays at 2.
i=2, j=0: pattern[0] = 'a' vs text[2] = 'c' — still no match, so nothing advances here.
Mismatch with j already 0 means there is nothing to reuse: just slide the text pointer, i = 3.
i=3, j=0: pattern[0] = 'a' equals text[3] = 'a'. Advance to i = 4, j = 1; matched "a".
i=4, j=1: pattern[1] = 'b' equals text[4] = 'b'. Advance to i = 5, j = 2; matched "ab".
i=5, j=2: pattern[2] = 'a' equals text[5] = 'a'. Advance to i = 6, j = 3; matched "aba".
i=6, j=3: pattern[3] = 'b' equals text[6] = 'b'. Advance to i = 7, j = 4; matched "abab".
Now j = 4 equals m = 4 — the whole pattern has been consumed, so we have a full match.
Return i - j = 7 - 4 = 3. "abab" starts at index 3 of "abcabab". Final answer is 3.

Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome.desc: Input s = "aab". It is not empty, so we skip the early return and do real work.
Build temp = s + "$" + reversed(s) = "aab" + "$" + "baa" = "aab$baa". The '$' guarantees the two halves never overlap.
n = len(temp) = 7. The longest prefix of temp that is also a suffix tells us the longest palindromic prefix of "aab".
lps = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] — one slot per character of temp.
length = 0: the length of the prefix-suffix border matched so far.
i = 1, because lps[0] is always 0.
i=1: temp[1] = 'a' equals temp[length] = temp[0] = 'a' — the border can grow.
length becomes 1: one character of the border is confirmed.
lps[1] = 1: the prefix "aa" has border "a".
i advances to 2, the letter 'b' of the original half.
i=2: temp[2] = 'b' vs temp[length] = temp[1] = 'a' — mismatch, so take the else branch.
length = 1 is not 0, so there is a shorter border to fall back to before giving up.
length = lps[length-1] = lps[0] = 0. Notice i does NOT move — we retry index 2 against a shorter border.
Retry i=2: temp[2] = 'b' vs temp[0] = 'a' — still a mismatch.
Now length is already 0, so lps[2] = 0: "aab" has no border.
i advances to 3, which is the separator '$'.
i=3: temp[3] = '$' vs temp[0] = 'a' — mismatch, and length is 0.
lps[3] = 0. The '$' can never match a letter, which is exactly why it stops the two halves from bleeding into each other.
i advances to 4, the first character of the reversed half.
i=4: temp[4] = 'b' vs temp[0] = 'a' — mismatch with length already 0.
lps[4] = 0, then i moves on to 5.
i=5: temp[5] = 'a' equals temp[0] = 'a' — a border starts forming across the '$'.
length becomes 1 and lps[5] = 1: prefix "a" also ends the string so far.
i advances to 6, the final character.
i=6: temp[6] = 'a' equals temp[length] = temp[1] = 'a' — the border extends.
length = 2 and lps[6] = 2: the prefix "aa" of temp is also its suffix "aa".
i becomes 7, which is not < n = 7, so the LPS loop ends with lps = [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2].
lps[-1] = 2 means the longest palindromic PREFIX of "aab" is "aa" (length 2). Return len(s) - 2 = 3 - 2 = 1: adding one 'b' in front gives "baab".

Anagram Check.desc: s = "cat" and t = "act". Both have length 3, so len(s) != len(t) is false and we keep going.
count = 26 zeros, one bucket per lowercase letter. Bucket 0 is 'a', bucket 2 is 'c', bucket 19 is 't'.
First iteration: i = 0. We will handle s[0] and t[0] in the same pass — one adds, the other subtracts.
s[0] = 'c'; ord('c') - ord('a') = 2, so count[2] += 1 becomes 1.
t[0] = 'a'; index 0, so count[0] -= 1 becomes -1. Negative just means t has that letter more often so far.
Second iteration: i = 1, looking at s[1] = 'a' and t[1] = 'c'.
s[1] = 'a' -> count[0] += 1, taking it from -1 back up to 0. The earlier debt is repaid.
t[1] = 'c' -> count[2] -= 1, taking it from 1 down to 0.
Third iteration: i = 2, the last pair s[2] = 't' and t[2] = 't'.
s[2] = 't'; ord('t') - ord('a') = 19, so count[19] += 1 becomes 1.
t[2] = 't' -> count[19] -= 1 returns it to 0. i now reaches 3, so the counting loop ends.
Verification pass: walk every bucket. First val = count[0] = 0 (the 'a' bucket).
0 != 0 is false, so bucket 'a' is balanced and we do not return False.
Next val = count[1] = 0, the 'b' bucket — untouched by either string, so balanced.
Still zero, keep scanning. Buckets 'c' (index 2) and 't' (index 19) are the only two we ever touched.
Reaching index 19, the 't' bucket: it was incremented once by s and decremented once by t.
count[19] = 0, so no early return here either. The remaining buckets up to index 25 are all untouched zeros.
Every one of the 26 buckets ended at 0, so "cat" and "act" use exactly the same letters. Return True.

Count and Say.desc: We want the 4th term of the count-and-say sequence. n = 4 is greater than 0, so we skip the empty-string guard.
curr = "1" — the 1st term is fixed. We will rebuild it three times to reach the 4th term.
Outer loop pass 1 of 3 (range(1, 4)): turn term 1 into term 2 by reading "1" out loud.
next_str = [] — an empty list we append pieces to, because joining a list is far cheaper than += on strings.
i = 0, the scan position inside curr = "1".
0 < len(curr) = 1, so there is a run to describe.
count = 1: we have seen the character at index 0 once so far.
Inner loop test: i+1 = 1 is not < len(curr) = 1, so there is no next character — the run is just one '1'.
Append str(count) = "1" to next_str.
Append the character itself, curr[0] = '1'. So we said "one 1" = "11".
i moves to 1, which ends the while loop for this pass.
curr = "".join(['1','1']) = "11". That is term 2.
Outer loop pass 2 of 3: read "11" out loud.
i = 0, count = 1 for the character '1' at index 0.
Inner check: i+1 = 1 < 2 and curr[0] = '1' equals curr[1] = '1' — the run continues.
count becomes 2 — we have now seen two '1's in a row.
i moves to 1, the last character of the run.
Inner check again: i+1 = 2 is not < 2, so the run of '1's stops here with count = 2.
Append "2" (the count).
Append curr[1] = '1' (the character). We said "two 1s" = "21".
i becomes 2, so the while loop ends for this pass.
curr = "21". That is term 3.
Outer loop pass 3 of 3: read "21" out loud. This time there are two separate runs.
i = 0, count = 1 for '2'.
Inner check: curr[0] = '2' does not equal curr[1] = '1', so this run has length 1.
Append "1" then '2': "one 2".
i moves to 1, and 1 < 2 so the while loop runs a second time for the same term.
New run: count resets to 1 for curr[1] = '1'.
Inner check: i+1 = 2 is not < 2, so this run is a single '1'.
Append "1" and '1': "one 1". next_str is now ['1','2','1','1'].
i becomes 2, ending the while loop.
curr = "1211" — that is "one 2, one 1", term 4. The outer loop has now run all 3 times.
Return curr = "1211". The sequence went 1 -> 11 -> 21 -> 1211. Final answer is "1211".

Compare Version Numbers.desc: version1 = "1.01.3.0" split on '.' gives v1_parts = ['1', '01', '3', '0'] — four revision chunks.
version2 = "1.1.3" splits into v2_parts = ['1', '1', '3'] — only three chunks.
n1 = 4 and n2 = 3. The lengths differ, which is exactly the tricky case this loop is designed for.
Loop over range(max(4, 3)) = range(4), so i goes 0, 1, 2, 3 — we cover every chunk of the longer version.
i=0: 0 < n1 = 4, so num1 = int(v1_parts[0]) = int('1') = 1.
i=0: 0 < n2 = 3, so num2 = int(v2_parts[0]) = int('1') = 1.
Is 1 < 1? No, so version1 is not behind at this chunk.
Is 1 > 1? No either — the chunks tie, so we must look at the next chunk to break the tie.
Second iteration: i = 1.
i=1: num1 = int('01'). This is the classic trap — as a STRING '01' != '1', but int('01') = 1.
i=1: num2 = int(v2_parts[1]) = int('1') = 1. Converting to int made the leading zero harmless.
Compare again: 1 < 1 is false, so no -1 is returned here.
1 > 1 is false too, so chunk 1 also ties and we continue.
Third iteration: i = 2.
i=2: num1 = int(v1_parts[2]) = int('3') = 3.
i=2: num2 = int(v2_parts[2]) = int('3') = 3.
Compare chunk 2: 3 < 3 is false, so version1 is not behind.
3 > 3 is false. Still tied after three chunks — and version2 has run out of chunks.
Fourth iteration: i = 3. Only version1 has a chunk here, so this is where the padding rule matters.
i=3: 3 < n1 = 4, so num1 = int(v1_parts[3]) = int('0') = 0.
i=3: 3 < n2 = 3 is FALSE, so the missing chunk is treated as 0. num2 = 0 — "1.3" and "1.3.0" mean the same release.
Compare the padded chunk: 0 < 0 is false, so still tied.
0 > 0 is false. The loop finishes without ever returning early.
Every chunk tied, so the versions are equal: return 0. "1.01.3.0" == "1.1.3".

Longest Palindromic Prefix.desc: s = "abaxyz". It is non-empty, so we do not return the empty string early.
temp = s + "$" + s[::-1] = "abaxyz" + "$" + "zyxaba" = "abaxyz$zyxaba". A prefix of temp that is also a suffix is a prefix of s that reads the same backwards — a palindromic prefix.
n = len(temp) = 13: six letters, the '$', then six reversed letters.
lps = thirteen zeros, one per character of temp.
length = 0 — no border matched yet.
i = 1, since lps[0] is always 0 for a single character.
i=1: temp[1] = 'b' vs temp[0] = 'a' — mismatch.
length is already 0, so lps[1] = 0 and there is nothing to fall back to.
i advances to 2, the second 'a' of "aba" inside temp.
i=2: temp[2] = 'a' equals temp[0] = 'a' — a one-character border appears.
length becomes 1: the border is one character long.
lps[2] = 1: "aba" starts and ends with 'a'.
i advances to 3, the letter 'x' that will break the border.
i=3: temp[3] = 'x' vs temp[length] = temp[1] = 'b' — mismatch after a partial border.
length = 1 is not 0, so before writing 0 we retreat to the next shorter border.
length = lps[length-1] = lps[0] = 0. Crucially i stays at 3 — we retry the same character.
Retry i=3: temp[3] = 'x' vs temp[0] = 'a' — still a mismatch, and now length is 0.
lps[3] = 0, then i moves to 4.
i=4: temp[4] = 'y' vs temp[0] = 'a' — mismatch, so lps[4] = 0 and i becomes 5.
The same 'no match, write 0, advance' branch repeats for i = 5 ('z'), i = 6 ('$'), i = 7 ('z'), i = 8 ('y') and i = 9 ('x') — none of them equal temp[0] = 'a'.
i=10: temp[10] = 'a' equals temp[0] = 'a' — the reversed half finally starts matching the prefix.
length = 1, lps[10] = 1.
i=11: temp[11] = 'b' equals temp[length] = temp[1] = 'b' — the border grows.
length = 2, lps[11] = 2.
i=12: temp[12] = 'a' equals temp[2] = 'a' — the border grows once more.
length = 3, lps[12] = 3: the prefix "aba" of temp is also its suffix "aba".
i becomes 13, which is not < n = 13, so the LPS construction ends.
max_len = lps[-1] = 3 — the longest prefix of "abaxyz" that also appears reversed at the end is 3 characters long.
Return s[:3] = "aba". That is the longest palindromic prefix of "abaxyz".

Implement strstr().desc: haystack = "acaabc", needle = "aab". The needle is not empty, so we skip the return-0 shortcut.
n = len(haystack) = 6.
m = len(needle) = 3.
lps = [0, 0, 0] — the failure table for "aab", one entry per needle character.
length = 0: length of the longest proper prefix of "aab" that is also a suffix, so far.
i = 1 because lps[0] is always 0.
i=1: needle[1] = 'a' equals needle[length] = needle[0] = 'a' — a border of length 1 exists.
length becomes 1 since both of the first needle characters are 'a'.
lps[1] = 1: in "aa" the prefix "a" is also the suffix.
i advances to 2, the last needle character 'b'.
i=2: needle[2] = 'b' vs needle[length] = needle[1] = 'a' — mismatch, take the else branch.
length = 1 is not 0, so fall back to a shorter border before writing a 0.
length = lps[length-1] = lps[0] = 0. i is deliberately NOT advanced — index 2 is retried.
Retry i=2: needle[2] = 'b' vs needle[0] = 'a' — mismatch again, and now length is 0.
lps[2] = 0: "aab" has no proper prefix that is also a suffix.
i becomes 3, which is not < m = 3, so the table is finished: lps = [0, 1, 0].
Search phase. i = 0 scans the haystack and never moves backwards.
j = 0 scans the needle and also counts how many characters currently match.
i=0, j=0: needle[0] = 'a' equals haystack[0] = 'a' — a promising start.
i advances to 1, moving one step along the haystack.
j advances to 1. Matched so far: "a".
Is j = 1 equal to m = 3? No, the needle is not fully matched yet.
i=1, j=1: needle[1] = 'a' but haystack[1] = 'c' — mismatch after one matched character.
j = 1 is not 0, so use the table instead of rewinding i.
j = lps[j-1] = lps[0] = 0. The needle slides so that its start lines up with haystack index 1; i stays put at 1.
i=1, j=0: needle[0] = 'a' vs haystack[1] = 'c' — not equal, so nothing advances in this if.
Mismatch with j already 0 means no prefix to reuse, so slide the haystack pointer: i = 2.
i=2, j=0: needle[0] = 'a' equals haystack[2] = 'a'. Advance both: i = 3, j = 1; matched "a".
i=3, j=1: needle[1] = 'a' equals haystack[3] = 'a'. Advance both: i = 4, j = 2; matched "aa".
i=4, j=2: needle[2] = 'b' equals haystack[4] = 'b'. Advance both: i = 5, j = 3; matched "aab".
Now j = 3 equals m = 3 — every needle character has been consumed, so this is a full match.
Return i - j = 5 - 3 = 2. "aab" begins at index 2 of "acaabc". Final answer is 2.

Postorder Traversal.desc: The tree is root 1 with left subtree 2 (children 4 and 5, and 5 has a left child 7) and right subtree 3 (only a right child 6). res will collect the postorder order: left subtree, right subtree, then node.
root = node 1 is not None, so we skip the early return on line 11. stack holds the chain of ancestors we have descended through but not finished. It starts empty.
curr = root = node 1: curr is the node we still have to descend from.
last_visited = None. This single variable is what makes one stack enough: it remembers the node we just output, so we can tell 'coming down' from 'coming back up'.
stack is empty but curr = 1 is not None, so the loop runs.
curr = 1 is truthy, so we are still descending: remember 1 and keep going left.
Push node 1. stack = [1].
curr = 1.left = node 2, so the descent continues into the left subtree.
Push node 2 as well: stack = [1, 2], the ancestors we still owe output to.
curr = 2.left = node 4, one level deeper down the left spine.
Push node 4. stack = [1, 2, 4] — the leftmost spine of the tree is now stacked.
curr = 4.left = None: node 4 is a leaf, so the descent bottoms out here.
curr is None, so we inspect (not pop) the top of the stack: peek_node = node 4.
Node 4 has no right child, so the condition is False: there is nothing left to explore below 4.
Output node 4: res = [4]. Postorder's first value is always the deepest-leftmost leaf.
Pop node 4 and set last_visited = 4. stack = [1, 2].
curr is still None, so peek again: peek_node = node 2, which we descended past earlier.
node 2 has a right child (node 5) and last_visited = 4 is not that child, so node 2 is NOT finished: we must go right before we may print 2.
curr = node 5. Node 2 deliberately stays on the stack, waiting for its right subtree.
Push node 5. stack = [1, 2, 5].
curr = 5.left = node 7, so we descend again — this is where a 3-node example would have nothing left to show.
Push node 7. stack = [1, 2, 5, 7], the deepest the stack ever gets.
curr = 7.left = None; node 7 is a leaf.
peek_node = 7 has no right child, so output it: res = [4, 7].
Pop node 7, last_visited = 7. stack = [1, 2, 5].
peek_node = node 5, whose right child is None, so the condition is False and 5 is ready.
Output node 5 after its only child 7: res = [4, 7, 5].
Pop node 5, last_visited = 5. stack = [1, 2].
peek_node = node 2 for the second time. Without last_visited we would now walk into node 5 again and loop forever.
peek_node.right is node 5 and last_visited is also node 5, so the condition is False: 2's right subtree is already done.
Output node 2, after both of its subtrees: res = [4, 7, 5, 2].
Pop node 2, last_visited = 2. stack = [1] — the whole left half of the tree is finished.
peek_node = root 1; its right child is node 3 and last_visited = 2 is not node 3, so we owe the right subtree a visit.
curr = node 3. The root stays parked on the stack.
Push node 3. stack = [1, 3].
curr = 3.left = None: node 3 has no left child at all, so the descent stops after one push.
peek_node = 3 has right child 6 and last_visited = 2 is not 6, so curr = node 6.
Push node 6. stack = [1, 3, 6], then curr = 6.left = None.
peek_node = 6 is a leaf, so output it: res = [4, 7, 5, 2, 6].
Pop node 6, last_visited = 6. stack = [1, 3].
peek_node = 3, and last_visited = 6 IS 3's right child, so line 26 is False and node 3 is printed: res = [4, 7, 5, 2, 6, 3].
Pop node 3, last_visited = 3. stack = [1].
peek_node = root 1 and last_visited = 3 is its right child, so the root is finally output last: res = [4, 7, 5, 2, 6, 3, 1].
Pop the root. stack = [] and curr is None, so the while condition on line 18 is finally false.
Return res = [4, 7, 5, 2, 6, 3, 1]: every node appears after both of its subtrees, produced with one stack and no recursion.

Level Order Traversal.desc: Input tree is [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]: root 3 with children 9 and 20, and 20 in turn has children 15 and 7. res starts as an empty list of levels.
Guard against the empty tree: root is node 3, which is truthy, so we skip the early return and start a real BFS.
Seed the queue with the root only: queue = [3]. A deque is used because popleft() is O(1), unlike list.pop(0).
Outer loop check: queue = [3] is non-empty, so there is a level to process. This iteration handles level 0.
level_size = len(queue) = 1. Snapshotting the size NOW is the whole trick: children pushed later in this pass belong to the next level, not this one.
curr_level = [] — a fresh bucket that will collect the values of every node sitting at level 0.
Inner loop, iteration 1 of level_size = 1. We will drain exactly one node here even if the queue grows meanwhile.
node = queue.popleft() takes node 3 off the front. queue is momentarily empty.
Record the value: curr_level = [3]. Level 0 contains just the root.
Does node 3 have a left child? Yes, node 9, so the condition is True and we enqueue it.
queue.append(9). The queue now holds [9] — the first member of the NEXT level.
Does node 3 have a right child? Yes, node 20, so this condition is True as well.
queue.append(20), giving queue = [9, 20]. Level 0 is now fully drained and level 1 is fully queued.
The inner for-loop ran level_size = 1 times and stops. Push the finished bucket: res = [[3]].
Outer loop check again: queue = [9, 20] is non-empty, so we start level 1.
level_size = len(queue) = 2 — exactly the two nodes that live on level 1, captured before any of their children arrive.
curr_level = [] again, a fresh bucket for level 1.
Inner loop, iteration 1 of 2 for this level.
node = queue.popleft() = node 9; queue shrinks to [20].
curr_level = [9]. Node 9 is a leaf, so nothing new will be queued from it.
node 9 has no left child (None is falsy) and, on line 31, no right child either — both enqueue lines are skipped entirely.
Inner loop, iteration 2 of 2 — the second and last node of level 1.
node = queue.popleft() = node 20; the queue is empty again for a moment.
curr_level = [9, 20]. Note the left-to-right order is preserved purely by FIFO queue discipline.
node 20 has a left child 15, so queue.append(15) makes queue = [15].
node 20 also has a right child 7, so queue.append(7) makes queue = [15, 7] — all of level 2, in order.
Level 1 is complete: res = [[3], [9, 20]].
queue = [15, 7] is still non-empty, so a third pass begins for level 2.
level_size = 2 for the two nodes 15 and 7.
curr_level = [] one last time, for the deepest level of this tree.
Iteration 1: node = queue.popleft() = node 15, leaving queue = [7].
curr_level = [15]. Node 15 is a leaf, so both child checks fail and nothing is enqueued.
Iteration 2: node = queue.popleft() = node 7, and now the queue is truly empty.
curr_level = [15, 7]. Node 7 is a leaf too, so no children are added.
Level 2 is complete: res = [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]].
Outer loop check: the queue is empty, so `while queue` is False and the BFS stops. Every node entered and left the queue exactly once.
Return res = [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]] — the node values grouped level by level, top to bottom, left to right.

Maximum Depth of Binary Tree.desc: Call maxDepth(root) on the tree [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]: node 3 has children 9 and 20, and node 20 has children 15 and 7.
Base-case test: root is node 3, which is not None, so we fall through and must ask both children for their depths.
Recurse left first: left_depth of node 3 will come from maxDepth(node 9). The current frame pauses here until node 9 answers.
New frame entered with root = node 9. The call stack is now maxDepth(3) -> maxDepth(9).
Node 9 is not None, so this frame also has to recurse into its children before it can answer.
Node 9 has no left child, so this call is maxDepth(None) — the recursion is about to hit bottom.
In the None frame the test `not root` is True: an empty tree has been reached.
Return 0 for the empty left subtree of node 9. This is the value that stops the recursion from going deeper.
Back in node 9's frame: left_depth = 0. Now recurse right, which is also None.
The right child of node 9 is None as well, so that call immediately returns 0.
Node 9 now has left_depth = 0 and right_depth = 0, so it returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1 — a leaf has depth 1.
Back in the root's frame: left_depth = 1 (from node 9). Now the right branch is explored with maxDepth(node 20).
New frame with root = node 20. Unlike node 9, this node has two children, so its subtree is one level taller.
Node 20 is not None, so we keep descending instead of returning 0.
Recurse into node 20's left child, node 15.
New frame with root = node 15, the deepest-left node of the right subtree. Stack is maxDepth(3) -> maxDepth(20) -> maxDepth(15).
Node 15 is not None, so it must still ask its two (empty) children.
Node 15 has no left child, so maxDepth(None) is called for its left side.
That empty call returns 0, giving node 15 a left_depth of 0.
Node 15 now recurses right, which is also None.
The right side of node 15 is empty too, so it returns 0.
Node 15 returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1 to node 20 — another leaf of depth 1.
Back in node 20's frame: left_depth = 1. Now recurse into its right child, node 7.
New frame with root = node 7, the last unexplored node of the tree.
Node 7 is not None, so the same leaf pattern repeats one more time.
Node 7 has no left child; maxDepth(None) is called.
It returns 0, so node 7's left_depth is 0.
Node 7 recurses right, which is None as well.
That call returns 0 too, so node 7 has no non-empty children.
Node 7 returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1 back up to node 20.
Node 20 finally has left_depth = 1 (node 15) and right_depth = 1 (node 7), so it returns 1 + max(1, 1) = 2 for its own subtree.
The root frame now has left_depth = 1 (node 9) and right_depth = 2 (node 20). It returns 1 + max(1, 2) = 3.

Check if Binary Tree is Balanced.desc: Tree: root 1 has left child 2 (with leaves 4 and 5) and right child 3, whose only child 6 has a single right child 7. Seven nodes, deliberately lopsided on the right.
Kick off one postorder pass with check(1). The helper returns a real height when a subtree is balanced and the poison value -1 the moment it is not.
Node 1 is not None, so we skip the base case and must measure both of its subtrees.
Descend left: call check(2) to measure the root's left subtree first.
Node 2 is not None either; keep going down.
Descend left again: call check(4), the leftmost leaf.
Node 4 exists, so its own two children get measured before it reports anything.
check(4.left) hits the empty-node base case and returns height 0.
left_h = 0 for node 4, which is not the -1 poison value, so we carry on.
check(4.right) is also the empty base case, so right_h = 0.
abs(0 - 0) = 0, comfortably within 1, so node 4 is balanced.
Return 1 + max(0, 0) = 1: node 4 is a leaf of height 1.
Back in check(2): left_h = 1, not -1, so the left side is fine and we can look right.
Call check(5), node 2's right child, now that its left side reported height 1.
Node 5 is a real node, so it too runs the full body.
Both of node 5's children are None so left_h = right_h = 0; the difference is 0 and check(5) returns height 1.
right_h = 1 for node 2, again not the poison value.
abs(1 - 1) = 0 for node 2 - its two leaves are level, so the subtree {2, 4, 5} is balanced.
check(2) returns 1 + max(1, 1) = 2. The whole left half of the tree has now been certified.
Back in check(1): left_h = 2, not -1, so the root's left side is fine so far.
Now the root's right side: call check(3), the branch that will actually fail.
Node 3 is not None. It has no left child at all but a chain hanging on the right.
check(3.left) is the empty base case, so left_h = 0 for node 3.
left_h = 0 is a legitimate height, not -1, so we keep measuring.
Call check(6), node 3's only child and the whole of its right subtree.
Node 6 is real; it also has no left child, only a right child 7.
check(6.left) returns 0, so left_h = 0 for node 6 as well.
Call check(7), the deepest node on this chain.
Node 7 is a leaf with two empty children, so it returns height 1.
Back in check(6): right_h = 1 from leaf 7, and it is not the -1 poison value.
abs(0 - 1) = 1 for node 6, which is exactly the allowed limit, so node 6 is still balanced.
check(6) returns 1 + max(0, 1) = 2, so node 3 sees a right subtree of height 2.
Back in check(3): right_h = 2 and it is not -1, so nothing has failed yet - the failure is about to come from node 3 itself.
abs(0 - 2) = 2 which is greater than 1: node 3 has an empty left side but a right side of height 2, so this subtree is unbalanced.
Return the poison value -1 from check(3) instead of a height.
Back in check(1): right_h == -1, so the failure detected two levels down has arrived at the root.
Return -1 immediately - the root never even compares its own heights, and no further node is visited.
check(root) came back as -1, so the expression is False: this tree is not height-balanced.

Diameter of Binary Tree.desc: The tree has 9 nodes and leans left. max_diameter = [0] is a one-element list so the nested helper can mutate it.
height(root) is called on node 1. Every node will be asked for its height exactly once, bottom-up.
Node 1 first needs its left height, so it recurses into node 2 before doing anything else.
Node 2 also postpones its own work and recurses left into node 4.
Node 4 recurses left into node 7. The call stack is now 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 7.
Node 7 recurses left into node 9, the deepest node on this branch.
Node 9 has no left child, so height(None) hits the base case and returns 0 — left_h = 0 for node 9.
Node 9 asks for its right height; node 9 is a leaf, so this call also returns 0.
At leaf 9 the through-path is left_h + right_h = 0 + 0 = 0 edges, so max_diameter stays 0.
Node 9 returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1, the height of a single leaf.
Back in node 7 with left_h = 1; its right child is None so right_h = 0.
Through node 7 the path is 1 + 0 = 1 edge, which beats the old 0, so max_diameter becomes 1.
Node 7 returns 1 + max(1, 0) = 2 to its parent, node 4.
Node 4 has left_h = 2 from node 7 and no right child, so right_h = 0.
Through node 4 the path measures 2 + 0 = 2 edges (9-7-4), so max_diameter rises to 2.
Node 4 returns height 1 + max(2, 0) = 3 up to node 2.
Node 2 now has left_h = 3 and starts its right recursion into node 5.
Node 5 has no left child at all, so its left_h is 0 and only its right side can grow.
Node 5 recurses right into node 8, mirroring what node 4 did on the other side.
Node 8 has no left child either, so left_h = 0 for node 8.
Node 8 recurses right into node 10, the deepest node of the right branch of node 2.
Leaf 10 has left_h = right_h = 0, so its candidate 0 leaves max_diameter at 2.
Node 10 returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1 as the height of leaf 10.
Node 8 has left_h = 0 and right_h = 1, candidate 1, which does not beat max_diameter = 2.
Node 8 returns 1 + max(0, 1) = 2 to node 5.
Node 5 has left_h = 0, right_h = 2, candidate 2 — a tie with max_diameter, so nothing changes.
Node 5 returns 1 + max(0, 2) = 3, so node 2 finally has both heights.
The key moment: node 2 has left_h = 3 and right_h = 3, so the path 9-7-4-2-5-8-10 is 6 edges and max_diameter jumps from 2 to 6.
Node 2 returns 1 + max(3, 3) = 4 as its height to the root.
The root now has left_h = 4 and recurses into its right child, node 3.
Node 3 is a leaf: left_h = right_h = 0, candidate 0, max_diameter untouched at 6.
Node 3 returns height 1 back to the root, node 1.
At the root left_h + right_h = 4 + 1 = 5, which is LESS than 6, so the best path never touches the root.
The root returns height 1 + max(4, 1) = 5, and the recursion is finished.
Answer: 6 edges, the path 9-7-4-2-5-8-10 that passes through node 2 rather than the root.

Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.desc: The tree is root -30 with left child 4 and right child -8; 4 has left child 11; 11 has children 7 and -2; -8 has children 13 and 6. max_sum starts at negative infinity so the very first real path wins.
Kick off the post-order walk with dfs(root = -30). Nothing is computed at a node until both of its children have reported back.
node = -30 is not None, so we do not take the base case and instead recurse into its children.
To get left_gain for -30 we must first call dfs on its left child, node 4. The recursion dives down the left spine.
node = 4 is not None either, so it also has to ask its children before it can answer.
Node 4 calls dfs on its left child 11. We are now three levels deep and still descending.
node = 11 is not None, so the descent continues into its own left child.
Node 11 calls dfs on its left child 7. Node 7 is a leaf, so this is the bottom of this branch.
Leaf 7 calls dfs(None) for its missing left child, and the base case returns 0 — 'an absent subtree contributes nothing'.
Back in node 7: left_gain = max(0, 0) = 0.
Node 7's right child is also None, so dfs returns 0 and right_gain = max(0, 0) = 0.
The best path that TOPS OUT at node 7 is 0 + 7 + 0 = 7, i.e. the single node 7 by itself.
max_sum jumps from -inf to 7 — the first real candidate the algorithm has seen.
Node 7 reports 7 + max(0, 0) = 7 upward. This is a BRANCH value: what a parent can hang onto if it comes down through 7.
Node 11 receives 7 from the left, so left_gain = max(7, 0) = 7 — worth keeping.
Now node 11 calls dfs on its right child -2 to find out whether that side is worth anything.
Node -2 is a leaf: both gains are 0, so current_path_sum = -2 + 0 + 0 = -2.
max_sum = max(7, -2) stays 7. A lone negative node never improves the answer, but the code still has to consider it.
Node -2 returns -2 + max(0, 0) = -2 upward — a negative branch value.
Here is the clamp that makes the algorithm work: right_gain = max(-2, 0) = 0. Node 11 REFUSES the -2 branch rather than dragging its parent's total down.
The best path topping out at node 11 is 7 + 11 + 0 = 18, i.e. the path 7 -> 11 (the -2 side is dropped).
max_sum improves from 7 to 18.
Node 11 returns 11 + max(7, 0) = 18 to its parent. A branch can only go down ONE side, so we take the larger gain, not the sum.
Node 4 sets left_gain = max(18, 0) = 18.
Node 4 has no right child at all, so dfs(None) returns 0 and right_gain = max(0, 0) = 0.
current_path_sum at node 4 is 18 + 4 + 0 = 22 — the path 7 -> 11 -> 4.
max_sum improves again, from 18 to 22. This is the value that will end up being the answer.
Node 4 returns 4 + max(18, 0) = 22 to the root.
The root -30 finally gets its left_gain = max(22, 0) = 22 and can start on the right subtree.
The root calls dfs on its right child -8, which has two leaf children of its own.
Node -8 first calls dfs on its left child 13, a leaf.
Leaf 13 has both gains 0, so current_path_sum = 13. max_sum = max(22, 13) stays 22.
Node 13 returns 13 + max(0, 0) = 13 to its parent -8.
Node -8 now calls dfs on its right child 6, the last unvisited leaf.
Leaf 6 gives current_path_sum = 6, which does not beat the running max_sum of 22.
Node 6 returns 6 upward, so node -8 has left_gain 13 and right_gain 6, both positive and both kept.
At node -8 the through-path uses BOTH children: 13 + (-8) + 6 = 11, the path 13 -> -8 -> 6.
max_sum = max(22, 11) stays at 22. The right subtree's best internal path loses to 7 -> 11 -> 4.
Node -8 returns -8 + max(13, 6) = 5 upward. Even though the node itself is negative, going down through 13 still nets a positive 5.
The root's right_gain = max(5, 0) = 5, so it keeps the right branch too.
The best path THROUGH the root is 22 + (-30) + 5 = -3. The -30 is so costly that crossing the root is a bad idea.
max_sum = max(22, -3) stays 22 — proof that the winning path never had to touch the root.
dfs(root) returns -30 + max(22, 5) = -8, but nobody is above the root to use it, so this branch value is discarded.
Return max_sum[0] = 22, achieved by the path 7 -> 11 -> 4 buried in the left subtree, not by anything passing through the root.

Check Identical Trees.desc: Compare p = 5(3(1,4), 8(7)) with q = 5(3(1,4), 8) — identical except q's node 8 has no left child.
Both roots exist, so the both-null base case does not fire here.
Neither root is null either, so there is no structural mismatch at the top.
p.val = 5 equals q.val = 5, so the roots match and the recursion may continue.
Evaluate the left half of the and first: compare p.left = 3 with q.left = 3.
At the pair (3, 3) neither side is null, so this is a real comparison.
3 == 3, so node 3 matches and its own children get compared.
Recurse further left into the pair (1, 1), the leftmost node of both trees.
1 == 1: the leftmost leaf matches in value.
Node 1 still recurses: compare its left children, which are null in both trees.
Both nodes are null, so this missing subtree is identical in p and q.
Return True for that null-null pair below node 1.
The and moves on to node 1's right children, also null on both sides.
True again, so node 1 is fully verified and returns True to node 3.
Node 3's left side came back True, so now compare its right children: 4 against 4.
4 == 4, and node 4 is a leaf in both trees.
Both of node 4's null child pairs return True, so node 4 returns True.
Node 3's whole subtree matched, so True travels back up to the root.
The root's left operand is True, so the right operand runs: compare node 8 with node 8.
The pair (8, 8) is not both null, so keep checking it.
8 == 8, so the values still agree; the difference must be found lower down.
Compare the left children of the two 8s: p has node 7 there, q has nothing.
'not p and not q' is false, because p is the real node 7.
'not p or not q' is true: q is null while p is node 7, so the shapes differ here.
Return False for this pair — the first and only mismatch in the whole walk.

vars.reason: p has a left child 7, q does not

Check Identical Trees.desc: That False short-circuits node 8's and, so node 8's right children are never compared.
The root's and collapses to False as well: p and q are not identical trees.

Zig Zag Traversal.desc: The root (value 1) exists, so the empty-tree shortcut is skipped and the BFS is set up.
queue is seeded with the root only: queue = [1].
result starts empty; one inner list will be appended per level.
left_to_right = True, so level 0 will be read in normal order. This flag flips every level.
Loop check: queue = [1] is non-empty, so process level 0.
level_size = len(queue) = 1 - snapshotting the size is what keeps levels separate while the queue keeps growing.
Allocate a fixed-size slot list level_nodes = [0]; values are written by index, never appended.
i=0: pop node 1 from the front of the queue. queue is momentarily empty.
left_to_right is True so index = i = 0; store level_nodes[0] = 1.
Node 1 has a left child, so 2 joins the queue.
Node 1 also has a right child, so 3 joins the queue: queue = [2, 3].
Level 0 is complete: result = [[1]].
Flip the flag: left_to_right becomes False, so level 1 will be filled right to left.
New iteration: level_size = 2 for the level holding nodes 2 and 3.
i=0: pop node 2, the LEFT-most node of this level.
Direction is right-to-left, so index = level_size-1-i = 2-1-0 = 1: node 2 belongs at the END of this level's list.
Write level_nodes[1] = 2, leaving slot 0 still waiting.
Node 2's left child 4 is enqueued for the next level.
Node 2's right child 5 is enqueued too: queue = [3, 4, 5].
i=1: pop node 3, the second and last node of level 1.
index = 2-1-1 = 0, so node 3 lands at the FRONT even though it was popped second - that is the whole zigzag trick.
Write level_nodes[0] = 3; the level reads [3, 2], the reverse of BFS order.
Node 3 has no left child, so nothing is enqueued from this branch - the tree is lopsided here.
Node 3's right child 6 is enqueued: queue = [4, 5, 6].
Level 1 appended reversed: result = [[1], [3, 2]].
Flip again: left_to_right = True, so level 2 goes back to plain left-to-right.
level_size = 3 for the level [4, 5, 6]; level_nodes = [0, 0, 0].
i=0: pop node 4, the first node of level 2.
left_to_right is True again, so index = i = 0: level_nodes = [4, 0, 0].
Node 4 is a leaf - no left child and no right child - so the queue does not grow.
i=1: pop node 5, which sits under node 2.
index = i = 1, so level_nodes = [4, 5, 0].
Node 5's only child, the left child 7, is enqueued: queue = [6, 7].
i=2: pop node 6, the last node of level 2.
index = i = 2: level_nodes = [4, 5, 6], filled straight through this time.
Node 6's left child 8 is enqueued: queue = [7, 8].
Node 6's right child 9 is enqueued: queue = [7, 8, 9].
Level 2 appended in order: result = [[1], [3, 2], [4, 5, 6]].
Flip once more: left_to_right = False for the deepest level.
level_size = 3 for the bottom level [7, 8, 9], which came from two different parents.
i=0: pop node 7, child of node 5.
index = 3-1-0 = 2, so node 7 goes to the last slot: level_nodes = [0, 0, 7].
i=1: pop node 8, child of node 6.
index = 3-1-1 = 1: level_nodes = [0, 8, 7].
i=2: pop node 9, the final node in the queue.
index = 3-1-2 = 0: level_nodes = [9, 8, 7], the exact reverse of the popping order.
The queue is empty - no node enqueued anything at the bottom level - so the while loop ends.
Return the zigzag traversal [[1], [3, 2], [4, 5, 6], [9, 8, 7]]: direction alternated on all 4 levels.

Boundary Traversal.desc: The tree is root 1, left child 2 (children 3 and 6, and 3 has only a RIGHT child 4) and right child 7 (only a right child 8, whose children 9 and 10 are leaves). result = [] will be filled in three passes.
root is not None, so we do not return early.
is_leaf(1) checks 1.left and 1.right: both exist, so the root is not a leaf and belongs on the boundary.
Append the root: result = [1]. The root is added once, by hand, so the three helpers never have to worry about it.
PASS 1: add_left_boundary(root.left = node 2). Note it starts at 2, not at the root.
curr = node 2 — the walk down the left edge begins.
curr is node 2, so the while loop body runs.
is_leaf(2) is False (it has children 3 and 6), so node 2 counts as a left-boundary node.
Append 2: result = [1, 2].
2.left = node 3 exists, so curr = 3 — the ordinary case, keep hugging the left edge.
is_leaf(3)? 3.left is None but 3.right = node 4, so it is NOT a leaf and does belong to the left boundary.
Append 3: result = [1, 2, 3].
Node 3 has no left child, so the fallback fires: curr = 3.right = node 4. The 'left boundary' is the leftmost path that still exists, and here it has to lean right.
is_leaf(4) is True, so node 4 is skipped here. Leaves are deliberately left to pass 2 — otherwise 4 would be printed twice.
Node 4 has neither child, so curr becomes None.
curr is None, the while loop ends, and pass 1 is done with result = [1, 2, 3].
PASS 2: add_leaves(root). This one starts at the ROOT and walks the whole tree, collecting leaves left to right.
node = 1 is not None, so no early return.
is_leaf(1) is False, so we do not record the root; instead recurse into both subtrees.
Recurse left: add_leaves(node 2). Node 2 is not a leaf either, so it recurses again into add_leaves(node 3).
Node 3 is not a leaf, so it recurses into add_leaves(3.left), and 3.left is None.
node is None, so this call returns immediately — the guard on line 18 is what lets the recursion be written without checking children first.
Recurse right from node 3: add_leaves(node 4).
is_leaf(4) is True, so append 4: result = [1, 2, 3, 4]. This is the first genuine leaf.
Node 2's own right recursion: add_leaves(node 6).
Node 6 has no children, so append 6: result = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6]. Node 6 is an INTERIOR leaf — it is on neither boundary, and only this pass can find it.
The left half is exhausted; back at the root, recurse right: add_leaves(node 7). Node 7 has no left child, so its line-25 call returns at once via line 19.
add_leaves(7.right = node 8). Node 8 is not a leaf, so it recurses into its two children.
add_leaves(node 9): it is a leaf, so append 9. result = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9].
add_leaves(node 10): also a leaf, so append 10. Pass 2 ends with result = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10]; the four leaves came out strictly left to right.
PASS 3: add_right_boundary(root.right = node 7).
curr = node 7 and temp = []. The right boundary is collected top-down into temp first, because it has to be emitted bottom-up.
is_leaf(7) is False (it has a right child 8), so node 7 is a right-boundary node.
temp = [7]. Nothing is written to result yet.
7.right = node 8 exists, so curr = 8 — mirror image of the left walk.
Node 8 has children 9 and 10, so it is not a leaf: temp = [7, 8].
curr = 8.right = node 10.
is_leaf(10) is True, so it is skipped — pass 2 already recorded it.
Node 10 has no children, so curr = None and the loop stops.
Extend result with reversed(temp) = [8, 7], giving result = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 8, 7]. Reversing is what makes the traversal one continuous anticlockwise loop.
Return [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 8, 7]: root, down the left edge (1-2-3), across the leaves (4, 6, 9, 10), then back up the right edge (8, 7). Every one of the 9 nodes appears exactly once.

Vertical Order Traversal.desc: A full three-level tree: root 1, children 2 and 3, leaves 4, 5, 6, 7. col_map starts empty and will bucket nodes by their column.
Seed the BFS queue with (root 1, row 0, col 0). Rows grow downward, columns shift -1 going left and +1 going right.
Pop (node 1, row 0, col 0) from the front of the queue.
Record node 1 in column 0: col_map[0] = [(0, 1)].
