Push the left child as (node 2, row 1, col -1).
Push the right child as (node 3, row 1, col 1). Level 0 is done.
Pop (node 2, row 1, col -1) - the first node of level 1.
col_map[-1] = [(1, 2)] - node 2 is the only node one column to the left.
Push node 4 as (row 2, col -2): left of a col -1 node lands at col -2, the leftmost column in the tree.
Push node 5 as (row 2, col 0). Notice this puts node 5 back in the ROOT's column.
Pop (node 3, row 1, col 1), the other node on level 1.
Record node 3 one column right of the root: col_map[1] = [(1, 3)].
Push node 6 as (row 2, col 0): left of a col +1 node also lands in column 0, so node 6 joins nodes 1 and 5 there.
Push node 7 as (row 2, col 2), the rightmost column.
Pop (node 4, row 2, col -2), the first of the four leaves.
col_map[-2] = [(2, 4)] - a column with exactly one occupant.
Node 4's children are both None, and the code pushes them anyway as (None, 3, -3) and (None, 3, -1).
Pop (node 5, row 2, col 0) - a leaf that lands in the root's own column.
Append to the EXISTING bucket: col_map[0] = [(0, 1), (2, 5)]. Column 0 now holds two nodes from different rows.
Pop (node 6, row 2, col 0) - the same column as node 5 and the same row too.
col_map[0] = [(0, 1), (2, 5), (2, 6)]. Nodes 5 and 6 share coordinates (row 2, col 0), so only their values can separate them later.
Pop (node 7, row 2, col 2), the last real node.
col_map[2] = [(2, 7)]. Every node has now been bucketed.
Node 7's two None children are pushed as well, so the queue still holds eight placeholder entries.
Pop the first placeholder, (None, 3, -3).
`if node:` is False for a placeholder, so nothing is recorded and no children are pushed - this is how the BFS terminates.
The other seven None entries drain the same way and the queue empties, ending the BFS.
Sorting the keys gives columns -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, left to right. Start with col = -2.
Column -2 holds only [(2, 4)], so sorting is a no-op.
Strip the row numbers and keep only values: result = [[4]].
Column -1 holds only [(1, 2)], giving [2]; result = [[4], [2]].
Column 0 is the interesting one: [(0, 1), (2, 5), (2, 6)]. The key (row, val) puts row 0's node 1 first, then breaks the row-2 tie between 5 and 6 by value.
Column 1 holds [(1, 3)] and column 2 holds [(2, 7)], each a single node.
Both are appended, completing result = [[4], [2], [1, 5, 6], [3], [7]].
Return the five columns in left-to-right order: [[4], [2], [1, 5, 6], [3], [7]].

Top View of Binary Tree.desc: The tree has 7 nodes. root = node 1 is not None, so the early-exit guard is skipped.
col_map = {} will remember the FIRST value seen in each column; later arrivals in a taller column are hidden.
queue = [(node 1, col 0)]. The root defines column 0 and BFS guarantees we meet shallower nodes first.
min_col = max_col = 0. These are widened as we go so the answer can be read off without sorting keys.
Pop (node 1, col 0) from the front of the queue.
Column 0 is unseen, so col_map[0] = 1. The root is visible from above.
Node 1 has a left child, so push (node 2, col -1) — a left step subtracts one column.
Node 1 also has a right child, so push (node 3, col +1).
Pop (node 2, col -1), the first node of depth 1.
Column -1 is new, so col_map[-1] = 2 and node 2 is part of the top view.
min_col = min(0, -1) = -1: the visible window has grown one column to the left.
Push node 2's left child: (node 4, col -2).
Push node 2's right child: (node 5, col -1 + 1 = 0) — that lands back under the root's column.
Pop (node 3, col +1), the other node of depth 1.
Column 1 is new, so col_map[1] = 3.
max_col = max(0, 1) = 1: the window now stretches from column -1 to column 1.
Node 3 has no left child, so nothing is pushed for the left side.
Push node 3's right child: (node 6, col 2).
Pop (node 4, col -2), the leftmost node in the whole tree.
Column -2 is new, so col_map[-2] = 4.
min_col = min(-1, -2) = -2, the final left edge of the view.
Node 4 is a leaf, so neither the left nor the right push happens.
Pop (node 5, col 0) — node 5 sits at depth 2 in the same column as the root.
Column 0 is ALREADY in col_map (holding the root value 1), so the if fails and node 5 is skipped: it is hidden directly beneath node 1.
Node 5 still contributes children: push (node 7, col 0 + 1 = 1).
Pop (node 6, col 2), the rightmost node.
Column 2 is new, so col_map[2] = 6 and node 6 becomes the right end of the top view.
max_col = max(1, 2) = 2, so the columns finally run from -2 to 2, five in total.
Pop the last entry (node 7, col 1).
Column 1 already maps to node 3, which sits one level higher, so node 7 is hidden too and nothing is recorded.
The queue is empty, so the BFS loop ends after processing all 7 nodes.
Read col_map for columns -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 in order: the top view is [4, 2, 1, 3, 6]; nodes 5 and 7 never appear.

Bottom View of Binary Tree.desc: Call bottomView on the tree 1 -> left 2, right 3, and 2 -> right 5. Columns: 1 at 0, 2 at -1, 3 at +1, 5 at 0.
Root is not None, so we skip the empty-tree shortcut.
col_map starts empty; it will map column index -> the LAST value seen in that column.
Seed the BFS queue with the root at column 0.
Track the column range as we go so we never have to sort the keys later.
Queue is not empty, so we enter the BFS loop.
Pop the front pair: node = 1, col = 0.
Write col_map[0] = 1 unconditionally — later nodes in column 0 are deeper, so they are allowed to overwrite this.
min_col = min(0, 0) = 0, the leftmost column so far.
max_col = max(0, 0) = 0, the rightmost column so far.
Node 1 has a left child (2), so we will queue it.
Push (2, col - 1) = (2, -1): moving left decreases the column by one.
Node 1 also has a right child (3).
Push (3, col + 1) = (3, 1): moving right increases the column by one.
Second pass of the BFS loop: the queue still holds two pairs.
Pop the front pair: node = 2, col = -1.
Column -1 is seen for the first time: col_map[-1] = 2.
min_col = min(0, -1) = -1, we have moved further left.
Node 2 has no left child, but it does have a right child (5).
Push (5, -1 + 1) = (5, 0): node 5 lands back in column 0, right underneath the root.
Third pass of the loop with two pairs still queued.
Pop node = 3 at col = 1.
Column 1 is new: col_map[1] = 3.
max_col = max(0, 1) = 1, we have moved further right. Node 3 is a leaf so nothing is queued.
Fourth pass of the loop: one pair left, the deep node 5.
Pop node = 5 at col = 0 — the same column as the root, but one level deeper.
This is the key step: col_map[0] is OVERWRITTEN from 1 to 5, because in BFS the last node written to a column is the lowest one.
The queue is now empty (node 5 is a leaf), so the BFS loop ends.
Read the columns in order from min_col = -1 to max_col = 1: [col_map[-1], col_map[0], col_map[1]] = [2, 5, 3]. That is the bottom view.

Node 1 is not null, so we do not hit the base case and keep going.
depth (0) matches len(result) (0). Add 1 to result
Node 3 is not null, so this call continues past the base case.
depth (1) matches len(result) (1). Add 3 to result
Back at node 1. Recurse left: Call solve(2, 1)
Node 2 is not null, so this call continues past the base case.
depth (1) does not match len(result) (2). Skip adding 2.
Node 5 is not null, so this call continues past the base case.
depth (2) matches len(result) (2). Add 5 to result

Node 1 is not null, so we do not hit the base case and keep going.
depth (0) matches len(result) (0). Add 1 to result
Node 2 is not null, so this call continues past the base case.
depth (1) matches len(result) (1). Add 2 to result
Node 5 is not null, so this call continues past the base case.
depth (2) matches len(result) (2). Add 5 to result
Back to node 1. Recurse right: Call solve(3, 1)
Node 3 is not null, so this call continues past the base case.

Symmetric Binary Tree.desc: The tree is root 1 with children 2 and 2; the left 2 has children 3 and 4, the right 2 has children 4 and 3. Deeper down, the left 3 has a left child 5 and the right 3 has a right child 5, while the left 4 has a left child 8 whose mirror slot under the right 4 is empty.
root is not None, so we compare its two subtrees against each other: isMirror(root.left = 2, root.right = 2). Call A.
Call A: t1 = 2 and t2 = 2 are both real nodes, so 'not t1 and not t2' is False and the both-empty shortcut does not apply.
Call A: neither side is None, so 'not t1 or not t2' is also False. We fall through to the real comparison.
Call A: t1.val == t2.val gives 2 == 2 = True, so Python evaluates the next operand of the 'and' chain.
Call A recurses on the OUTER pair: isMirror(t1.left = 3, t2.right = 3). Call B. Note the crossing — left's left is matched with right's right.
Call B: both 3s exist, so the both-null test is False.
Call B: neither 3 is None, so the one-sided-null test is False too.
Call B: 3 == 3 is True, so the two outer grandchildren agree in value and we keep going down.
Call B recurses: isMirror(left 3's LEFT child 5, right 3's RIGHT child 5). Call C — the outermost pair on this side.
Call C: both 5s are present, so we skip the both-null shortcut.
Call C: 5 == 5 is True. These two leaves are at mirrored positions and hold equal values.
Call C recurses on isMirror(5.left = None, 5.right = None). Call D — both arguments are missing children.
Call D: 'not None and not None' is True — two absent subtrees are trivially mirrors of each other.
Call D returns True. This is the base case that terminates the whole recursion at the fringe of the tree.
Call C now evaluates its second recursive call: isMirror(5.right = None, 5.left = None). Call E, again both empty.
Call E: both arguments are None, so the both-null test is True again.
Call E returns True, so call C has 5 == 5 and True and True — call C itself returns True. The 5/5 leaf pair is confirmed mirrored.
Back in call B: its first branch was True, so the 'and' continues to isMirror(left 3's RIGHT child = None, right 3's LEFT child = None). Call F.
Call F: both children are absent, so the both-null test is True — the inner slots under the two 3s match because both are empty.
Call F returns True, so call B returns True as well. The entire outer pair 3/3 with their 5/5 descendants is verified symmetric.
Call A's first branch came back True, so it evaluates the INNER pair: isMirror(t1.right = 4, t2.left = 4). Call G.
Call G: both 4s exist, so the both-null test is False.
Call G: neither 4 is None, so the one-sided-null test is False.
Call G: 4 == 4 is True. The values still match at this level — the tree has looked perfectly symmetric so far.
Call G recurses on isMirror(left 4's LEFT child = 8, right 4's RIGHT child = None). Call H. This is the pair where the mirror breaks: one side has a node, the other has nothing.
Call H: t1 = 8 is a real node, so 'not t1 and not t2' is False — this is NOT the both-empty case.
Call H: 'not t1 or not t2' is True because t2 is None while t1 = 8 exists. Exactly one side is missing, so the shapes cannot mirror.
Call H returns False. Note that no value comparison was ever needed — the structural mismatch alone settles it.
Call G's first recursive operand is False, so the 'and' short-circuits: line 13 is never evaluated and call G returns False without ever inspecting the 4s' other children.
Call A had True from its outer pair but False from this inner pair, so 'True and False' makes call A return False.
isSymmetric returns False. The tree matched on values everywhere it compared, and it was the missing mirror of node 8 under the right-hand 4 that broke the symmetry.

Root to Node Path.desc: Search the tree 1(2(4, 5(7)), 3(_, 6)) for target 6, starting from the root with an empty result.
Node 1 is a real node, so this is not the null base case.
Append the root's value: path = [1].
1 != 6, so the target must be somewhere below the root.
Recurse into the left child, node 2.
Append node 2's value: path = [1, 2].
2 is not the target 6 either, so descend again.
Recurse left once more into node 4.
Append 4: path = [1, 2, 4].
4 != 6, and node 4 is a leaf, so both of its children will fail.
Recurse into node 4's left child, which does not exist.
A null node cannot be on the path, so this call returns False right away.
Node 4's right child is null too, so that returns False as well.
Dead end: pop 4 off the path, leaving path = [1, 2]. This is the backtracking step.
Node 4 reports False up to its parent, node 2.
Node 2's left branch failed, so try its right child, node 5.
Append 5: path = [1, 2, 5].
5 != 6 — a near miss in value, but not the node we are looking for.
Recurse into node 5's only child, node 7.
Append 7: path = [1, 2, 5, 7], the deepest this wrong branch goes.
7 != 6, and node 7 is a leaf with two null children.
Both children of 7 returned False, so pop 7: path = [1, 2, 5].
Node 5 has no right child, so that call returns False and node 5 is out of options.
Pop 5 off the path as well: path = [1, 2].
Node 2 has now failed on both sides, so pop 2 as well: path = [1].
Node 2 returns False, and the entire left subtree of the root is discarded.
Back at the root: its left call was False, so recurse into the right child, node 3.
Append node 3's value: path = [1, 3].
3 != 6, so keep going under node 3.
Node 3 has no left child, so that recursive call returns False.
Recurse into node 3's right child, node 6.
Append 6: path = [1, 3, 6].
node.val 6 equals the target 6 — the node has been found.
Return True, which means line 19 never runs here, so 6 stays on the path.
The True propagates through node 3 and then the root, and no ancestor pops itself.
Return result = [1, 3, 6]: the unique root-to-node path down to the target.

Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.desc: Call on the tree 3 -> (5, 1), 5 -> (6, 2), 1 -> (0, 8), with p = node 6 and q = node 2. The expected answer is node 5.
Frame(3): root is not None and node 3 is neither p (6) nor q (2), so we must search both sides.
Frame(3): recurse into the left subtree, calling the function on node 5.
Frame(5): node 5 is not p (6) and not q (2) either, so keep descending.
Frame(5): recurse left into node 6.
Frame(6): node 6 IS p, so the base case fires — we stop digging and report this node upward.
Frame(6) returns node 6 to its caller, frame(5).
Frame(5): left is now node 6. Next we recurse right into node 2.
Frame(2): node 2 IS q, so the base case fires again.
Frame(2) returns node 2 upward to frame(5).
Frame(5): left = 6 and right = 2 are BOTH non-null, which means p and q were found in different subtrees of node 5.
Frame(5) therefore returns node 5 itself — this is the split point, the lowest common ancestor of 6 and 2.
Back in frame(3): the left call finished with left = 5.
Frame(3): now recurse into the right subtree, calling the function on node 1.
Frame(1): node 1 is neither p nor q, so it keeps searching its own children.
Frame(1): recurse left into node 0.
Frame(0): node 0 is not p or q, and it is a leaf, so both of its recursive calls will hit the None base case.
The calls on node 0's two None children return None straight away (root is falsy).
Frame(0): left = None and right = None, so the 'both sides found something' test fails.
Frame(0) returns None: nothing of interest lives under node 0.
Frame(1): left = None; the right call on node 8 behaves exactly the same and also returns None.
Frame(1): both sides are None, so node 1 is not an ancestor of p or q.
Frame(1) returns None back to frame(3).
Frame(3): left = node 5 but right = None, so node 3 is NOT the split point — both targets sit on the left.
Frame(3) returns whichever side is non-null, i.e. node 5. The final answer is node 5, the LCA of 6 and 2.

Maximum Width of Binary Tree.desc: Call widthOfBinaryTree on the tree [1, 3, 2, 5, 3, null, 9]. Root is not None, so we do not return 0.
max_width starts at 0; every level will try to beat it.
Seed the queue with the root and give it heap index 0. A node with index i has children 2i+1 and 2i+2, exactly as in an array-based complete tree.
Level 0 begins: the queue is not empty.
size = 1, so level 0 contains exactly one node.
min_idx = 0, the index of the leftmost node of this level. Subtracting it keeps indices small.
Reset first and last for this level.
Iterate the level, i = 0 of 1.
Pop (node 1, idx 0) from the front of the queue.
Normalise: cur_id = 0 - 0 = 0.
i == 0, so this is the leftmost node of the level: first = 0.
i == size - 1 too (the level has a single node), so last = 0 as well.
Left child 3 exists, so push it with index 2*0 + 1 = 1.
Right child 2 exists, so push it with index 2*0 + 2 = 2.
Level 0 width = last - first + 1 = 0 - 0 + 1 = 1, so max_width becomes 1.
Level 1 begins: the queue holds nodes 3 and 2.
size = 2 nodes on this level.
min_idx = 1, the raw index of node 3, the leftmost node of level 1.
Level 1, i = 0: process the first (leftmost) node of this level.
Pop (node 3, idx 1).
Normalise: cur_id = 1 - 1 = 0. This rebasing is what stops indices from exploding on deep trees.
i == 0, so first = 0.
Node 3 has a left child 5: push it with index 2*0 + 1 = 1.
Node 3 also has a right child 3: push it with index 2*0 + 2 = 2.
Level 1, i = 1 (the last node of this level).
Pop (node 2, idx 2).
Normalise: cur_id = 2 - 1 = 1.
i == size - 1, so last = 1: node 2 is the rightmost node of level 1.
Node 2 has no left child but has right child 9: push it with index 2*1 + 2 = 4. That gap of missing index 3 is exactly the null that must be counted later.
Level 1 width = 1 - 0 + 1 = 2, so max_width becomes max(1, 2) = 2.
Level 2 begins with three queued nodes: 5, 3 and 9.
size = 3 nodes on the last level.
min_idx = 1, the index of node 5.
i = 0: pop (node 5, idx 1); cur_id = 0 so first = 0. Node 5 is a leaf, nothing is pushed.
i = 1: pop (node 3, idx 2); cur_id = 2 - 1 = 1. It is neither the first nor the last node, and it is a leaf.
i = 2: pop (node 9, idx 4), the final node of the level.
Normalise: cur_id = 4 - 1 = 3.
i == size - 1, so last = 3.
Level 2 width = 3 - 0 + 1 = 4 — the two missing slots between 3 and 9 are counted, exactly what the problem asks. max_width becomes 4.
The queue is empty, all levels are done, so we return the answer 4.

Children Sum Property.desc: changeTree(root) is called on the root, value 5. It is not None, so there is work to do.
The root has both children (40 and 60), so it is not a leaf and the property must be enforced here.
child_sum starts at 0 and will accumulate whichever children exist.
Left child exists: child_sum += 40 -> 40.
Right child exists: child_sum += 60 -> 100.
Is root.val=5 > child_sum=100? No. The children are already far bigger, so no value is pushed down - this branch of the if is skipped entirely.
Recurse into the left subtree rooted at 40 before touching the root's own value.
Node 40 has children 9 and 3, so it is not a leaf either.
Fresh child_sum = 0 for this frame.
child_sum += left child 9 -> 9.
child_sum += right child 3 -> 12.
Now 40 > 12 is True: the parent is too big and we are forbidden to shrink it, so both children must be lifted instead.
Left child is overwritten with the parent value: 9 becomes 40, an increment as required.
Right child likewise: 3 becomes 40. The subtree is now temporarily 40 with children 40 and 40, i.e. 40 vs a child sum of 80.
Recurse into the left child (now 40).
That node has no children at all, so the leaf base case returns immediately - leaves may hold any value.
Recurse into the right child (also 40); it is a leaf too and returns at once.
Post-order phase for node 40: recompute tot_sum from scratch, because the children may have grown during the recursion.
tot_sum += left child's final value 40 -> 40.
tot_sum += right child's final value 40 -> 80.
Node 40 is raised to 80 so it equals 40+40 exactly. The left subtree now satisfies the property.
Back in the root frame: recurse into the right subtree, node 60.
Node 60 has no left child but does have a right child 7, so it is not a leaf.
child_sum = 0 for node 60.
There is no left child, so the if is False and the missing child simply contributes nothing.
Only the right child counts: child_sum += 7 -> 7.
60 > 7, so the single child has to be lifted up to the parent value.
The left-push is guarded by 'if root.left' - there is no left child here, so this half of the push-down is skipped.
The right child jumps from 7 to 60, matching its parent.
changeTree(root.left) is still called even though the left child is None.
The None base case fires and the call returns straight away - this is why the missing child costs nothing.
changeTree on the right child (now 60) hits the leaf base case and returns.
Post-order for node 60: tot_sum = 0.
No left child, so nothing is added from the left side.
tot_sum += right child 60 -> 60.
Node 60 is set to 60. The value does not change, but it is now genuinely equal to the sum of its one child.
Both recursive calls are done, so the root's own post-order update begins with tot_sum = 0.
tot_sum += left child's final value 80 -> 80.
tot_sum += right child's final value 60 -> 140.
The root jumps from 5 to 140 = 80 + 60. Every internal node now equals its children's sum and no value was ever decreased.

Nodes at Distance K.desc: Call distanceK on the tree 3 -> (5, 1), 5 -> (6, 2), 2 -> (7, 4), 1 -> (0, 8) with target = node 5 and k = 2. parent_map starts empty.
Kick off the DFS that records, for every node, who its parent is. That is the missing 'upward' edge a tree does not normally have.
Inside the helper for node 3: it is not None, so we record it.
parent_map[3] = None because the root has no parent.
Recurse into the left child, passing node 3 as the parent.
parent_map[5] = 3. The same happens for 6 and 2 under 5, and for 7 and 4 under 2.
Now recurse into the right subtree of 3, which fills in 1, 0 and 8 the same way.
The tree is now effectively an undirected graph. Start BFS at the target node 5 with distance 0.
Mark the target as visited so we never walk back into it.
result will collect the values of every node exactly k = 2 hops away.
BFS loop starts; the queue holds one entry.
Pop (node 5, dist 0).
dist (0) is not equal to k (2), so node 5 itself is not part of the answer.
dist (0) < k (2), so it is worth expanding all three neighbours of node 5.
Left child 6 exists and is unvisited.
Push (6, dist + 1) = (6, 1) and mark 6 visited.
Right child 2 exists and is unvisited.
Push (2, 1) and mark 2 visited.
Look up the parent of node 5 in the map: it is node 3.
Push (3, 1) as well — this upward hop is what a plain tree traversal could never do.
Next BFS iteration with three queued nodes, all at distance 1.
Pop (node 6, dist 1).
1 < 2, so expand node 6. It is a leaf, and its only other neighbour is its parent 5, which is already visited — nothing new is queued.
Pop (node 2, dist 1).
Left child 7 is unvisited: push (7, 2).
Right child 4 is unvisited: push (4, 2).
Pop (node 3, dist 1).
Node 3's left child 5 is already visited, but its right child 1 is not: push (1, 2). Its parent is None, so nothing else is added.
Pop (node 7, dist 2).
dist (2) == k (2): node 7 is exactly two hops from the target.
Append 7 to the result. Note we do NOT expand it further, which keeps the search from going past distance k.
Pop (node 4, dist 2).
dist == k again, so append 4.
Pop (node 1, dist 2) — reached by going UP to 3 and then down to 1.
dist == k, so append 1.
The queue is now empty, so the BFS loop ends.
Return [7, 4, 1]: the three nodes at distance exactly 2 from node 5.

Burn a Binary Tree.desc: Start with an empty parent_map. The tree gives us child pointers only, so we must record the upward edges ourselves before the fire can climb.
target_node is None for now; the DFS will set it the moment it meets the node whose value is 4.
Kick off dfs(root=1, parent=None). Tree is 1 -> left 2, right 3, and node 2 -> left 4. Target value is 4.
Node 1's value (1) is not the target, so we simply record parent_map[node 1] = None — the root has no parent.
Recurse into the left child: dfs(node 2, parent node 1).
Record parent_map[node 2] = node 1 so the fire can later climb from 2 back up to 1.
Recurse deeper into node 2's left child: dfs(node 4, parent node 2).
Check node 4: node.val (4) == target_val (4) is True — this is where the fire starts.
Save the actual node object in target_node so BFS can start from a node reference, not just a value.
Record parent_map[node 4] = node 2 as well; node 4 has no children so this DFS branch is finished.
Unwinding back to the root, dfs(node 3, parent node 1) runs and records parent_map[node 3] = node 1. Every node now knows its parent.
BFS setup: the queue starts with the burning source (node 4) at time 0.
visited holds node 4 already, so the fire will never come back to its own starting point.
max_time = 0 will hold the second at which the LAST node catches fire — that is the answer.
The queue is not empty, so we enter the BFS loop and process the fire second by second.
Pop (node 4, time 0): node 4 is already burning at second 0.
max_time = max(0, 0) = 0. Nothing burned later than second 0 yet.
Node 4 has no left child (and no right child either), so the fire cannot spread downward from here.
Look up parent_map[node 4] = node 2 — the only neighbour of a leaf is its parent.
Node 2 was unvisited, so mark it burnt and enqueue it with time 0 + 1 = 1.
Pop (node 2, time 1): node 2 catches fire one second after the target.
max_time = max(0, 1) = 1 — the fire front is now one second old.
Node 2's left child is node 4, but node 4 is already in visited, so we do NOT push it back — this is what stops the fire looping.
Parent of node 2 is node 1 and it is unvisited: enqueue (node 1, time 1 + 1 = 2).
Pop (node 1, time 2): the root catches fire at second 2.
max_time = max(1, 2) = 2.
The root's right child node 3 has not burnt yet, so the fire finally crosses to the right half of the tree.
Enqueue (node 3, time 2 + 1 = 3) and mark it visited.
Pop (node 3, time 3): the last unburnt node catches fire at second 3.
max_time = max(2, 3) = 3. Node 3 is a leaf whose only neighbour (node 1) is already visited, so nothing new is enqueued.
The queue is now empty, so every node has burnt and the BFS loop exits.
Return max_time = 3: starting at leaf 4, the whole tree is on fire after 3 seconds.

Count Total Nodes in Complete Binary Tre.desc: Enter countNodes with the root (node 1). Tree is level-order [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] — six nodes, last level partially filled.
Call get_left_height(node 1): walk the LEFTMOST spine and count how many nodes we meet.
Node 1 exists, so h becomes 1.
Step to node.left = node 2 and keep walking left.
Node 2 exists, so h becomes 2.
Step to node.left = node 4.
Node 4 exists, so h becomes 3.
node.left of the leaf 4 is None, so the while condition will now fail.
get_left_height returns 3 — the left spine holds 3 nodes.
Now call get_right_height(node 1): walk the RIGHTMOST spine the same way.
Node 1 exists, so h becomes 1.
Step to node.right = node 3.
Node 3 exists, so h becomes 2.
Node 3 has no right child (only a left child 6), so node becomes None and the walk stops.
get_right_height returns 2 — the right spine is one node shorter than the left one.
Compare lh == rh: 3 == 2 is False, so this whole tree is NOT perfect and the formula does not apply here.
Fall back to counting: 1 (for the root) + countNodes(node 2) + countNodes(node 3). Python evaluates the left call first.
Inside countNodes(node 2): the left spine is 2 -> 4, so lh = 2.
The right spine of node 2 is 2 -> 5, so rh = 2 as well.
lh == rh: 2 == 2 is True — the subtree rooted at 2 is PERFECT, so we can count it without visiting a single extra node.
Return (1 << 2) - 1 = 3 for the subtree {2, 4, 5}. This is the shortcut that beats the O(n) traversal.
Now the right call runs: countNodes(node 3), which is not None.
Left spine of node 3 is 3 -> 6, so lh = 2.
Right spine of node 3 is just 3 itself, so rh = 1.
2 == 1 is False, so node 3's subtree is not perfect and we must split it further.
Return 1 + countNodes(node 6) + countNodes(None) for the subtree rooted at 3.
For the leaf node 6 both spines have length 1, so lh == rh is True.
Return (1 << 1) - 1 = 1 for the single node 6.
countNodes(None) hits the base case and returns 0 — node 3 has no right child.
Node 3's subtree therefore totals 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 nodes.
Back at the root: 1 + 3 (perfect subtree of 2) + 2 (subtree of 3) = 6 nodes in total.

Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and.desc: Build in_map from inorder [9, 3, 15, 20, 7] so any value's inorder position is an O(1) lookup instead of a scan.
pre_idx = 0 is the single shared cursor into preorder; every node we create consumes exactly one preorder value.
Call helper(0, 4) — build the tree from the entire inorder range.
Base check: in_start (0) > in_end (4) is False, so this range holds at least one node.
root_val = preorder[0] = 3. In preorder the very first unconsumed value is always the root of the current range.
Create TreeNode(3), the root of the whole tree.
Advance pre_idx to 1 so the next recursive call picks up the following preorder value.
in_map[3] = 1: in inorder, everything at indices 0..0 is the left subtree and 2..4 is the right subtree.
Build the left subtree first with helper(0, 0) — the single inorder slot holding value 9.
root_val = preorder[1] = 9 becomes the root of this one-element range.
pre_idx moves to 2 after consuming 9.
in_map[9] = 0, so node 9's left range is 0..-1 and its right range is 1..0 — both empty.
helper(0, -1) hits the base case (0 > -1) and returns None: node 9 has no left child.
helper(1, 0) likewise returns None, so node 9 is a leaf and is returned as the left child of 3.
Back at the root: build the right subtree with helper(2, 4), the inorder slice [15, 20, 7].
root_val = preorder[2] = 20 — the right child of the root.
pre_idx advances to 3.
in_map[20] = 3, so 20's left range is 2..2 ([15]) and its right range is 4..4 ([7]).
helper(2, 2) builds 20's left child from the single inorder slot 2.
root_val = preorder[3] = 15, a leaf that becomes 20's left child.
pre_idx advances to 4; both recursive ranges of 15 are empty, so it returns as a leaf.
helper(4, 4) builds 20's right child from inorder slot 4.
root_val = preorder[4] = 7, the last value; it becomes 20's right child.
pre_idx becomes 5 — every preorder value has now been consumed exactly once.
Node 20 is complete (left 15, right 7) and is returned as the root's right child.
The root node 3 now has left child 9 and right child 20 and is returned to the top-level call.
Return the finished tree: level order [3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7].

Construct Binary Tree from Postorder and.desc: Build in_map from inorder [9, 3, 15, 20, 7] for O(1) root-position lookups.
post_idx starts at the LAST index (4) because postorder must be read right to left: root, then right subtree, then left subtree.
helper(in_start, in_end) will own one inorder range at a time; the top-level call covers the whole array.
helper(0, 4): in_start (0) > in_end (4) is False, so the range is non-empty.
root_val = postorder[4] = 3 — the final postorder value is always the overall root.
Create TreeNode(3) as the root of the tree.
Decrement post_idx to 3; the next value we read will be the root of the RIGHT subtree.
in_map[3] = 1, so inorder indices 0..0 form the left subtree and 2..4 form the right subtree.
Build the RIGHT subtree first: helper(2, 4) over the inorder slice [15, 20, 7].
root_val = postorder[3] = 20 becomes the root's right child.
post_idx drops to 2.
in_map[20] = 3: node 20's left range is 2..2 ([15]) and its right range is 4..4 ([7]).
Again right first: helper(4, 4) builds node 20's right child.
root_val = postorder[2] = 7 — exactly the value we expect on the right of 20.
post_idx drops to 1; node 7's two sub-ranges are empty, so it stays a leaf.
helper(5, 4) for node 7's right side returns None because 5 > 4.
Now node 20's LEFT subtree: helper(2, 2), the single inorder slot holding 15.
root_val = postorder[1] = 15, node 20's left child.
post_idx drops to 0; only the very first postorder value remains.
Node 20 is finished with left child 15 and right child 7, and is returned as the root's right child.
Back at the top call: build the LEFT subtree with helper(0, 0).
root_val = postorder[0] = 9, the root's left child.
post_idx becomes -1: every postorder value has now been consumed exactly once.
Node 9 is a leaf and is returned as the root's left child.
Node 3 now has left child 9 and right child 20; return it to the top-level caller.
The finished tree in level order is [3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7] — matching the original traversals.

Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.desc: serialize is called on root 1. The tree is deliberately lopsided: 2 has only a left child (4), 3 has two children (5 and 6), and 5 has a single left child (7). root is not None, so we do not return the empty string.
Seed the BFS queue with the root. The queue will also be allowed to hold None children — those are exactly what becomes '#'.
res collects one token per pop, in strict level order.
The queue is non-empty so the loop on line 11 starts, and node = queue.pop(0) = node 1. Popping from the front is what makes this a queue rather than a stack.
node 1 is real, so res = ['1'].
Append 1.left = node 2 to the queue.
Append 1.right = node 3. queue = [2, 3] — level 2 is now lined up.
Pop node 2 from the front.
node 2 is real, so its value is recorded: res = ['1', '2'].
Append 2.left = node 4. queue = [3, 4].
Append 2.right, which is None. The None is pushed anyway — that missing child is a position the decoder must know about. queue = [3, 4, None].
Pop node 3 and record it: res = ['1', '2', '3'].
Push 3.left = node 5 and 3.right = node 6. queue = [4, None, 5, 6].
Pop node 4, a leaf, and record it: res = ['1', '2', '3', '4'].
A leaf still pushes both of its Nones: queue = [None, 5, 6, None, None].
Pop the first None — the one 2 pushed for its missing right child.
res = ['1','2','3','4','#']. That '#' is the placeholder that will keep 4 and 5 from being mistaken for siblings.
Pop node 5 and record it: res = ['1','2','3','4','#','5']; then push its child 7 and one None. queue = [6, None, None, 7, None].
Pop node 6 and record it: res = ['1','2','3','4','#','5','6']; it is a leaf, so two Nones go on the queue.
The next two pops are node 4's Nones, so two more '#' tokens land: res = [...,'6','#','#'].
Pop node 7, the deepest node, and record it: res = [...,'#','#','7']. Its own two Nones are queued.
Five Nones remain (5's right, 6's two, 7's two) and each becomes a '#'. Now the queue is empty and line 11 ends the loop.
Return '1,2,3,4,#,5,6,#,#,7,#,#,#,#,#' — 7 values plus 8 markers, one token per slot of the level-order layout.
deserialize is handed data = '1,2,3,4,#,5,6,#,#,7,#,#,#,#,#'. It is non-empty, so there is a tree to rebuild. Nothing exists yet.
values[0] is the root, so root = TreeNode(1). Everything else will be attached to it as a child of an already-built node.
queue = [root]. This queue mirrors the one serialize used, so the nodes come off in exactly the order their children were written.
i = 1: values[0] is spent, so the reading head sits on the first CHILD token.
The queue is non-empty and i = 1 < 15, so the rebuilding loop runs.
curr = queue.pop(0) = node 1. The next two tokens are, by construction, exactly node 1's two children.
values[1] = '2' is not '#', so a real left child exists.
curr.left = TreeNode(2), and line 44 pushes node 2 so it can collect its own children later. queue = [2].
i = 2, now pointing at the right-child token.
values[2] = '3' is not '#', so curr.right = TreeNode(3) and node 3 joins the queue. queue = [2, 3]; i becomes 3.
curr = node 2. Its children are the tokens at i = 3 and i = 4.
values[3] = '4', so curr.left = TreeNode(4) and node 4 is queued. queue = [3, 4].
i = 4 and values[4] = '#', so the condition is False: node 2 keeps right = None and nothing is queued. This is the marker doing its job.
curr = node 3, and tokens 5 and 6 are '5' and '6', so it gains both children. queue = [4, 5, 6] and i = 7.
curr = node 4: values[7] and values[8] are both '#', so it stays a leaf and i advances to 9. Nothing is pushed, which is how the queue eventually drains.
curr = node 5 and values[9] = '7', so curr.left = TreeNode(7). queue = [6, 7]; the deepest node of the tree is restored.
i = 10 and values[10] = '#', so node 5 has no right child. i advances to 11.
curr = node 6. Tokens 11 and 12 are '#', '#', so it is confirmed a leaf and i reaches 13.
curr = node 7, the last node in the queue. Tokens 13 and 14 are '#', '#', so it too is a leaf and i reaches 15.
queue is empty and i = 15 is no longer < len(values) = 15, so the loop stops. Both stopping conditions fire together, which is the sign the encoding was consumed exactly.
Return root. The rebuilt tree is identical to the original, including 2's missing right child and 5's single left child — the shape information lived entirely in the '#' markers.

Morris Inorder Traversal.desc: Tree: root 4 with left subtree {2, 1, 3} and right subtree {6, 5}. result starts empty; the expected inorder answer is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
curr = root, node 4. There is no stack and no recursion anywhere - the tree itself will hold our place.
Node 4 HAS a left child (node 2), so we may not visit 4 yet; its entire left subtree must be emitted first.
pred starts at curr.left = node 2, then walks as far right as it can inside the left subtree.
pred.right is node 3, which is not None and not curr, so the walk continues.
pred = node 3, the rightmost node of 4's left subtree - which is exactly 4's inorder predecessor.
Node 3 has no right child, so the walk stops here.
pred.right is None, meaning this subtree has never been threaded before - so this is a first visit to node 4.
CREATE THE THREAD: 3.right = 4. Node 3's unused right pointer now doubles as a return path back up to 4.
curr = 4.left = node 2 and we descend, knowing the thread will bring us back.
Node 2 also has a left child (node 1), so 2 cannot be visited yet either.
pred = curr.left = node 1, the start of the predecessor hunt for node 2.
Node 1 has no right child, so the inner while loop never runs; node 1 is already the predecessor.
Create a second thread: 1.right = 2. Two temporary back-edges now exist, 1 -> 2 and 3 -> 4.
curr = 2.left = node 1, descending into the deepest left node.
Node 1 has NO left child, so nothing precedes it - it is safe to emit.
Visit node 1, the smallest value: result = [1].
curr = 1.right, which is the THREAD we built, so we land back on node 2 without any stack.
Node 2 still has a left child, so the code takes the same branch as before and re-finds its predecessor.
pred = node 1 and this time pred.right == curr (node 2), so the loop stops on the thread rather than on a None.
pred.right is NOT None, so we are on the SECOND visit to node 2: its left subtree is finished.
TEAR THE THREAD DOWN: 1.right = None, restoring node 1 to its original shape. Only the 3 -> 4 thread remains.
With its left subtree finished, visit node 2: result = [1, 2].
curr = 2.right = node 3, a genuine edge this time.
Node 3 has no left child, so it is emitted straight away.
Visit node 3: result = [1, 2, 3]. The whole left subtree of 4 is now done.
curr = 3.right, which is the surviving thread, so we climb back to node 4 - the reason the thread was built ten steps ago.
Node 4 still has a left child, so we hunt for the predecessor again: pred = node 2.
2.right = node 3 which is neither None nor curr, so pred advances to node 3.
Now pred.right == curr (node 4) - we have found our own thread, so the walk stops.
Cut it: 3.right = None. The tree is now exactly as it started, with no threads left.
Visit the root at last: result = [1, 2, 3, 4], exactly halfway through.
curr = 4.right = node 6, moving into the untouched right subtree.
Node 6 has a left child (node 5), so the whole thread dance repeats on the right subtree.
pred = node 5, which has no right child, so it is immediately node 6's predecessor.
Create the third and final thread of the run: 5.right = 6.
curr = 6.left = node 5, descending under the freshly built thread.
Node 5 has no left child, so visit it: result = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
curr = 5.right = node 6, climbing back up the thread we just built.
pred is node 5 again and pred.right is not None, so this is node 6's second visit.
Cut the last thread: 5.right = None. The tree is fully restored.
Visit node 6: result = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
curr = 6.right = None - node 6 never had a real right child.
curr is None, so the outer while loop ends. Every thread that was created has also been removed.
Return [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], produced with O(1) extra memory and a tree left byte-for-byte unchanged.

Morris Preorder Traversal.desc: The tree has 6 nodes: 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 with children 4 and 5, and node 3 with a single left child 6. result starts empty.
curr = root = node 1. No stack and no recursion are allowed, so the tree itself has to remember the way back.
curr = 1 HAS a left child (node 2), so the else branch runs: we must first build a way back before descending.
pred starts at curr.left = node 2 — the search for node 1's inorder predecessor begins here.
pred = 2 has a right child (node 5) and that child is not curr, so keep walking right.
pred = node 5, the rightmost node of node 1's left subtree and therefore its inorder predecessor.
pred = 5 has no right child, so the while condition fails and the search stops at node 5.
pred.right is None, which means this subtree has never been visited: take the thread-creating branch.
THREAD CREATED: 5.right = node 1. Node 5's empty right pointer now doubles as a return link to the root.
Preorder means root first, so node 1 is emitted now: result = [1].
curr = curr.left = node 2. We descend into the left subtree knowing node 5 can bring us back.
curr = 2 also has a left child (node 4), so again the else branch runs.
pred = curr.left = node 4. Node 4 has no right child at all, so the inner while loop never runs and node 4 IS the predecessor.
THREAD CREATED: 4.right = node 2. Two temporary threads now exist at once: 5 -> 1 and 4 -> 2.
Node 2 is emitted before its subtree, giving result = [1, 2].
curr = curr.left = node 4, the leftmost node of the tree.
curr = 4 has no left child, so the simple branch runs: visit it and move right.
result = [1, 2, 4] after emitting the leaf 4.
curr = curr.right, but 4.right is the THREAD we planted, so this jump lands back on node 2 with no stack at all.
curr = 2 again, and it still has a left child, so the else branch runs a second time.
pred = curr.left = node 4 once more — the same predecessor search as before.
The loop condition sees pred.right == curr == node 2, so it stops immediately: this is the tell-tale of a second visit.
pred.right is NOT None, so the if fails and control falls to the else: the left subtree is already finished.
THREAD REMOVED: 4.right = None restores the tree to its original shape. Node 2 is not re-emitted.
curr = curr.right = node 5, the real right child of node 2.
result = [1, 2, 4, 5]; the whole left subtree of the root has now been emitted.
5.right is still the very first thread we planted, so curr jumps all the way back up to the root, node 1.
curr = 1 again and it still has a left child, so the predecessor search repeats.
pred = node 2, the start of the same rightmost-walk we did at the very beginning.
2.right = 5 is not curr, so the loop steps once more and pred = node 5.
Now pred.right == curr == node 1, so the loop stops: the thread proves the left subtree is done.
THREAD REMOVED: 5.right = None. Every borrowed pointer has now been given back on the left half.
curr = 1.right = node 3, so the traversal moves into the right subtree of the root.
curr = 3 has a left child (node 6), so one more thread has to be built.
pred = curr.left = node 6, and since node 6 has no right child the inner loop does not move.
THREAD CREATED: 6.right = node 3, the third and last thread of the traversal.
Node 3 is emitted before its subtree: result = [1, 2, 4, 5, 3].
curr = curr.left = node 6, descending into node 3's only child.
Node 6 has no left child, so it is emitted at once: result = [1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6].
curr follows 6.right, the thread, back up to node 3.
Second visit to node 3: pred = node 6 again, and pred.right already points at curr.
THREAD REMOVED: 6.right = None. The tree is now exactly as it was before the traversal started.
curr = 3.right, which is None because node 3 has no right child.
curr is None, so the while loop ends after visiting all 6 nodes with O(1) extra memory.
Return the preorder [1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6], produced without a stack and with every borrowed pointer restored.

Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List.desc: curr starts at the root. Tree is 1 with left subtree (2 -> children 3 and 4) and right child 5 -> right child 6.
curr is not None, so enter the loop; we will rewire one node per iteration.
Node 1 has a left child (node 2), so its left subtree must be spliced onto the right spine.
prev starts at curr.left = node 2; we now walk to the rightmost node of the left subtree.
Node 2 has a right child (node 4), so prev moves to node 4.
Node 4 has no right child, so the walk stops: node 4 is the LAST node of node 1's left subtree in preorder.
Hook the old right subtree underneath: node 4's right becomes node 5, so nothing is lost.
Move the left subtree over to the right: node 1's right becomes node 2.
Clear node 1's left pointer — the flattened list must have no left children.
Advance curr to its (new) right child, node 2. Chain so far: 1 -> 2 -> ...
Loop again with curr = node 2.
Node 2 still has a left child (node 3), so the same surgery repeats one level down.
prev = curr.left = node 3.
Node 3 has no right child, so it is already the rightmost node of node 2's left subtree.
Attach node 2's old right subtree (node 4, which now leads to 5 and 6) under node 3.
Node 2's right becomes node 3.
Node 2's left pointer is cleared.
curr moves to node 3. Chain so far: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6.
Loop again with curr = node 3.
Node 3 has no left child, so there is nothing to splice — we just walk on.
curr moves to node 4.
Node 4 has no left child either.
curr moves to node 5.
Node 5 has no left child (its only child, node 6, is on the right).
curr moves to node 6, the last node of the chain.
Node 6 is a leaf, so no splice is needed.
curr becomes None because node 6 has no right child.
curr is None, so the loop ends. The tree is now the right-skewed chain 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 with every left pointer None.

Floor in BST.desc: floor = -1 is the 'nothing found yet' sentinel; we will overwrite it whenever we meet a value that is <= key.
curr starts at the root, node 8. BST is 8 with left child 4 (children 2 and 6) and right child 12 (children 10 and 14). We want floor(5).
curr is not None, so we can still descend.
Is curr.val (8) == key (5)? No, so no instant answer here.
key (5) < curr.val (8) is True: 8 is too big to be a floor, and so is everything in its right subtree.
Move left to node 4, discarding the root and its whole right subtree in one step.
curr = node 4 is not None, so continue.
Is curr.val (4) equal to the key (5)? No, so we cannot return early.
key (5) < curr.val (4) is False, so we fall into the else branch: 4 is smaller than the key.
4 <= 5, so node 4 is a legitimate candidate: record floor = 4.
Move RIGHT to node 6 to hunt for a value that is still <= 5 but larger than 4.
curr = node 6 is not None, so keep going.
Is curr.val (6) equal to the key (5)? No, so we cannot return early.
key (5) < curr.val (6) is True, so 6 is too big — do NOT touch floor.
Move left from node 6, but node 6 is a leaf, so curr becomes None.
curr is None: we have fallen off the bottom of the tree and the loop ends.
Return floor = 4 — the greatest value in the BST that does not exceed 5.

Ceil in BST.desc: ceil = -1 is the sentinel meaning 'no value >= key found yet'.
curr starts at the root, node 8. BST is 8 with left child 4 (children 2 and 6) and right child 12 (children 10 and 14). We want ceil(5).
curr is not None, so enter the descent loop.
key (5) > curr.val (8) is False, so 8 is >= 5 and therefore a valid candidate.
Record ceil = 8. It may not be the tightest answer, but it is the best one seen so far.
Move LEFT to node 4 to look for a smaller value that is still >= 5.
curr = node 4 is not None, so continue.
Is curr.val (4) equal to the key (5)? No, so we cannot return early.
key (5) > curr.val (4) is True: 4 is too small, so the ceil must live in node 4's right subtree.
Move right to node 6, leaving ceil untouched at 8.
Is curr.val (6) equal to the key (5)? No, so we cannot return early.
key (5) > curr.val (6) is False, so 6 qualifies as a candidate.
Update ceil to 6 — tighter than the previous candidate 8.
Move left from node 6, but it is a leaf, so curr becomes None.
curr is None, so the loop ends after visiting only 3 of the 7 nodes.
Return ceil = 6 — the smallest value in the BST that is at least 5.

Insert Node in BST.desc: root is node 4, not None, so we do not need the 'create a fresh tree' shortcut. BST is 4 with left child 2 (children 1 and 3) and right child 7; we insert val = 5.
curr starts at the root; we keep the root reference untouched so we can return it at the end.
Enter the infinite loop — it only ends via a break, once the new node has been attached.
Is val (5) < curr.val (4)? No, so 5 belongs somewhere in node 4's right subtree.
Take the else branch, which handles 'val is greater than or equal to the current node'.
curr.right is node 7, an existing child, so there is no free slot here yet.
Second iteration of the descent loop with curr = node 7.
Is val (5) < curr.val (7)? Yes, so 5 belongs in node 7's left subtree.
Check curr.left: node 7 has no left child, so the condition is False.
The else branch means we have found the empty slot where the search for 5 would have failed — that is exactly where 5 must live.
Attach the new node: node 7's left child becomes TreeNode(5).
break out of the loop — the insertion is done and the BST property still holds (4 < 5 < 7).
Return the original root, node 4. The tree is now level order [4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 5] and its inorder is the sorted list [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7].

Delete Node in BST.desc: deleteNode(root = node 5, key = 3). BST is 5 with left child 3 (children 2 and 4) and right child 6 (right child 7). root is not None, so we search on.
key (3) < root.val (5) is True, so the node to delete must be in the left subtree.
Recurse: root.left = deleteNode(node 3, 3). Whatever comes back is re-attached as node 5's left child.
Inside deleteNode(node 3, 3): root is not None.
key (3) < root.val (3) is False.
key (3) > root.val (3) is also False — so this IS the node we must delete.
Case check 1: root.left is node 2, so the node is not childless-on-the-left; we cannot simply return the right child.
Case check 2: root.right is node 4, so both children exist — this is the hard, two-children case.
Start hunting for the inorder successor: temp = root.right = node 4.
temp.left is None, so the leftmost node of the right subtree is node 4 itself — the smallest value greater than 3.
Copy the successor value into the current node: this node now holds 4 instead of 3, and the BST order (2 < 4 < 5) still holds.
The value 4 now appears twice, so delete it from the RIGHT subtree: root.right = deleteNode(node 4, 4).
Inside deleteNode(node 4, 4): root is not None.
key (4) < root.val (4) is False, so we do not walk left.
4 > 4 is False, so this is the duplicate successor node we came to remove.
root.left is None here — the easy case at last.
Return root.right, which is also None: node 4 simply disappears.
Back in the node that now holds 4: its right child is set to None, so its only child is node 2 on the left.
Return this repaired subtree (value 4, left child 2) up to the caller.
Back at the top call: node 5's left child is reassigned to the returned subtree rooted at 4.
Return node 5. Inorder is now [2, 4, 5, 6, 7] — the value 3 is gone and the BST property is intact.

Kth Smallest Element in BST.desc: Initialize an empty stack. It will hold ancestors whose left side we are still exploring. Our tree is [3,1,4,null,2] and k=2.
Start the walk at the root: node points to 3.
count = 0 — we have not visited (popped) any value yet.
Outer loop check: the stack is empty but node is 3 (not None), so we enter the loop.
Inner loop check: node 3 exists, so we start sliding left toward the smallest value.
Push 3 onto the stack — we must visit its whole left subtree before visiting 3 itself.
Step left: node = 3.left = 1. Smaller values always live to the left.
Inner check again: node 1 exists, so we keep sliding left.
Push 1 onto the stack, on top of 3.
Step left: node = 1.left = None — node 1 has no left child, we've hit the smallest value's spot.
Inner check: node is None, so the slide-left loop ends. The top of the stack (1) is the smallest unvisited value.
Pop the stack: node = 1. This is the 1st value in ascending order.
count becomes 1 — we have now visited 1 value (the minimum, 1).
Is count (1) equal to k (2)? No — the 1st smallest is not what we want, keep going.
Move into 1's right subtree: node = 1.right = 2. Values there are bigger than 1 but smaller than 3.
Outer loop check: node is 2, so we continue — there is still tree to explore.
Inner check: node 2 exists, so we try to slide left from it.
Push 2 onto the stack, above 3.
Step left: node = 2.left = None — 2 is a leaf, nothing smaller below it.
node is None so the inner loop ends; pop the stack: node = 2, the next value in ascending order.
count becomes 2 — this pop is the 2nd smallest value of the whole tree.
Is count (2) equal to k (2)? YES — the value we just popped is the answer.
Return node.val = 2. Notice we never touched node 4 — early exit saved that work.

Lowest Common Ancestor in BST.desc: Start the descent at the root: node = 6. We are looking for the LCA of p=3 and q=5 in [6,2,8,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5].
Loop check: node 6 exists, so we inspect where p and q lie relative to it.
Are both targets smaller than 6? p=3 < 6 is true AND q=5 < 6 is true — both live in 6's left subtree.
Step left: node = 6.left = 2. The LCA cannot be 6, because 2's subtree already contains both targets.
Loop check: node 2 exists — compare the targets against 2 next.
Are both smaller than 2? p=3 < 2 is false, so this condition fails immediately.
Are both larger than 2? p=3 > 2 is true AND q=5 > 2 is true — both targets sit in 2's right subtree.
Step right: node = 2.right = 4. We keep descending as long as both targets stay on one side.
Loop check: node 4 exists — test the targets against 4.
Both smaller than 4? p=3 < 4 is true but q=5 < 4 is false — they are NOT both on the left.
Both larger than 4? p=3 > 4 is false — they are not both on the right either.
Neither condition held, so we fall into the else branch: 3 and 5 straddle node 4 (3 < 4 < 5) — the paths to p and q split here.
Return node 4. It is the deepest node whose subtree contains both 3 (its left child) and 5 (its right child) — the LCA.

Construct BST from Preorder Traversal.desc: Create the shared cursor idx = [0]. It points at the next unused preorder value (8) and only ever moves forward.
Kick off build(inf): the root of the whole tree has no upper limit on its value.
Guard check: idx=0 is in range and preorder[0]=8 <= inf, so 8 belongs in this (root) subtree.
val = 8 — the first preorder value is always the root of the entire BST.
Consume 8: the cursor advances to idx=1. No other call will ever see 8 again.
Create the node for 8. The tree so far is just this root.
Build 8's LEFT subtree: call build(bound=8) — only values smaller than 8 may live there.
Guard: preorder[1]=5 <= bound 8, so 5 belongs under 8 on the left.
val = 5 — it becomes the root of 8's left subtree.
Consume 5: cursor advances to idx=2.
Create the node for 5 (it will be attached as 8.left when this call returns).
Build 5's LEFT subtree: call build(bound=5) — only values below 5 allowed.
Guard: preorder[2]=1 <= bound 5, so 1 belongs here.
val = 1 — the root of 5's left subtree.
Consume 1: cursor advances to idx=3. Next unused value is 7.
Create the node for 1.
Build 1's LEFT subtree: call build(bound=1) — values below 1 only.
Guard: preorder[3]=7 > bound 1 — 7 is too big to sit anywhere under 1's left side.
Return None WITHOUT consuming 7 — node 1 gets no left child, and 7 stays available for an ancestor.
Build 1's RIGHT subtree: call build(bound=5) — 1's right side inherits ITS caller's bound of 5.
The guard fails again (7 > 5), so return None — node 1 is a leaf. 7 must belong even higher up.
Return node 1 to its caller; back in 5's frame, line 13 completes: 5.left = 1.
Build 5's RIGHT subtree: call build(bound=8) — values between 5 and 8 land here.
Guard: preorder[3]=7 <= bound 8 — 7 finally found the subtree it belongs to.
val = 7 is consumed (idx advances to 4, lines 10-11) and its node is created — it will be 5's right child.
Build 7's LEFT subtree: call build(bound=7). The next value is 10.
10 > 7, so the guard fails: return None — 7 has no left child.
Build 7's RIGHT subtree: call build(bound=8). Still looking at 10.
10 > 8 too — return None. Node 7 is a leaf; 10 doesn't fit anywhere under 8's LEFT side.
Return node 7; back in 5's frame, line 14 completes: 5.right = 7.
Node 5's subtree is finished — return node 5; back in the ROOT frame, line 13 completes: 8.left = 5.
Build 8's RIGHT subtree: call build(bound=inf) — the right side inherits the root's unlimited bound.
Guard: preorder[4]=10 <= inf, so 10 belongs in the root's right subtree.
val = 10 — the root of 8's right subtree.
Consume 10: idx becomes 5 — every preorder value has now been used.
Create the node for 10; it will attach as 8.right.
Both of 10's child calls (build(10), then build(inf)) hit idx == 5 — the list is exhausted, so each returns None instantly: 10 is a leaf.
Return node 10; back in the root frame, line 14 completes: 8.right = 10.
The root frame returns node 8 — the whole tree is assembled: 8 with left 5 (children 1, 7) and right 10.
build(inf) hands back the root 8; bst_from_preorder returns it. Final level order: [8, 5, 10, 1, 7].

Inorder Successor in BST.desc: Initialize successor = None — we have not yet seen any value greater than x=8. Tree: [20,8,22,4,12,null,null,null,null,10,14].
Start the descent at the root: node = 20.
Loop check: node 20 exists, so we compare it against x=8.
Is 20 > 8? Yes — 20 comes after 8 in sorted order, so it is a valid successor candidate.
Record the candidate: successor = 20. It may be too big, but it is the best we have seen.
Step LEFT to find something smaller that is still > 8: node = 20.left = 8.
Loop check: node 8 exists — compare it with x.
Is 8 > 8? No — strict inequality fails, so 8 itself can never be its own successor.
Take the else branch and step RIGHT: node = 8.right = 12. Anything <= 8 (including 8's left subtree) is ruled out.
Loop check: node 12 exists — keep walking.
Is 12 > 8? Yes — 12 is a valid candidate and it is smaller (closer to 8) than our current candidate 20.
Update the candidate: successor = 12, replacing 20. Each update strictly tightens the answer.
Step LEFT again looking for something between 8 and 12: node = 12.left = 10.
Loop check: node 10 exists — one more comparison.
Is 10 > 8? Yes — 10 beats 12 as the closest value above 8 seen so far.
Update: successor = 10. Can anything between 8 and 10 exist below? Only in 10's left subtree.
Step LEFT: node = 10.left = None — 10 has no left child, so nothing between 8 and 10 exists.
Loop check: node is None — the descent has fallen off the tree, so the search is over.
Return successor — the node holding 10, the smallest value strictly greater than 8. Matches the inorder [4,8,10,12,14,20,22].

BST Iterator.desc: BSTIterator is constructed on the tree [7,3,15,null,null,9,20]; __init__ receives the root node 7. Sorted order will be 3, 7, 9, 15, 20.
Create an empty stack. Invariant: the stack always holds exactly the chain of nodes whose values are still owed, top = next smallest.
Call _push_left(7) to stage the path from the root down to the tree's minimum value.
node 7 is not None, so push it: stack=[7]. 7 must wait until its whole left subtree is served.
Step left: node = 7.left = 3, heading toward smaller values.
Push 3 as well: stack=[7, 3]. 3 is now the top — the smallest pending value.
node = 3.left = None, so the while loop ends: the left spine [7, 3] is fully staged and the constructor finishes.
First next(): pop the top -> node 3, the minimum of the whole tree. stack=[7].
Stage 3's successors: _push_left(3.right) is _push_left(None) — 3 has no right child, so nothing is pushed.
Return 3 — the first value of the sorted sequence.
Second next(): pop 7, the next smallest. The stack is briefly empty.
_push_left(7.right = 15) runs: push 15 -> stack=[15].
Step left from 15: node = 15.left = 9 — 9 comes before 15 in sorted order, so it must sit above 15 on the stack.
Push 9 -> stack=[15, 9]; 9.left is None so this spine ends here.
Return 7. Notice the stack again holds exactly the pending left spine [15, 9] — never the whole tree.
hasNext(): the stack holds 2 nodes, so len(self.stack) > 0 is True — more values remain.
Third next(): pop 9 off the top. stack=[15].
9 has no right child, so _push_left(None) stages nothing new.
Return 9 — sorted order emitted so far: 3, 7, 9.
Fourth next(): pop 15. stack=[] for a moment.
_push_left(15.right = 20): push 20 -> stack=[20]; 20 has no left child so the dive stops immediately.
Return 15. Only the value 20 is still owed to the caller.
Fifth next(): pop 20, the maximum. stack=[].
Return 20 — the full sorted sequence 3, 7, 9, 15, 20 has now been emitted.
hasNext(): the stack is empty -> False. Every node was pushed once and popped once — that is the amortized O(1) argument made visible.

Two Sum in BST.desc: findTarget starts with k=12 on the BST [5,3,6,2,4,null,7]. Create arr=[], soon to hold the inorder (sorted) values.
Kick off the recursive inorder walk from the root node 5.
inorder(5) first recurses left into 3, which recurses left into 2, which calls inorder on 2's empty left child.
That call sees node=None and returns immediately — time to visit 2 itself.
Append 2, the smallest value in the tree: arr=[2].
2 has no right child, so recursion unwinds to 3 and appends it: arr=[2, 3].
inorder(3) now descends into its right child 4 (values just above 3 live there).
4 is appended: arr=[2, 3, 4]. The root's whole left subtree is finished.
Back at the root: append 5 -> arr=[2, 3, 4, 5].
The right subtree visits 6 (no left child) and then its right child 7: arr=[2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] — sorted, exactly as the BST promised.
Set two pointers on the sorted array: lo=0 (value 2) and hi=5 (value 7).
lo=0 < hi=5, so the pair-search loop runs — at least two distinct nodes remain in range.
9 is not 12, and 9 < 12: the sum is too small. hi already sits on the LARGEST value, so only a bigger left value can help.
Advance lo to 1 (value 3); the pair (2, anything) is permanently ruled out for reaching 12.
s = arr[1] + arr[5] = 3 + 7 = 10, still below 12.
Too small again -> lo=2 (value 4).
s = arr[2] + arr[5] = 4 + 7 = 11. One short of the target.
Still too small -> lo=3 (value 5).
s = arr[3] + arr[5] = 5 + 7 = 12 — exactly k!
The check s == k is finally true: 5 and 7 come from two different nodes of the tree.
Return True: the BST contains two distinct nodes (5 and 7) whose values sum to 12.

Recover BST.desc: recoverTree starts on [3,1,4,null,null,2]. A correct BST on these values would read 1,2,3,4 in inorder — we will watch for a drop. Create the empty stack.
The walker node starts at the root (value 3); it will dive down left spines.
prev = None: no node has been visited in inorder yet, so there is nothing to compare against.
first and second start as None — they will capture the two offending nodes when a drop appears.
Outer loop runs (node=3 is not None). The inner dive pushes 3: stack=[3].
Step left: node = 3.left = 1.
Push 1 as well: stack=[3, 1]; then node = 1.left = None will end the dive.
Pop the top: node=1 is the FIRST value in inorder order. stack=[3].
prev is None — 1 has no predecessor to compare with, so no drop check happens on the first visit.
prev now points at node 1: the baseline for the next comparison.
node = 1.right = None: 1 has no right subtree, so we will return to the stack.
The stack still holds [3]: pop it. Inorder so far: 1, 3.
prev.val=1 < node.val=3: the sequence rises, exactly what a healthy BST does. No offender yet.
prev moves forward to node 3.
node = 3.right = 4: inorder continues into the right subtree.
Push 4 (stack=[4]), step to 4.left = 2 and push it too: stack=[4, 2].
Pop node=2. Inorder so far: 1, 3, 2 — the sequence just went DOWN!
Drop detected: prev.val=3 > node.val=2. These two nodes are the corrupted pair (or its endpoints).
first was None, so first = prev — the node holding 3, a large value that appeared too early.
second = node — the node holding 2. If a later drop appeared, second would be overwritten there; with an adjacent swap it will not.
prev moves on to node 2 and the traversal continues normally.
node = 2.right = None; back to the stack, which still holds [4].
Pop node=4. Inorder so far: 1, 3, 2, 4.
prev.val=2 < 4: no second drop. The swapped values were inorder NEIGHBOURS — first=node(3), second=node(2) is exactly right.
node = 4.right = None and the stack is empty — the outer loop is about to end.
Swap the two VALUES: the node that held 3 now holds 2 and vice versa. The tree becomes [2,1,4,null,null,3] with inorder 1,2,3,4 — a valid BST, shape untouched.

Largest BST in Binary Tree.desc: largestBst runs on [5,2,4,1,3]. Define sentinels NEG=-inf and POS=+inf, used by empty-subtree reports and poisoned ranges.
Call solve(5) on the root. Whatever report it produces, its size slot [0] will be the final answer.
solve(5) needs its left report first, so it recurses into node 2 — post-order means children always report before parents.
solve(2) likewise recurses into ITS left child, node 1.
solve(1) calls solve(None) for 1's left child: the base case returns (0, inf, -inf) — a size-0 report whose range can never block a parent.
Back in solve(1): the left report unpacks to l_size=0, l_min=inf, l_max=-inf.
1's right child is also None -> right report (0, inf, -inf): r_size=0, r_min=inf, r_max=-inf.
BST test at 1: l_max=-inf < 1 < r_min=inf — trivially true for a leaf; the sentinels do their job.
Leaf 1 reports (0+0+1, min(inf,1), max(-inf,1)) = (1, 1, 1): a BST of size 1 spanning values [1, 1].
solve(2) receives its left report: l_size=1, l_min=1, l_max=1.
solve(2) recurses right into leaf 3, which reports (1, 3, 3) by the same leaf pattern: r_size=1, r_min=3, r_max=3.
BST test at 2: l_max=1 < 2 < r_min=3 — true. Everything left of 2 tops out at 1, everything right starts at 3.
Merge at 2: size=1+1+1=3, mn=min(1,2)=1, mx=max(3,2)=3. solve(2) reports (3, 1, 3) — the subtree {1,2,3} is one valid BST.
solve(5) receives its left report: l_size=3, l_min=1, l_max=3 — a 3-node BST lives on its left.
solve(5) recurses right into leaf 4 -> right report (1, 4, 4): r_size=1, r_min=4, r_max=4.
BST test at 5: l_max=3 < 5 holds, BUT 5 < r_min=4 FAILS — the right subtree contains 4, smaller than the root. The whole tree is not a BST.
Broken at the root: report (max(3, 1), -inf, inf) = (3, -inf, inf). The poisoned range would make any ancestor's test fail — here there is none.
solve(root) returned (3, -inf, inf); its [0] slot is 3. The largest BST subtree is {1, 2, 3} rooted at node 2 — answer 3.

DFS Traversal.desc: We run dfsOfGraph(V=5, adj=[[1,2],[0,3],[0,4],[1],[2]]) — the same graph as BFS (edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-4) but now we go as DEEP as possible before backtracking.
dfs = [] will collect vertices in the order we first touch them.
visited = [False]*5 — one flag per vertex, shared by every recursive call because it is captured by the inner function.
The nested function traverse(node) is defined here; nothing runs yet. Defining it inside dfsOfGraph lets it read 'visited', 'dfs' and 'adj' without passing them around.
traverse(0) is the actual kick-off: we start the depth-first walk at vertex 0.
Inside traverse(0): visited[0] = True. Marking on ENTRY is what guarantees we never re-enter vertex 0.
dfs.append(0) -> dfs = [0].
for neighbor in adj[0]: adj[0] = [1, 2]; the first neighbour is 1.
visited[1] is False, so the condition holds and we dive into 1 right now — we do NOT look at neighbour 2 yet. That postponement is the essence of DFS.
traverse(1) is called. Frame for vertex 0 is paused mid-loop, remembering that neighbour 2 is still pending.
Inside traverse(1): visited[1] = True.
dfs.append(1) -> dfs = [0, 1].
adj[1] = [0, 3]; first neighbour is 0.
visited[0] is True, so 'not visited[0]' is False — we skip 0 and avoid infinite recursion back into our own parent.
Next neighbour of 1: neighbor = 3.
visited[3] is False, so traverse(3) is called — the stack is now 0 -> 1 -> 3, three frames deep.
Inside traverse(3): line 6 sets visited[3] = True, then dfs.append(3) -> dfs = [0, 1, 3]. Note 3 is recorded BEFORE 2, unlike BFS.
adj[3] = [1] only, and visited[1] is True, so the for-loop finds nothing new.
traverse(3) falls off the end and returns. We BACKTRACK into the paused frame of vertex 1, right after its traverse(3) call.
Back in traverse(1), the for-loop over adj[1] = [0, 3] has no items left, so this frame also finishes.
traverse(1) returns. We backtrack into vertex 0's frame, which still had neighbour 2 waiting.
The for-loop in traverse(0) resumes and hands us the second neighbour: neighbor = 2.
visited[2] is still False, so traverse(2) is called. Stack is 0 -> 2.
Inside traverse(2): visited[2] = True on line 6, then dfs.append(2) -> dfs = [0, 1, 3, 2].
adj[2] = [0, 4]. Neighbour 0 is already visited, so it is skipped.
Neighbour 4 is unvisited, so traverse(4) is called. Stack is 0 -> 2 -> 4.
Inside traverse(4): visited[4] = True, then dfs.append(4) -> dfs = [0, 1, 3, 2, 4]. All 5 vertices are now visited.
adj[4] = [2] and visited[2] is True, so nothing new. traverse(4) returns, then traverse(2) returns, then traverse(0) returns — the stack unwinds to empty.
return dfs gives [0, 1, 3, 2, 4]: we went deep 0 -> 1 -> 3, backtracked, then went deep 0 -> 2 -> 4.

Number of Provinces.desc: We call findCircleNum on a 4x4 matrix. Cities 0-1 share a road and cities 2-3 share a road; there is no road between the two pairs, so the answer should be 2.
n = 4: the matrix has 4 rows, so there are 4 cities numbered 0, 1, 2 and 3.
parent = [0, 1, 2, 3]. Before reading a single road, every city is the leader of a province containing only itself.
size = [1, 1, 1, 1]: each of the four provinces currently holds exactly one city. We only trust size[i] when i is a leader.
components = 4. This counter is the answer-in-progress: it starts at n and drops by one every time two provinces merge.
Outer loop starts with i = 0. We will pair city 0 with every city that comes after it.
Inner loop starts at j = i + 1 = 1. We deliberately skip j <= i because the matrix is symmetric: cell (1,0) repeats what cell (0,1) already told us.
isConnected[0][1] = 1, so there is a direct road between city 0 and city 1. We must union them.
To merge, we first need the LEADER of each city, not the city itself. We call find(0) and then find(1).
Inside find(0): parent[0] is 0, which equals x, so the while condition is False and we never enter the loop. City 0 is already a leader.
find(0) returns 0 - the leader of city 0 is city 0 itself.
Now find(1): parent[1] is 1, again its own parent, so the loop body is skipped and find(1) will return 1. Back in the caller we get a = 0 and b = 1.
a = 0 and b = 1 are different leaders, so cities 0 and 1 really do live in separate provinces right now. Time to merge.
Union by size: size[0] = 1 is NOT less than size[1] = 1, so the condition is False and we skip the swap. Root a = 0 stays the bigger (here: tied) tree.
parent[1] = 0. City 1 now points at city 0, so parent becomes [0, 0, 2, 3] and both cities answer 'my leader is 0'.
size[0] += size[1] gives size[0] = 2: province 0 now holds two cities. size[1] is stale but harmless because 1 is no longer a leader.
components drops from 4 to 3. Provinces are now {0,1}, {2}, {3}.
Inner loop advances to j = 2 with i still 0.
isConnected[0][2] = 0 - no road from city 0 to city 2 - so the whole union block is skipped.
j = 3 next: isConnected[0][3] = 0 as well, so nothing happens and the inner loop for i = 0 is finished.
Outer loop moves to i = 1. Note we only look at columns 2 and 3 for this row - column 0 and 1 are behind the diagonal.
j = 2: isConnected[1][2] = 0, no road, skip.
j = 3: isConnected[1][3] = 0 too, so row 1 adds no new information. components is still 3.
Outer loop moves to i = 2.
Inner loop starts at j = 3, the only column to the right of the diagonal in row 2.
isConnected[2][3] = 1: cities 2 and 3 are directly connected, so we union them.
find(2) walks nowhere because parent[2] = 2, and find(3) likewise returns 3. So a = 2 and b = 3.
a = 2 differs from b = 3, so these are two distinct provinces and the merge proceeds.
size[2] = 1 is not less than size[3] = 1, so once again no swap is needed.
parent[3] = 2, so parent becomes [0, 0, 2, 2]: city 3 now hangs under leader 2.
size[2] becomes 2 - the province led by city 2 holds cities 2 and 3.
components drops from 3 to 2. The provinces are now {0,1} and {2,3}.
Outer loop reaches its last value, i = 3.
range(4, 4) is empty, so the inner loop body never runs for i = 3 and both loops finish.
We return components = 2. Two roots survive in parent = [0, 0, 2, 2] - cities 0 and 2 - which is exactly the number of provinces.

Number of Islands.desc: Guard check: grid = [["1","1","0"],["0","1","0"],["0","0","1"]] is non-empty and its first row is non-empty, so we do NOT return 0 early. Note the cells are the STRINGS "1" and "0", not the numbers 1 and 0, because that is what the problem hands us - and in Python 1 == "1" is False, so if you retype this grid with bare numbers the code returns 0 islands and never tells you why.
Cache the dimensions: rows = 3 and cols = 3. These bound every neighbour check later.
Initialise count = 0 — no islands discovered yet; the scan is about to begin.
Outer scan starts with row r = 0; the inner loop will walk columns 0, 1, 2 of this row.
Cell (0,0) holds "1" — land that no BFS has sunk yet. We just discovered a brand-new island!
Count the new island: count goes from 0 to 1. Now we must sink ALL of it so it is never re-counted.
Sink the starting cell: grid[0][0] becomes "0". The grid itself is our visited marker — no extra set needed.
Seed the BFS queue with the island's first cell: queue = [(0,0)].
Pop the oldest cell: (row, col) = (0, 0). The queue is empty for now; we spread from here.
Check (0,0)'s neighbours: down (1,0) is "0" — fail; up (-1,0) is out of bounds — fail; right (0,1) is "1" — PASS!
Sink neighbour (0,1) immediately — sinking on arrival guarantees no cell ever enters the queue twice.
Append (0,1) to the queue so we can later spread from it. Left neighbour (0,-1) is out of bounds, so (0,0) is done.
Pop (0,1) — the BFS frontier advances one ring outward from the island's first cell.
Neighbours of (0,1): down (1,1) is "1" — PASS! (up is out of bounds; right (0,2) and left (0,0) are "0").
Sink (1,1): the third and last cell of this island turns to water on arrival.
Append (1,1); queue = [(1, 1)]. Every discovered land cell is queued exactly once.
Pop (1,1) and try to spread. Note the "1" at (2,2) touches (1,1) only DIAGONALLY — it is not a neighbour.
All four checks fail: down (2,1)="0", up (0,1) sunk, right (1,2)="0", left (1,0)="0". Nothing new to enqueue.
The queue is empty — BFS for island #1 is complete and all 3 of its cells are sunk. Back to the outer scan.
Second island discovered: count goes from 1 to 2.
Sink (2,2). The grid is now entirely water — nothing left for the scan to find.
Seed the new BFS: queue = [(2,2)] for island #2.
Pop (2,2): down and right are out of bounds, up (1,2) and left (2,1) are "0" — this island was a single cell.
Scan finished (r=2, c=2 was the last cell). Return count = 2 — the grid contained exactly two islands.

Flood Fill Algorithm.desc: Read the clicked pixel (sr,sc) = (1,1): old = 1. Only pixels wearing colour 1 will be repainted.
Guard: old (1) != color (2), so there IS work to do — we do not return early.
Cache dimensions: rows = 3, cols = 3. Every neighbour probe will be bounds-checked against these.
Seed the BFS queue with the start pixel: queue = [(1, 1)].
Paint the start pixel NOW: image[1][1] = 2. Painting before the loop means (1,1) can never re-enter the queue.
Pop the oldest pixel: (r, c) = (1, 1). We now try to spread paint to its four neighbours.
Neighbour down (2,1): it holds 0, not old (1) — this pixel is a wall, the paint stops here.
Neighbour up (0,1): in bounds and holds 1 == old — the paint can spread there!
Paint (0,1) on arrival: it becomes 2 the moment it is discovered, so it can never be enqueued twice.
Append (0,1) to the queue. Next neighbour right (1,2) holds 0 — wall; left (1,0) holds 1 — spreads!
Paint left neighbour (1,0) to 2 and it joins the frontier.
Append (1,0). Queue is now [(0, 1), (1, 0)] — the first BFS ring around the click is complete.
Pop (0,1). Its down neighbour (1,1) is already 2 (fails == old), and up (-1,1) is out of bounds.
Right neighbour (0,2) holds 1 == old — paint spreads to the top-right corner.
Paint (0,2) to 2 immediately upon discovery.
Left neighbour (0,0) also holds 1 — the last unpainted pixel of the top row is reachable.
Paint (0,0) to 2 and enqueue it. Queue: [(1, 0), (0, 2), (0, 0)].
Pop (1,0). Down neighbour (2,0) holds 1 == old — one more pixel to claim below.
Paint (2,0) to 2 and enqueue it. Up (0,0) and right (1,1) are already 2; left (1,-1) is out of bounds.
Pop (0,2): down (1,2) is 0 — wall; left (0,1) is already 2; other neighbours out of bounds. Nothing spreads.
Pop (0,0): both in-bounds neighbours (0,1) and (1,0) are already painted 2 — no new work.
Pop (2,0): up (1,0) is 2, right (2,1) is 0 — wall. Note (2,2) still holds 1: it only touches the region diagonally!
The queue is empty — every pixel connected to the click through colour-1 paths has been repainted.
Return the image: [[2,2,2],[2,2,0],[2,0,1]]. The 0-walls and the diagonal 1 at (2,2) survived untouched.

Detect Cycle in Undirected Graph (BFS).desc: Input: V=4, edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 2-3 (a triangle plus a tail). Initialise visited = [F, F, F, F].
Outer loop tries start = 0 first — if the graph were disconnected, later starts would cover other components.
visited[0] is False, so vertex 0 belongs to an unexplored component — we do NOT skip it.
Seed the BFS queue with (0, -1): vertex 0 with sentinel parent -1, because a root has no parent.
Mark visited[0] = True at enqueue time — marking on pop would let 0 be enqueued again via its neighbours.
Pop the oldest entry: node = 0, parent = -1. We now scan 0's neighbour list [1, 2].
First neighbour of 0: nei = 1. Which of the three cases applies — unvisited, parent, or visited non-parent?
visited[1] is False — case 1: a normal first discovery of vertex 1 through the edge 0-1.
Mark visited[1] = True immediately, so no other branch can discover vertex 1 'for the first time' again.
Enqueue (1, 0): when vertex 1 is popped later it will remember it was reached FROM vertex 0.
Second neighbour of 0: nei = 2, also unvisited — another normal discovery via edge 0-2.
Mark visited[2] = True. Vertices 1 and 2 are now BOTH claimed as children of 0 — same BFS level.
Enqueue (2, 0). Queue is now [(1, 0), (2, 0)] and vertex 0's neighbour scan is finished.
Pop the next entry: node = 1, parent = 0. Scan 1's neighbour list [0, 2].
nei = 0 is visited, so check the elif: is 0 != parent? No — 0 IS the parent, this is just edge 0-1 seen backwards. Ignore it.
Next neighbour of 1: nei = 2 — the third side of the triangle, the edge 1-2.
visited[2] is True AND 2 != parent (0): vertex 2 was already reached via 0-2, and now again via 1-2 — two distinct paths!
Return True: the two meeting paths 0->2 and 0->1->2 close the triangle 0-1-2. The tail vertex 3 never needed visiting.
